name: SHapley Additive exPlanations
description: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) explains one prediction by sharing out the gap between that prediction and a baseline, usually the model's average output over a background dataset, among the input features. Each feature receives a signed score, where positive means it pushed the prediction above the baseline and negative means it pushed it below. The scores are Shapley values from game theory, meaning each is the feature's average effect over every order in which the features could be added, and together they add up exactly to the gap. Exact calculation is costly, so tools usually estimate the scores by sampling or use shortcuts for particular model types, such as a fast exact method for tree ensembles, and averaging the absolute scores over many predictions gives a global ranking of features. In a fairness use, the difference in average output between two groups is shared out feature by feature in the same way, showing which inputs account for the gap.

example_use_cases.description: Analysing a customer churn prediction model to understand why a specific high-value customer was flagged as likely to leave, revealing that recent support ticket interactions and declining purchase frequency were the main drivers.

A lender's model validation team investigates why a loan approval model approves one applicant group less often than another. They compute SHAP values for every applicant, compare the group averages feature by feature, and see which inputs, such as postcode or credit history length, account for most of the gap, so they know what to scrutinise first.

limitations.description: Common estimators fill in a 'missing' feature by sampling its value independently of the others. With correlated features, such as income and postcode, the model is then evaluated on unrealistic combinations and credit can be split between correlated features in ways that mislead. Check feature correlations before reading individual scores.

Exact values need the model evaluated on every subset of features, which grows exponentially with the number of features. Sampling estimators trade accuracy for speed, and explaining many predictions from a slow model, or a model with hundreds of features, can take hours. Tree ensembles have a much faster exact algorithm.

Scores are relative to a baseline set by the background dataset, and a different background gives different scores. Explaining an applicant against all customers says something different from explaining them against previously approved customers, so the choice must be made on purpose and reported.

SHAP describes what the model has learned, not how the world works. A large contribution does not show that changing that feature would change the real outcome, so the scores should not be used to advise people on what to change.

Averaging absolute scores into a global ranking can hide features that matter a great deal for a small subgroup, or that push in opposite directions for different people. Inspect the spread of per-prediction scores, not only the mean.

sample_claims.text: For each declined application, the features with the largest SHAP contributions to the refusal match the lender's documented underwriting criteria.
Across the validation set, administrative fields such as ward code and admission day contribute negligibly to the readmission model's predictions compared with clinical measurements.

The difference in approval rates between applicant groups on the benefits eligibility model is accounted for mainly by the documented eligibility criteria, and the share of the gap attributed to postcode and other proxy inputs is reported.
The explanation shown to each fraud analyst accounts for the whole gap between the transaction's risk score and the average score.

name: Permutation Importance
description: Permutation Importance measures how much a trained model relies on each input feature. For each feature, the values in a dataset are shuffled at random, which breaks the link between that feature and the outcome, and the model is scored again. The fall in score, for example in accuracy, is the feature's importance: a large fall means the model depends on the feature, and little or no fall means it does not. Repeating the shuffle several times shows how much the result varies. The method works with any model, but it shows what the model uses, not what causes the outcome in the world.

example_use_cases.description: Assessing which patient characteristics (e.g., age, blood pressure, cholesterol) matter most to a medical diagnosis model by shuffling each one in turn on held-out patients and recording the drop in performance, so a clinician can judge whether the model relies on clinically relevant factors.

A bank's model-risk team shuffles each input to a card-fraud model in turn on held-out transactions, to check the model leans on transaction behaviour and not on a field that leaks the answer, such as a case-handling code recorded after fraud was confirmed.

A flood-forecasting team shuffles each rainfall, river-level and soil-moisture input of a model trained on historic data, to check that forecasts depend on the physical drivers hydrologists expect and not on a calendar variable.

limitations.description: When features are strongly correlated, shuffling one leaves the model able to rely on its correlated partner, so both can show low importance even though the model uses them. Shuffling also creates feature combinations that do not occur in real data, which can distort the scores.

Computationally expensive for large datasets or complex models. The model is scored once per feature per shuffle, so cost grows with the number of features, the number of repeats and the size of the evaluation data. No retraining is needed.

The score for a feature includes the effect of its interactions with other features and cannot separate them from its own effect. If two features interact, shuffling either one lowers the score, so importances need not add up to the model's total performance.
The ranking can change with the scoring metric, particularly for imbalanced classification, where accuracy and F1-score can give different pictures of which features matter.

Scores computed on training data can reflect overfitting: a feature the model has memorised can look important even though it does not help on new data. Use held-out data, and repeat the shuffle to see how much the scores vary.

sample_claims.text: The fraud model's accuracy on held-out data falls sharply when transaction amount or merchant category is shuffled and barely changes when customer postcode is shuffled.
The diagnostic model's accuracy on held-out patients depends on established clinical risk factors and not on administrative fields such as hospital identifier.
The environmental monitoring model's forecasts are most sensitive to atmospheric variables that domain experts consider physically relevant
The recommendation-model audit reports performance changes from shuffling behavioural and demographic inputs under a stated metric, without treating small drops as proof of feature independence.

name: Mean Decrease Impurity
description: Mean Decrease Impurity (MDI) scores how much each feature contributes to a tree-based model, such as a random forest, by looking at how the model's decision trees split the training data. Each split sends cases into two groups, and a good split makes each group more uniform in its outcome, which is a drop in impurity, measured with a score such as Gini impurity. For each feature, MDI adds up the drops from every split that uses it, weights each by the share of training cases reaching that split, and averages over all trees. The scores are usually scaled to sum to one, so they show relative importance. Because they come from the training data, they describe how the model was built, not how well each feature predicts on new data.

example_use_cases.description: Determining the most influential genetic markers in a decision tree model predicting disease susceptibility, by identifying which markers consistently lead to the purest splits between healthy and diseased patient groups.

A model-validation team reviews a gradient-boosted loan-default model and ranks its inputs by MDI before sign-off. They investigate any identifier-like or many-valued field, such as customer ID or postcode, that ranks near the top, because MDI favours such fields and they may reflect overfitting rather than real predictive signal.

An environmental analytics team fits a random forest to forecast air quality and uses MDI to choose which weather stations' readings to drop from a simpler model. They then confirm on held-out data that accuracy holds, because MDI alone reflects the training data.

limitations.description: MDI favours features with many distinct values, because more possible split points give more chances of a good split by chance. Strobl and colleagues found that uninformative continuous or many-category variables were preferred over informative ones when predictors differed in type or number of categories.

Scores are calculated from the training data, so a feature can rank high because the model fitted noise in it. A high score does not show that the feature helps predictions on unseen data, and scikit-learn recommends permutation importance on held-out data as the alternative.

MDI gives only a non-negative score for each feature. It does not show whether higher values of a feature raise or lower the prediction, so it cannot support a claim about the direction of a feature's effect.

Scores vary from tree to tree, and the scikit-learn example plots this spread as error bars. A forest with few trees, or a small training set, can therefore give a ranking that shifts when the model is refitted.
Correlated predictors compete for splits. One can mask another's importance, and changing the fitted ensemble or candidate-feature settings can change their relative ranks.

sample_claims.text: The five features with the highest mean decrease in impurity in the readmission-risk forest are the clinical risk factors that the clinical team documented as expected drivers.
No identifier-like or many-valued field, such as customer ID or postcode, ranks in the top ten by mean decrease in impurity in the loan-default model.
The mean-decrease-impurity ranking of the delivery-time forest is stable across 20 refits on bootstrap samples of the training data, with the same top five features each time.
Three meteorological variables account for over half of the total importance in the air-quality forecasting forest, and the model documentation names them.

name: Coefficient Magnitudes (in Linear Models)
description: Coefficient Magnitudes explains a linear model by reading its fitted coefficients. Each coefficient shows how much the prediction changes when its feature rises by one unit while every other feature stays fixed, and its sign gives the direction. Because a coefficient's size depends on the units of its feature, the features are first put on a common scale, for example by standardising them or by multiplying each coefficient by its feature's standard deviation. The features with the largest scaled coefficients are then read as having the strongest influence on the model's predictions. This gives a global view of the model without needing a separate explanation method.

example_use_cases.description: An estate agency's data team standardises the inputs of a linear house-price model, then ranks the absolute coefficients to show valuers which property attributes move the estimate most. Valuers check that the signs match their experience, for example that more floor area raises the price, before the model guides asking prices.

A lender's model-risk team documents a linear credit-scoring model for its regulator by publishing the standardised coefficient of every input. The reviewer can read off the direction and relative weight of each input without a separate explanation tool, and can query any input that carries more weight than policy allows.

A public health analyst fits a logistic regression to predict emergency readmission and reports standardised coefficients to clinicians, who see which patient characteristics push the predicted risk up or down. The analyst refits on resamples first, to check that the large coefficients keep their sign.

limitations.description: Raw magnitudes have output-per-input units and cannot be ranked across differently scaled variables. Express comparable input changes explicitly; changing metres to centimetres makes the corresponding coefficient smaller for the same predictions.

Coefficients concern the encoded model inputs while other inputs are held fixed. If the model includes transformed variables or interactions, inspecting one coefficient does not give the whole effect of changing an original variable.

Correlated predictors can have unstable or shared coefficients even when predictions change little. Scaling does not remove this problem, and regularisation can change which correlated feature receives a large weight.

Each coefficient is conditional on the other features in the model. A feature can have a negative coefficient while rising with the outcome on its own, so a coefficient read in isolation can mislead about the feature's plain relationship to the outcome.

A coefficient is a conditional association in the fitted model, not a causal effect. Its magnitude alone also does not give a particular applicant's contribution, which depends on that applicant's feature values.

sample_claims.text: Before coefficient sizes were used to rank influence in the valuation model, inputs were put on a common scale and strongly correlated input pairs were merged or reduced to one, so the ranking is not a product of units or collinearity.
The credit-scoring model is a linear model whose standardised coefficients are published in its documentation, so a reviewer can trace each score to its inputs without a separate explanation method.

The direction of every input's coefficient in the readmission-risk model agrees with clinical expectation, and none of the five largest standardised coefficients changes sign across 100 bootstrap refits.
Rainfall and soil nitrogen have the largest standardised coefficients in the crop-yield model, and their confidence intervals exclude zero.

name: Integrated Gradients
description: Integrated Gradients assigns input features scores for a prediction relative to a chosen reference input, called the baseline. It evaluates gradients, rates of output change, at points along a straight path from that reference to the actual input. Each feature's average gradient is multiplied by its change from the reference, and the resulting scores sum approximately to the output difference when enough numerical steps are used. For text, the path runs through continuous token representations rather than discrete word identifiers, and scores can be combined into highlighted words. In a protected-term variant, the reviewer fixes before the run a list of words or columns that name or record a protected characteristic, and reads the scores those inputs receive: a large score shows that the output rests partly on the characteristic, but a small score does not show that the model ignores it.

example_use_cases.description: An eye-screening programme evaluating a diabetic retinopathy grading model shows graders an Integrated Gradients heatmap beside each prediction, so they can see whether the regions driving a referral are lesions such as haemorrhages rather than camera artefacts, and uses the review to decide whether the model may assist grading.

A team building a question-answering assistant over an organisation's policy documents attributes each answer to the question's tokens and flags questions where the content words receive almost no attribution; those questions become test cases in which the content words are changed, to show whether the assistant actually reads the question.

A trust-and-safety team reviewing the posts its toxic-content classifier wrongly flagged fixes, before the run, a list of identity terms (names of religions, ethnicities and sexual orientations, chosen because the policy forbids penalising them) and computes Integrated Gradients against an all-padding baseline. Where a listed term ranks among the five most attributed tokens of a wrongly flagged post, the team adds counter-examples to the training data; a low score is not taken as clearance.

A lender's model-risk team audits a classifier that reads the free-text statements in loan applications. Before the run it lists the words that state a protected characteristic, such as a religion, a pregnancy or a disability, and computes Integrated Gradients against a documented reference statement for a sample of declined applications. Any listed word among the ten most attributed is reported for a swap test; the absence of such words does not show the model ignores them.

limitations.description: Attributions are measured against the baseline and no choice is neutral. Features that match the baseline score near zero even when the model relies on them: with a black-image baseline, dark pixels on the object get little credit. A comparison of blurred, noise and training-data baselines found none best, so the baseline is an assumption to state and to vary before drawing conclusions.

Requires gradient access to a differentiable model, so it cannot explain tree ensembles, rule-based components or a model reached only through an API. For text, the path runs through token embeddings whose intermediate points are not real words, and subword tokenisation splits a word across several scores that must be recombined before a reviewer can read them.

Each explanation needs one gradient computation per step along the path; the original authors found 20 to 300 steps were usually enough for the scores to sum to within 5% of the output difference. Explaining long documents, high-resolution images or a large audit sample therefore costs tens to hundreds of forward and backward passes per prediction.

A score shows how sensitive the output was to a feature along one straight path, not that the feature causes the outcome in the world or that removing it would change the decision. Maps over neighbouring pixels or tokens are often noisy, and a plausible-looking heatmap does not show that the model's reasoning is sound.

sample_claims.text: The retinopathy grading model's referral predictions are attributable to lesion regions in the retinal image rather than to imaging artefacts, as shown by Integrated Gradients review of a stratified sample of graded cases

The attribution scores given to credit analysts for each decision sum, within a stated tolerance, to the difference between the model's score for the applicant and its score for the documented reference applicant
The question-answering audit records token attributions for the documented reference and uses low content-word scores to select questions for separate perturbation tests.

None of the identity terms on the fixed list ranks among the five most attributed tokens, against the all-padding baseline, for the moderation classifier's decisions on the non-abusive posts in the audit set
The loan-screening bias review records the attribution ranks of specified protected-characteristic words in the reviewed statements, relative to documented reference inputs.

name: DeepLIFT
description: DeepLIFT (Deep Learning Important FeaTures) explains a single prediction of a neural network by dividing the difference between the model's output and its output on a reference input among the input features. The reference is a neutral input chosen for the problem, such as an all-zero image or a blurred copy of the input. The method measures how far each neuron's activation is from its value on the reference, then passes those differences backwards through the layers in one pass, applying a rule for each layer type. A plain gradient (the rate of change of the output with respect to an input) is zero where the output has levelled off, but DeepLIFT can still assign credit there. The scores add up to the output difference and mean something only relative to the reference chosen.

example_use_cases.description: A genomics group training a neural network to predict where a regulatory protein binds DNA computes DeepLIFT scores for each predicted binding region against a reference sequence with background base frequencies. They read off which short stretches of bases carry the score, compare them with known binding motifs, and decide whether the model has learned real regulatory sequence before using it to prioritise experiments.

A hospital imaging team is investigating a chest X-ray classifier that flags healthy patients as abnormal. For the false positives it computes DeepLIFT scores against a blurred copy of each image and checks whether the weight sits on the image border, where scanner labels are printed, rather than on lung tissue. It then decides whether to mask the labels and retrain.

A regional geohazard agency uses a neural network to rate landslide susceptibility from terrain, rainfall and land-cover layers. For a slope the model rates as high risk, DeepLIFT scores show which input layers drove the rating, and the agency compares them with the field investigation report before using the map for planning.

A lender's credit team sends each declined applicant a short statement of the factors that most lowered their score. For its neural network scorer it computes DeepLIFT scores against a documented reference applicant, the median approved applicant, and the statement lists the factors with the largest negative scores, which are the ones that pulled this score below the reference.

limitations.description: Every score is relative to a reference input, and the choice changes the picture. In the original paper an all-zero reference on CIFAR-10 images highlighted hard-to-interpret background pixels, while a blurred copy of the image highlighted object outlines. State the reference used and repeat the analysis with at least one alternative before drawing conclusions.

The Captum implementation supports only the Rescale rule, which can give all the credit to one of two inputs that jointly drive the output. In the paper's min(i1, i2) example Rescale scores only the smaller input, while the RevealCancel rule shares the credit. Where inputs interact, the scores can hide a dependency that a more complete rule would show.

Propagation rules must support the network operations. Captum implements the Rescale rule and a limited set of nonlinearities; inaccessible operations in built-in recurrent modules can prevent attribution unless a supported implementation is used.

Two networks that compute exactly the same function can receive different DeepLIFT scores, because differences between a neuron and its reference do not obey the chain rule that gradients obey (Sundararajan et al., 2017, App. B). The scores therefore describe how the model is built as well as what it computes, which matters when comparing a model with a re-implemented or compressed version of it.

Feature contributions account for a particular output difference, not a causal effect in the world or a guaranteed change after deleting that feature. Correlated genomic bases or financial variables make that distinction important.

sample_claims.text: The binding-site model's highest-scoring regions in the validation sequences coincide with known binding motifs, as shown by DeepLIFT scores against a reference sequence with background base frequencies
The chest X-ray classifier's DeepLIFT scores on its false-positive cases fall on lung tissue and not on image borders or printed labels, using a blurred copy of each image as the reference
For the audited landslide cases, the input layers with the largest DeepLIFT scores match the causes named in the field investigation reports

Each declined credit application is accompanied by its largest DeepLIFT scores against the documented reference applicant, and the reported approximation error of those scores is below a stated tolerance

name: Layer-wise Relevance Propagation
description: Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) explains a neural network's prediction by working backwards from the output to the inputs. It treats the prediction score as a quantity called relevance, then passes that relevance back through each layer in proportion to how much each neuron contributed in the forward pass. The rules for this redistribution are chosen to keep the total relevance roughly constant from layer to layer, so the input scores add up to the prediction apart from small amounts absorbed by bias terms and stabilisers. Different rules can be used for different types of layer. The result is a relevance score for each input, such as a pixel or a feature, with positive values for inputs that supported the prediction and negative values for inputs that counted against it.

example_use_cases.description: Identifying which pixels in chest X-rays contribute to pneumonia detection, helping radiologists verify AI diagnoses by highlighting anatomical regions the model considers relevant.

A perception team investigating a misclassified traffic-sign image draws the relevance map for the wrong class. The map shows the relevance sitting on a sticker and the background rather than on the sign itself, which tells the team to add training images with such clutter before the model is retested.

A bank's model-risk reviewers receive LRP relevance scores for a sample of declined applications scored by a neural network. They check that the inputs with the most relevance for the decline output are affordability measures and not proxy fields such as postcode, and file the scores with the decision record for audit.

limitations.description: Each layer type needs its own propagation rule, and a new layer type has none until someone derives one, so adapting LRP to a new architecture takes expertise and testing.
Rule selection (LRP-ε, LRP-γ and others) changes the resulting maps, so two analysts can produce different explanations of the same prediction, and choosing among them takes expertise.

Heatmaps are hard to validate. The original paper judges them by eye and with a pixel-flipping test, and notes that quality beyond visual assessment is an open question, so a plausible-looking map does not prove the model relies on the highlighted inputs.

Standard rules do not cover attention layers. Extensions for transformers, such as AttnLRP in the LXT library, exist but are recent and specific to certain architectures, so users of transformers or large language models must adopt them and confirm they match their model.

Bias handling and epsilon stabilisation can absorb or inject relevance, so input scores do not always sum exactly to the selected output. A report should document the accounting residual before claiming conservation.

sample_claims.text: On the audited sample of chest X-rays, the relevance for the pneumonia output lies mainly inside the lung fields and not on laterality markers, text or image borders.
For every audited credit decision, the relevance scores for the decline output are stored with the decision record, and they sum to the model's score within the stated tolerance.
In the reviewed true positives of the defect-detection network, most of the relevance falls on the defect itself and not on the background texture that differs between production lines.

Where the perception model misclassifies a traffic sign in the test set, the relevance map shows whether the evidence for the wrong class came from the sign or from its surroundings, and each case is recorded.

name: Contextual Decomposition
description: Contextual Decomposition explains why an LSTM, a neural network that reads text one word at a time, made a particular prediction. The user picks a word or phrase, and the method splits the network's output score into two parts: the part due to that phrase alone, and the part due to everything else, including how the phrase interacts with the words around it. Comparing a phrase's score with the scores of its parts reveals effects that word-by-word methods miss, such as a negation reversing the sentiment of the word that follows it. The split is tracked through the LSTM's internal gates, so the model itself is not changed or retrained. The output is a numerical score for each phrase examined.

example_use_cases.description: Analysing why an LSTM-based spam filter flagged an email by decomposing contributions from individual words ('free', 'urgent') versus their contextual interactions ('free trial' together).

A hospital analytics team checks an LSTM that flags clinical notes mentioning possible pneumonia. Contextual decomposition shows whether negated findings such as 'no evidence of pneumonia' push the score down, as intended, or whether the model reacts to the word 'pneumonia' alone, which tells the team if it needs retraining on negated examples before use.

A platform's trust-and-safety team handles an appeal against an LSTM toxicity classifier's removal of a post. The reviewing moderator is shown the phrases with the highest contextual decomposition scores, including whether a negation such as 'not stupid' was read correctly, so the moderator can judge whether the removal rested on the post's actual meaning.

limitations.description: Developed for LSTMs, whose gates the method uses to separate a phrase's own effect from its interactions. The source does not cover plain recurrent networks, transformers or attention models, so teams using those cannot apply the published method as it stands.
Needs internal states, gate parameters and classifier weights. Output labels or probabilities alone do not reveal the phrase-related and remaining-input components.

The user must choose each phrase to examine, and the published method handles contiguous phrases. The number of possible phrases grows quickly with text length, so scanning a whole document for interactions is costly and easy to leave incomplete.

The split relies on linearising the gate and activation functions and averaging over orderings of the terms. Interaction scores are therefore approximate, and the source validates them only on sentiment tasks (Stanford Sentiment Treebank, Yelp), so scores on other tasks need checking independently.

Components combine additively in hidden states and class scores before the probability transformation. They should not be read as independent probabilities or as the exact effect of deleting a phrase.

sample_claims.text: In the clinical-note classifier, negated findings such as 'no evidence of pneumonia' lower the score for that condition, as the contextual decomposition of the full phrase shows.
Each removal decision of the toxicity classifier that is sent to appeal can be traced to named words or phrases whose contextual decomposition scores account for most of the output score.

In the news-sentiment model used for credit monitoring, the contribution of a sentiment word changes sign when a negation or contrast precedes it, and contextual decomposition separates the word's own effect from its context.

For the audited support tickets, the routing model's decision is not driven by any single trigger word: phrase-level contextual decomposition scores account for more of the output than the strongest single-word score.

name: Taylor Decomposition
description: Taylor Decomposition explains one prediction of a neural network by splitting its output score into a contribution from each input, such as each pixel. It starts from a reference input, called a root point, that is close to the real input but for which the network's score is zero. Each input's contribution is the slope of the score with respect to that input at the root point, multiplied by how far the input sits from the root, and terms that involve several inputs at once are left out. Finding a good root point is slow for large networks, so the deep variant applies the same idea to one neuron at a time and passes the contributions backwards through the layers, which gives rules close to those of Layer-wise Relevance Propagation. The result is a relevance score for every input that can be drawn as a heatmap.

example_use_cases.description: A quality team uses a convolutional network to flag defective printed circuit boards. For each flagged board they draw the deep Taylor heatmap and check that the highlighted pixels sit on the defect and not on a board label, the edge or the background, before they trust the flags enough to stop manual inspection.

A hospital's model-validation group audits a ReLU network that classifies chest X-rays. For a sample of positive cases, deep Taylor relevance shows whether the evidence for the finding lies inside the lungs or on markers, text or borders added by the imaging equipment, before the group signs the model off for a pilot.

A bank's data science team has a ReLU network that scores small-business loan applications from tabular inputs. For a declined application, deep Taylor relevance lists which inputs supplied most of the score, so a reviewer can see whether the decision rests on repayment history and income or on a field such as postcode.

limitations.description: The explanation depends on the choice of root point, and different reference inputs give different attributions. Finding the nearest root needs an iterative optimisation that is slow for large networks and may not converge, which is why the source applies the deep variant to large image networks.

Plain Taylor decomposition uses only first-order terms, so joint effects of several inputs stay unattributed and the scores need not add up to the prediction. In the source's tests the nearest-root version lost a large share of the relevance, so its heatmaps can leave much of the prediction unexplained.

The deep variant's guarantees, scores that add up to the prediction and are never negative, are proved for ReLU-style layers with zero or negative biases, and iNNvestigate documents support for ReLU networks only. Other activations, positive biases or normalisation layers need workarounds that the proofs do not cover.

Heatmaps explain one input at a time and are hard to validate. The source judges them by eye and by checking that relevance is conserved on MNIST digits and ImageNet photos, so a plausible-looking map does not prove that the model relies on the highlighted inputs.

Requires access to internal layer operations and supported redistribution rules. A prediction-only service cannot supply this layer-wise decomposition, and an image-derived rule should not be assumed valid for arbitrary text or attention models.

sample_claims.text: For each audited decision, the deep Taylor relevance scores of the inputs sum to the network's output score within the agreed tolerance, so little of the prediction is left unattributed.
On the audited sample of chest X-rays, the deep Taylor relevance for the positive finding lies mainly inside the lung fields and not on markers, text or image borders.
In the reviewed true positives of the defect classifier, the highest-relevance pixels fall on the defect itself, so its flags do not depend on board labels or background texture.
The inputs given most relevance for declined applications in the credit network are affordability and repayment measures, not postcode or other fields that stand in for protected characteristics.

name: Sobol Indices
description: Sobol indices show how much of the variation in a model's output can be traced to each of its inputs. The analyst sets a range or probability distribution for every input and runs the model on a large, carefully designed sample of input combinations. The variance (spread) of the outputs is then split into shares. A first-order index is the share caused by one input varying on its own, and a total-order index also counts every interaction that input takes part in. A large gap between the two signals that an input matters mainly through interactions, and optional second-order indices show which pairs of inputs interact.

example_use_cases.description: Analysing a climate prediction model to determine which atmospheric parameters (temperature, humidity, pressure) contribute most to rainfall forecast uncertainty, helping meteorologists understand which measurements need the highest precision.

A risk team validating a portfolio valuation model asks which economic indicators (interest rates, inflation, GDP growth) drive most of the variation in predicted portfolio value. A large gap between an indicator's total-order and first-order indices shows it acts mainly through interactions, which tells the team which scenarios to stress-test together.

limitations.description: The standard sampling scheme needs N(2D+2) model runs for D inputs (N(D+2) without second-order indices), with N often in the thousands. A slow model, or one with dozens of inputs, quickly becomes impractical. Grouping related inputs, or screening first with a cheaper method such as Morris, reduces the cost.

Assumes the inputs vary independently. If real inputs are correlated, for example income and postcode, the sample contains combinations the model never meets in practice, and the indices can mislead about which inputs matter.

Needs a probability distribution or range for every input, and the indices depend on that choice, because widening one input's range raises its share of the variance. If the ranges do not reflect the real deployment population, the ranking describes a model the users will never face.

Variance is the only yardstick. When the output is heavily skewed or has several peaks, variance shares can be unreliable guides to which inputs matter, and a moment-independent method such as PAWN may suit better.

Estimates carry sampling error. With too few runs the confidence intervals can be as wide as the indices themselves, so small indices cannot be told apart from zero. Report the intervals SALib returns and check that the ranking holds when N is increased.

sample_claims.text: Our flood-model review reports atmospheric inputs' main and total shares of output variance under the documented independent input distributions.
The portfolio-model audit records first and total-order sensitivity indices, distinguishing main effects from overall interaction involvement.
Our clinical-model sensitivity review reports patient-input variance shares under the chosen distributions, without treating them as a decomposition of every source of prediction uncertainty.

name: Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations
description: LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations) explains individual predictions by approximating the complex model's behaviour in a small neighbourhood around a specific instance. It works by creating perturbed versions of the input (e.g., removing words from text, changing pixel values in images, or varying feature values), obtaining the model's predictions for these variations, and training a simple interpretable model (typically linear regression) weighted by proximity to the original instance. The coefficients of this local surrogate model reveal which features most influenced the specific prediction.

example_use_cases.description: Explaining why a specific patient received a high-risk diagnosis by showing which symptoms (fever, blood pressure, age) contributed most to the prediction, helping doctors validate the AI's reasoning.
Debugging a text classifier's misclassification of a movie review by highlighting which words (e.g., sarcastic phrases) confused the model, enabling targeted model improvements.

Showing insurance customers the claim features that most influenced an automated approval or denial. A reviewer first checks that the explanation is stable across repeated runs and plausible for that claim, because it approximates the model locally and may not match its full reasoning.

limitations.description: Explanations can be unstable due to random sampling, producing different results across multiple runs.
The linear surrogate may poorly approximate highly non-linear model behaviour in the local region.
Defining the neighbourhood size and perturbation strategy requires careful tuning for each data type.
Can be computationally expensive for explaining many instances due to repeated model queries.

Assumes features are independent when generating perturbations, producing unrealistic out-of-distribution samples for datasets with correlated features. This can generate misleading attribution scores when inputs share strong correlations (e.g., age and income in credit scoring, comorbidities in clinical data).

sample_claims.text: For the transactions the fraud model flags, the features that the explanation ranks highest are ones fraud analysts judge relevant to the flag.
Explanations of the same prediction, repeated with fresh random samples, name the same top features, so the stated reasons do not depend on chance.
The explanation for each high-risk patient prediction rests on recognised clinical risk factors and not on artefacts such as the recording site or record format.
The content moderation system provides interpretable explanations for individual moderation decisions without requiring access to model internals
Customers receive the main reasons for an individual automated claim decision, drawn from a local explanation of that decision and checked by a reviewer for plausibility.

name: Ridge Regression Surrogates
description: This technique approximates a complex model by training a ridge regression (a linear model with L2 regularisation) on the original model's predictions. The ridge regression serves as a global surrogate that balances fidelity and interpretability, capturing the main linear relationships that the complex model learned whilst ignoring noise due to regularisation. This approach is particularly useful when stakeholders need to understand the overall behaviour of a complex model through transparent linear coefficients.

example_use_cases.description: Approximating a complex ensemble model used for credit scoring with a ridge regression surrogate to identify the most influential features (income, credit history, debt-to-income ratio) and their linear relationships for regulatory compliance reporting.

Creating a ridge regression surrogate of a neural network used for medical diagnosis to understand which patient symptoms and biomarkers have the strongest linear predictive relationships with disease outcomes.

Creating an interpretable approximation of a complex insurance pricing model for regulatory compliance, enabling stakeholders to understand and validate the decision-making process through transparent linear relationships.

limitations.description: Linear approximation may miss important non-linear relationships and interactions captured by the original complex model.
Requires a representative dataset to train the surrogate model, which may not be available or may be expensive to generate.
Ridge regularisation may oversimplify the model by shrinking coefficients, potentially hiding important but less dominant features.
Surrogate fidelity depends on how well linear relationships approximate the original model's behaviour across the entire input space.

sample_claims.text: The model's global behavior is approximated by a simpler representation that captures dominant linear relationships across all predictions
The credit scoring model's decision logic can be explained through consistent linear weights applied uniformly across all applicant evaluations
The diagnostic system's predictions are attributable to weighted combinations of patient features that remain stable across the entire population
The environmental forecasting model's feature influences are represented through simplified linear coefficients that prioritize robust patterns over noise
The complex ensemble model's overall decision-making process is captured by an interpretable linear approximation that reveals primary feature contributions

name: Partial Dependence Plots
description: Partial Dependence Plots show how changing one or two features affects a model's predictions on average. The technique works by varying the selected feature(s) across their full range whilst keeping all other features fixed at their original values, then averaging the predictions. This creates a clear visualisation of whether increasing or decreasing a feature tends to increase or decrease predictions, and reveals patterns like linear trends, plateaus, or threshold effects that help explain model behaviour.

example_use_cases.description: Analysing how house prices change with property size in a real estate prediction model, revealing whether the relationship is linear or if there are diminishing returns for very large properties.
Examining how customer age affects predicted loan default probability in a credit scoring model, showing whether risk increases steadily with age or has specific age ranges with higher risk.
Visualising how temperature affects crop yield predictions in agricultural models, identifying optimal temperature ranges and potential threshold effects.

limitations.description: Assumes the plotted features are independent of the others. When they are correlated, the averaging pairs values that never occur together, so the curve partly reflects how the model behaves in regions with no data.

Shows only the average effect. If a feature acts in opposite directions for different groups of instances, the effects cancel and the curve can look flat, so interactions with other features stay hidden.
Limited to one or two features at a time, because higher-dimensional plots cannot be read. Effects that depend on three or more features together cannot be shown.
The basic method needs a pass over the whole dataset for every grid value, so cost grows with dataset size, the number of grid points and the time the model takes to predict.

sample_claims.text: The readmission model's average predicted risk rises with the number of prior admissions and does not fall at any point, as clinical guidance would expect.
The credit model's average predicted default probability falls as income rises, with no unexplained reversal at any income level.
The crop-yield model's average predicted yield peaks within the agronomically plausible temperature range and declines on either side.
The driving model's average predicted safe speed falls as visibility worsens across the full range of visibility values seen in testing.

name: Individual Conditional Expectation Plots
description: Individual Conditional Expectation (ICE) plots display the predicted output for individual instances as a function of a feature, with all other features held fixed for each instance. Each line on an ICE plot represents one instance's prediction trajectory as the feature of interest changes, revealing whether different instances are affected differently by that feature. This complements Partial Dependence Plots by showing heterogeneous effects across individual instances rather than just the average trend.

example_use_cases.description: Examining how house price predictions vary with property age for individual properties, revealing that whilst most houses follow a declining price trend with age, historic properties (built before 1900) show different patterns due to heritage value.

Analysing how individual patients' diabetes risk predictions change with BMI, showing that whilst most patients follow the expected increasing risk pattern, some patients with specific genetic markers show different response curves.

limitations.description: Plots can become cluttered and difficult to interpret when displaying many instances simultaneously.
Does not provide automatic summarisation of overall effects, requiring manual visual inspection to identify patterns.
Still assumes all other features remain fixed at their observed values, which may not reflect realistic scenarios.
Cannot reveal interactions between the plotted feature and other features for individual instances.

sample_claims.text: The model's feature-response relationship varies across individual patient subgroups in clinically interpretable ways
The prediction trajectories for individual samples reveal heterogeneous effects that differ from the population-average trend
The flood model shows distinct response patterns to rainfall intensity across different watershed characteristics
The loan pricing model's sensitivity to income varies across applicant profiles without averaging over these differences

name: Gradient Saliency
description: Gradient saliency (also called vanilla gradient saliency) is the simplest gradient-based explanation for image classifiers: it takes the gradient of the score for a chosen class (the network's output for that class before it becomes a probability) with respect to every input pixel, in one backward pass, to show which pixels that score is most sensitive to. The gradient says how much the score would change if that pixel changed slightly. The method keeps the size of each gradient and, for colour images, the largest across the colour channels, then shows one value per pixel as a heatmap. Because the sign is dropped, the map shows sensitivity but not whether a pixel supports or counts against the class. In a bias-diagnosis use, the maps are drawn for the errors of a classifier already known to err more for one group, to see whether the sensitive pixels sit on a cue linked to that group; the group-wise errors come from a separate check.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital imaging team validating a pneumonia detection model on chest X-rays computes gradient saliency for a sample of confirmed cases and checks whether the most sensitive pixels lie over the lungs rather than over tubes, monitoring leads or position markers. They use the result to decide whether the model is ready for a clinical pilot or needs retraining on cleaner images.

An agricultural technology company testing a plant disease classifier on leaf photographs taken in the field computes gradient saliency for the images it misclassifies. It checks whether the sensitive pixels sit on the diseased leaf area or on soil, trays and hands in the frame, and decides whether to collect photographs with more varied backgrounds.

A team studying dataset bias fine-tunes an image classifier to separate doctors from nurses in photographs and finds, on a gender-balanced test set, that it errs far more often for one gender. It then inspects gradient saliency on those errors. Where the most sensitive pixels sit on faces and hair rather than on uniforms or equipment, the model is using appearance linked to gender as a shortcut, so the team rebalances the training photographs and retrains.

limitations.description: Maps are noisy and can change sharply for tiny changes to the image, so one map is weak evidence. A study of upper-limb X-ray classifiers found that plain-gradient maps were less accurate at locating abnormalities, and less repeatable, than radiologists' markings (Venkatesh et al., 2024). Look at many images and more than one trained model before drawing a conclusion about the model.

The gradient is local. Where the model's output has flattened, for example once a feature is already strongly present, the gradient is near zero, so a pixel the model relies on can get almost no score. Sundararajan et al. (2017) show this with a one-ReLU example, which is why methods such as Integrated Gradients measure the change from a baseline instead.

Because only the size of each gradient is kept, the map cannot say whether a pixel supports or counts against the chosen class. Evidence that argues against the prediction looks the same as evidence for it, so a map cannot show that a pixel was used in the way a reviewer assumes.

A high score means the output is sensitive to a small change in that pixel, not that the model relied on it or that removing it would change the decision. Pixel-level scores are scattered and often capture only the most discriminative part of an object (Simonyan et al., 2013), so they rarely outline a whole lesion or object a reviewer can name.

sample_claims.text: For the pneumonia model's confirmed cases in the validation sample, gradient saliency places the most sensitive pixels over the lung fields and not over tubes, leads or position markers, in at least the proportion of cases the acceptance criteria set
The plant disease classifier's gradient saliency maps for its misclassified field photographs show sensitivity concentrated on the leaf area and not on soil, trays or hands in the frame
Gradient saliency maps used as evidence for this classifier were repeated on models retrained with different random seeds, and the sensitive regions agree across runs above the stated threshold

On the audit images, the retrained doctor-versus-nurse classifier's gradient saliency maps place the most sensitive pixels on uniforms and equipment rather than on faces and hair, the cue found on its errors before the training photographs were rebalanced

name: Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping
description: Grad-CAM (Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping) draws a heatmap over an image showing which regions most raise a convolutional neural network's score for a chosen class, which need not be the one the model predicted. The last convolutional layer produces a stack of feature maps, each a coarse grid recording where one learned pattern appears. Grad-CAM takes the gradient of the class score with respect to each map (how much the score changes as that map's values change), averages it to give the map a weight, and adds the weighted maps together. It keeps only the positive values, so the result marks regions that count in favour of the class, then enlarges the coarse grid to the image's size and lays it over the image, so the output shows broad regions rather than pixels. In a bias-diagnosis use, the maps are laid over the errors of a classifier already known to err more for one group, to see which image region the model relies on; the group-wise errors and the training-data counts come from separate checks.

example_use_cases.description: A dermatology AI team validating a melanoma classifier overlays Grad-CAM on dermoscopy images and compares the highlighted region with the lesion outline drawn by a clinician. Cases where the heat falls on a ruler, hair or skin markings are collected, and the team decides whether the training images need cleaning before the model goes to clinical evaluation.

A team developing the traffic sign recogniser for a driver assistance system overlays Grad-CAM on the test images it misclassifies. When the heat sits on the background or a shadow rather than on the sign, they add training images with similar backgrounds and lighting, then recheck the overlays before the release decision.

A team studying dataset bias fine-tunes an image classifier to separate doctors from nurses in photographs and finds, on a gender-balanced test set, that it errs far more often for one gender. It overlays Grad-CAM on those errors: heat on faces and hairstyles rather than on uniforms or equipment shows the model has learned a gender shortcut, and a count of the training photographs by gender shows why. The team rebalances the photographs, retrains and checks that the heat moves.

limitations.description: Needs the network's gradients and its last convolutional feature maps, so it cannot be run on a model reached only through an API, or on architectures without convolutional layers. The user must also choose which layer to use, and the paper reports that maps become progressively worse for earlier layers (Selvaraju et al., Sec 3).

The map has the resolution of the last convolutional layer (14 by 14 for VGG-16 and AlexNet), then is enlarged to the image. Small or irregular findings, such as a few-millimetre lesion or a thin sign pole, fall inside one or two cells, so the overlay cannot show whether the model attended to the finding or to its surroundings.

In a chest X-ray benchmark Grad-CAM generally located pathologies better than six other saliency methods but worse than radiologists, with the largest gap for small, complex-shaped findings, and it located them better when the model was confident (Saporta et al., 2022). The overlays are least reliable for the uncertain, hard cases where a reviewer most wants an explanation.

A bright region means features there raise the class score under a local linear approximation, not that the model relied on them. In the paper's own check, Grad-CAM's ranking of image patches agreed only moderately with occlusion, which masks patches and re-scores the image (rank correlation 0.254, Sec 5.3). The ReLU also hides regions that count against the class.

sample_claims.text: For the melanoma classifier's validation images, the Grad-CAM region for the predicted class overlaps the clinician-drawn lesion outline in at least the proportion of cases set in the acceptance criteria

For the traffic sign recogniser's misclassified test images, the Grad-CAM region falls on the sign face and not the background in all but a reported fraction of cases, and each remaining case has been reviewed
The land-cover classifier's Grad-CAM region for each class in the labelled satellite tiles falls on the matching surface type and not on shadows or neighbouring land

On the audit images, the retrained doctor-versus-nurse classifier's Grad-CAM regions fall on uniforms and equipment rather than on faces and hair, the cue found on its errors before the training photographs were rebalanced

name: Occlusion Sensitivity
description: Occlusion sensitivity shows which parts of an input a model's prediction is sensitive to. A region of the input, such as a square patch of an image, is hidden by replacing it with a neutral value like grey, and the change in the model's output is recorded, usually the probability of the class of interest. Sliding the patch across the whole input gives a map of how much the output changes when each region is hidden. A large drop marks a region the prediction depends on. The method treats the model as a black box, needing only its inputs and outputs, and is most often used on images.

example_use_cases.description: Testing which regions of a chest X-ray are critical for pneumonia detection by systematically covering different areas with grey patches and measuring how much the model's confidence drops for each occluded region.

Evaluating whether a facial recognition system relies on specific facial features by masking eyes, nose, mouth, or other regions to identify which areas cause the biggest drop in recognition accuracy.

Analysing agricultural crop disease classification models to verify that predictions focus on visible disease symptoms (discolouration, lesions, wilting) rather than background elements like soil or irrigation equipment, so that a model relying on the background is caught before use on farms with different surroundings.

limitations.description: Computationally expensive as it requires running inference multiple times for each region tested, scaling poorly with input size.

The choice of patch size, shape and stride changes the map. A patch that is too small may miss features that are informative only together, and one that is too large covers several relevant regions at once and blurs the result.

Cannot capture interactions between multiple regions that jointly contribute to the prediction but are individually less important. If two regions carry the same evidence, hiding either one alone may change little, so both can look unimportant.

The occluding patch is itself an unnatural input. A change in the output may reflect the model reacting to the grey or black patch and not to the missing content, and the map can change with the fill value chosen.

sample_claims.text: The diagnostic system's classifications remain stable when non-pathological image regions are masked or removed
On the images examined, the crop disease classifier's confidence falls when leaf lesions are masked and changes little when soil or background is masked.
The traffic-sign classifier's confidence in the correct class falls sharply only when the sign face is covered, not when the surrounding scenery is covered.
The image classifier's prediction does not depend on watermarks, borders or other artefacts, because masking them leaves the output unchanged on the test images.

name: Attention Weight Analysis
description: Attention weight analysis reads the weights an attention-based neural network assigns to the parts of its input, to see which positions it draws on at each step. The weights come from an ordinary forward pass and are plotted as heatmaps, one row per output step or token. In recurrent encoder-decoder models, such as early neural machine translation or image captioning, each output step has a row over the source words or image regions, read as a soft alignment in which weight is shared across several source positions. In transformers, each attention head (one of several parallel attention units in a layer) has its own matrix at every layer; the analyst views these per head and layer, or averages them over many inputs to profile a head, for example by how much attention it gives each kind of token, or how often its strongest attention lands on a labelled relation such as a verb and its object. The heatmaps show where each step looks; on their own they do not measure how much each input contributed to the prediction, because the weights leave out what is done with the attended values and information mixes between layers.

example_use_cases.description: A localisation team validating an in-house recurrent encoder-decoder translation model for equipment manuals plots the attention matrix for sample sentences and checks that each technical term draws most of its weight from its source counterpart. Sentences whose weight falls mainly on punctuation or the end-of-sentence marker go to a translator; the team first tests this screen on sentences with known errors, and does not treat a clean alignment as proof of a correct translation.

A team assessing an image-captioning model for an alt-text service overlays each generated word's attention weights on the image to check that nouns such as 'wheelchair' or 'crossing' fall on the matching objects. Captions whose nouns attend mainly to background regions are sent for manual review before release, as a screen only: a match does not show that the object produced the word.

A clinical NLP team reviewing a transformer that extracts medication details from discharge letters uses head and model views on a sample of letters to find heads whose attention links each drug name to its dose and frequency, then checks whether those heads behave the same way on letters from a second hospital before describing in the model documentation where those heads look, without claiming that the extraction depends on them.

A model-risk team reviewing a contract-clause classifier uses attention maps as a first look at which phrases the model draws on, then tests the highlighted phrases with an attribution or ablation method before reporting them, because its validation policy does not accept attention weights alone as evidence of what drove a decision.

limitations.description: A bright cell in a heatmap does not show that the input behind it caused the output. In recurrent text classifiers, attention often disagreed with other measures of which words mattered, and very different patterns gave the same prediction (Jain and Wallace 2019). Wiegreffe and Pinter (2019) reply that attention can be a believable account without being a faithful one. Neither tested transformers. Confirm any reading by masking the highlighted inputs and checking that the output changes.

In transformers each layer mixes information between tokens, so one layer's weights do not show which inputs a later representation depends on. In a small six-layer transformer, the classification token's weights agreed with deletion-based importance only in the first layer; rollout, which combines weights across layers, agreed better later (Abnar and Zuidema 2020). For a fine-tuned DistilBERT model the gain was small: rollout improves on raw weights but does not fix them.

Each input gives one matrix per head per layer (144 in BERT-base), and the most visible pattern is often uninformative. In BERT, over half the attention in layers 6 to 10 falls on the separator token, which Clark et al. (2019) suggest acts as a 'do nothing' option; Kobayashi et al. (2020) found these weights carry little information once vector size is counted. Profiling a head needs averaging over many inputs, since a few hand-picked examples can mislead.

The weights mean different things in different architectures. In recurrent translation models source attention reads as a word alignment (Bahdanau et al. 2015). In transformer translation models, averaging source attention over all layers gave poor alignments; better ones needed a chosen layer or a measure that counts vector size (Garg et al. 2019; Kobayashi et al. 2020). Check any alignment reading against reference alignments for the model being assessed.

Attention can be trained to look harmless while the model still uses what it hides. Pruthi et al. (2020) trained occupation classifiers to put almost no attention on gender words with little loss of accuracy; the models still used gender, yet reviewers shown the manipulated highlights judged no predictions gender-influenced, against 66% with the original attention. A heatmap showing no weight on a sensitive input is weak evidence; test by changing the input.

sample_claims.text: For a sample of equipment-manual sentences, the recurrent translation model's source attention put its largest weight on the source counterpart of each translated technical term, and sentences where it did not were reviewed by a translator.

In the reviewed sample of alt-text captions, the share of generated object nouns whose attention fell on the matching object in the image met the release threshold, and captions that fell short were checked by hand before release.
The attention heads identified as linking drug names to doses behave consistently across discharge letters from both hospitals in the validation set
Phrases that attention maps suggested were decisive for the clause classifier were confirmed by an independent attribution method before being reported to reviewers

name: Factor Analysis
description: Factor analysis looks for a small number of hidden factors that explain why a larger set of measured variables, such as a model's input features, tend to move together. Each variable is modelled as a weighted mix of the shared factors plus a part that is unique to it, including measurement error. The weights are called loadings, and they show which variables each factor is built from; for example, several credit-history features might all load on one 'repayment behaviour' factor. Unlike principal component analysis, which summarises as much of the total variation as it can, factor analysis models only the variation that variables share. Analysts usually rotate the factors afterwards, using varimax (factors stay uncorrelated) or oblimin (factors may correlate), so that each variable loads mainly on one factor and the factors are easier to name.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's model validation team finds that forty macroeconomic and credit-bureau inputs to a default-risk model are heavily correlated. Exploratory factor analysis groups them into four factors the team can name, such as growth, inflation, household debt and credit conditions, and the model is rebuilt on the factor scores so its drivers can be explained to the risk committee in four terms instead of forty.

A flood-forecasting team with sixty correlated gauge, soil-moisture and satellite inputs runs factor analysis on the training data to find a few underlying drivers, such as rainfall intensity, catchment wetness and river level. Forecast explanations are then reported per driver, which operators can relate to what they see on the ground.

limitations.description: The standard model is linear, with each variable a weighted sum of factors plus noise. Maximum-likelihood extraction also assumes roughly normal data, so skewed, binary or strongly non-linear variables can distort the loadings. Check distributions first, or choose an extraction method that does not require normality.

Factors are statistical summaries of correlation, not discovered causes. A factor labelled 'economic confidence' is the analyst's reading of which variables load together, and a different rotation or sample may support a different label.

Sensitive to the choice of number of factors and rotation method, which have no single correct answer and can change both which variables group together and how readable the factors are. Report the choices made and check that the structure is stable.
Requires a sample that is large relative to the number of variables. With small samples the loadings are unstable and change when a few cases are added or removed.

Describes the structure of the data fed into it, not how a trained model uses that data. Factors of a model's inputs say nothing about which factors the model relies on, unless the model is also built on or analysed with the factor scores.

sample_claims.text: The default-risk model's correlated inputs reduce to a small number of named factors that account for most of their shared variance, so its drivers can be explained at factor level.
The flood-forecasting inputs group into a few factors whose loadings domain experts recognise as physically meaningful drivers.
The number of factors retained, the extraction method and the rotation are documented, and the factor structure is stable when the analysis is repeated on a separate sample.

name: Principal Component Analysis
description: Principal Component Analysis transforms high-dimensional data into a lower-dimensional representation by finding the directions (principal components) that capture the maximum variance in the data. Each component is a linear combination of original features, with the first component explaining the most variance, the second component the most remaining variance orthogonal to the first, and so on. This technique reveals underlying patterns in data structure, enables visualisation of complex datasets, and helps identify which combinations of features drive the most variation in the data.

example_use_cases.description: Analysing customer behavior data with dozens of variables (purchase frequency, spending patterns, demographics) to identify the 2-3 main dimensions that explain customer segmentation, revealing whether customers cluster by spending level, product preferences, or shopping frequency.

Reducing dimensionality of image data for facial recognition systems by finding the principal components that capture the most variation in face shapes and expressions, helping understand which facial features contribute most to distinguishing between individuals.

limitations.description: Principal components are abstract linear combinations of original features that often lack clear real-world interpretation or meaning.
Only captures linear relationships between features, missing non-linear patterns and complex interactions in the data.
Results are highly sensitive to feature scaling - features with larger numerical ranges can dominate the principal components.
Information loss is inherent when reducing dimensions, and choosing the optimal number of components requires balancing simplicity with retained variance.

sample_claims.text: The feature space reveals latent factors that explain correlated environmental measurements without relying on predetermined variable groupings
The model's high-dimensional patient data is reducible to a small number of orthogonal patterns that capture most variation in clinical measurements
The financial indicators decompose into uncorrelated variance components that reveal which measurement combinations drive portfolio risk
The image representation preserves maximal variance through linear transformations that identify which pixel combinations distinguish between object categories
The customer behavior measurements organize into ordered variance patterns showing which feature combinations best separate distinct market segments

name: t-SNE
description: t-SNE (t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbour Embedding) is a non-linear dimensionality reduction technique that creates 2D or 3D visualisations of high-dimensional data by preserving local neighbourhood relationships. The algorithm converts similarities between data points into joint probabilities in the high-dimensional space, then tries to minimise the divergence between these probabilities and those in the low-dimensional embedding. This approach excels at revealing cluster structures and local patterns, making it particularly effective for exploratory data analysis and understanding complex data relationships that linear methods like PCA might miss.

example_use_cases.description: Analyzing genomic data with thousands of gene expression features to visualize how different cancer subtypes cluster together, revealing which tumors have similar molecular signatures and potentially similar treatment responses.

Exploring deep learning model embeddings to understand how a neural network represents different categories of images, showing whether the model groups similar objects (cars, animals, furniture) in meaningful clusters in its internal feature space.

limitations.description: Non-deterministic algorithm produces different results on each run, making it difficult to reproduce exact visualizations or compare results across studies.
Prioritizes preserving local neighborhood structure at the expense of global relationships, potentially creating misleading impressions about overall data topology.
Computationally expensive with O(n²) complexity, making it impractical for datasets with more than ~10,000 points without approximation methods.
Sensitive to hyperparameter choices (perplexity, learning rate, iterations) that can dramatically affect clustering patterns and require domain expertise to tune appropriately.

sample_claims.text: The model's internal representations reveal distinct local neighborhoods corresponding to clinically meaningful disease subtypes
Similar customer profiles cluster together in the reduced representation while maintaining separation between behaviorally distinct segments
The high-dimensional embedding space exhibits locally coherent structure that corresponds to interpretable data groupings
The sensor data's local proximity relationships in the reduced visualization reflect genuine environmental similarity patterns
Complex gene expression patterns are rendered into interpretable clusters that preserve biological relationships between nearby cell types

name: UMAP
description: UMAP (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection) is a non-linear dimensionality reduction technique that creates 2D or 3D visualisations of high-dimensional data by constructing a mathematical model of the data's underlying manifold structure. Unlike t-SNE, UMAP preserves both local neighbourhood relationships and global topology more effectively, using techniques from topological data analysis and Riemannian geometry. This approach often produces more interpretable cluster layouts while maintaining meaningful distances between clusters, making it particularly valuable for exploratory data analysis and understanding complex dataset structures.

example_use_cases.description: Analysing single-cell RNA sequencing data to visualise how different cell types cluster based on gene expression patterns, revealing developmental trajectories and identifying previously unknown cell subtypes in tissue samples.

Exploring customer segmentation by reducing hundreds of behavioural and demographic features to 2D space, showing how different customer groups relate to each other and identifying transition zones where customers might move between segments.

limitations.description: Hyperparameter choices (n_neighbors, min_dist, metric) significantly influence the embedding structure and can lead to very different interpretations of the same data.
While preserving global structure better than t-SNE, distances in the reduced space still don't directly correspond to distances in the original feature space.
Performance can be sensitive to the choice of distance metric, which may not be obvious for complex or mixed data types.
Like other manifold learning techniques, it assumes the data lies on a lower-dimensional manifold, which may not hold for all datasets.

sample_claims.text: The high-dimensional dataset's underlying cluster relationships are visualized while preserving meaningful distances between distinct groups
The data visualization reveals both local neighborhood patterns and global topology without sacrificing one for the other
The model's learned representations can be explored through low-dimensional projections that preserve the manifold structure of the original feature space
Complex dataset structures with non-linear relationships are comprehensible through two-dimensional visualizations that maintain topological fidelity

name: Prototype and Criticism Models
description: Prototype and Criticism Models provide data understanding by identifying two complementary sets of examples: prototypes represent the most typical instances that best summarise common patterns in the data, whilst criticisms are outliers or edge cases that are poorly represented by the prototypes. For example, in a dataset of customer transactions, prototypes might be the most representative buying patterns (frequent small purchases, occasional large purchases), whilst criticisms could be unusual behaviours (bulk buyers, one-time high-value customers). This dual approach reveals both what is normal and what is exceptional, helping understand data coverage and model blind spots.

example_use_cases.description: Analysing medical imaging datasets to identify prototype scans that represent typical healthy tissue patterns and criticism examples showing rare disease presentations, helping radiologists understand what the model considers 'normal' versus cases requiring special attention.

Evaluating credit scoring models by finding prototype borrowers who represent typical low-risk profiles and criticism cases showing unusual but legitimate financial patterns that the model might misclassify, ensuring fair treatment of edge cases.

Evaluating representation bias in hiring datasets by examining whether prototypes systematically exclude certain demographic groups and criticisms disproportionately represent minorities, revealing data collection inequities.

limitations.description: Selection of prototypes and criticisms is highly dependent on the choice of distance metric or similarity measure, which may not capture all meaningful relationships in the data.
Computational complexity can become prohibitive for very large datasets, as the method often requires pairwise comparisons or optimisation over the entire dataset.
The number of prototypes and criticisms to select is typically a hyperparameter that requires domain expertise to set appropriately.
Results may not generalise well if the training data distribution differs significantly from the deployment data distribution.
