sample_claims.text: The medical imaging dataset's coverage is characterised by both typical tissue patterns and rare pathological presentations requiring specialised attention
The credit model's validation set includes both representative borrower profiles and exceptional cases that deviate from standard lending patterns
The environmental monitoring system's training data reflects both common measurement conditions and unusual scenarios that test operational boundaries
The hiring dataset's representative candidates do not systematically exclude particular demographic groups whilst edge cases disproportionately represent minorities
The system's performance on atypical cases is documented alongside its behaviour on prototypical examples

name: Influence Functions
description: Influence functions estimate which training examples most affected a model's prediction on a particular test example. For each training example, they estimate how much the model's loss on the test example would change if that example counted slightly more or slightly less, which approximates removing it and retraining without actually doing so. The estimate combines the gradient of the loss at the test and training points with the Hessian (the matrix of second derivatives, which describes the curvature of the training loss). The output ranks training examples as helpful or harmful for that prediction; because the theory assumes a smooth, convex loss, for deep networks the ranking is approximate, pointing to examples worth inspecting for mislabelled or unrepresentative cases rather than proving why the model erred. In a bias-diagnosis use, the rejections of a group already known from a separate check to be rejected more often are explained one by one, to find the training records that drive them.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital analytics team finds that its readmission model misclassifies many children. For a misclassified child, influence functions single out a handful of paediatric training records with far more influence than any others, showing that the training data holds very few children. The team collects more paediatric data before deciding whether the model can be used on that group.

An email-security team asks why its spam filter blocked a legitimate supplier invoice. It lists the training emails with the most influence on that decision, finds near-duplicate phishing messages with a similar layout, and decides whether to relabel, remove or down-weight them before retraining the filter.

A bank's model-risk team has found, from a separate check of approval rates by group, that applicants from one protected group are rejected more often. It takes a sample of that group's rejected applications and lists, for each, the training loans with the greatest influence on the rejection. It reviews whether those records are historical rejections made under discontinued underwriting rules or by branches with a known bias, and decides whether to remove or re-weight them.

limitations.description: Exact influence needs the inverse of the Hessian, which is out of reach for networks with millions of parameters. Implementations approximate it with Hessian-vector products or block-diagonal and low-rank forms, which still costs extra passes over the training data for every prediction explained and adds error. Plan to explain a sample of decisions, not all of them.

Needs the full training set, the loss function and parameters at or near a minimum of the training loss. A model delivered as an API or a finished file, or trained on data the assessor cannot see, cannot be examined. For models that are early-stopped or not trained to a minimum, the paper adds a damping term to the Hessian, one more setting that can change the ranking.

The derivation assumes a convex, twice-differentiable loss. On a non-convex CNN the paper still found a 0.86 correlation with actual retraining, but a larger study found estimates often erroneous for deeper networks and dependent on architecture, weight decay and the test point (Basu et al., 2020). Check the estimates against real retraining on a few examples before relying on them.

Losses with kinks, such as the hinge loss of a support vector machine, break the method. In the paper, influence computed on the unsmoothed hinge loss considerably overestimated the effect of removal, and a smooth approximation of the loss was needed. Check that the loss is smooth for the model in hand, or smooth it for the calculation.

sample_claims.text: The training records most influential for the readmission model's errors on paediatric patients have been identified with influence functions and reviewed by a clinical data steward
No training record among the ten most influential for any audited declined application is a known data-entry or labelling error

For each false positive in the spam filter's audit sample, the ten most influential training emails were reviewed and the cause of the error, mislabelled or unrepresentative training data, was recorded
The training records most influential for the audited protected-group rejections were reviewed, and none comes from underwriting rules since withdrawn or from branches with a documented bias

name: Contrastive Explanation Method
description: The Contrastive Explanation Method (CEM) explains one prediction of a classifier, such as a neural network, by describing what is present and what is absent in the input. A pertinent positive is the smallest set of features already present that is enough for the model to give the same prediction. A pertinent negative is the smallest set of features not currently present that would change the prediction to a different class if they were added. CEM finds both by solving an optimisation problem that searches for the smallest change to the input, and it can use an autoencoder (a model trained to reconstruct realistic inputs) to keep the changed inputs realistic. An explanation reads like 'this digit is a 3 because these strokes are present and because a short bar at the top is absent', since adding that bar would make it a 5.

example_use_cases.description: A procurement team uses a neural-network model that rates invoices as low, medium or high risk. For a high-risk invoice, the pertinent positives are the few triggered events that are enough for that rating, such as a large amount and a vendor with only a PO box. The pertinent negatives are events that did not occur but would lower the rating if they had, such as the vendor being registered. Reviewers check both before blocking payment.

A clinician reviews a decision-support model that suggests flu rather than pneumonia for a patient. The pertinent positives are the findings that are enough for that suggestion, such as cough, cold and fever. The pertinent negatives are findings that are absent but would move the suggestion to pneumonia if present, such as sputum and chills. The clinician compares both with their own reasoning to judge whether the model weighs the right findings.

A council uses a model to screen applications for housing support. When an application is declined, the pertinent negatives show which missing items, such as proof of tenancy, would have changed the outcome if present. A caseworker checks that each item is something the applicant can provide, then includes it in the decision notice.

limitations.description: Each explanation needs its own optimisation run for a single instance, so explaining many decisions is slow. Models whose gradients cannot be accessed need numerical gradient estimates, which slows it further.

Several settings shape the result, including how strongly the search favours small changes, how confident the model must be in the new class, and whether an autoencoder is used. Different settings can give different pertinent positives and negatives for the same instance, so they need checking with someone who knows the domain.

Changed inputs can be unrealistic. Without an autoencoder trained on good-quality data, a pertinent negative may describe an input that could never occur, so the explanation says little about real cases. Where data is scarce or poor, a good autoencoder may not be possible.

Absence has to be defined by the user. CEM adds or removes features relative to a value that stands for no signal, such as a blank pixel, and a poor choice gives meaningless pertinent negatives. This is natural for images and binary indicators, and needs domain judgement for continuous or categorical tabular data.

A pertinent negative is the smallest change the model responds to, not advice a person can act on. It may involve a feature that cannot be changed, such as age, and nothing in the method checks that the change is feasible. It is most useful when the two classes are close; if they are very different, there can be too many pertinent negatives to read.

sample_claims.text: For the invoices the risk model rates high, compliance reviewers judge that the pertinent positives are sufficient grounds for the rating and the pertinent negatives are events that would lower it.
For each flagged patient record, the pertinent positives and negatives match the findings clinicians use to tell the model's diagnosis from the nearest alternative.
On the instances tested, keeping only the pertinent positive leaves the model's prediction unchanged, and adding the pertinent negative changes it to a different class.
Each applicant declined for credit is told which absent factors, if present, would have changed the model's decision, and a reviewer has confirmed that each is something the applicant could change.
Caseworkers can tell an applicant which missing information, if provided, would change the eligibility model's outcome for that application.

name: ANCHOR
description: ANCHOR generates high-precision if-then rules that explain individual predictions by identifying the minimal set of feature conditions that guarantee a specific prediction with high confidence. It searches for 'anchor' conditions (e.g., 'age > 30 AND income < £50k') that ensure the model gives the same prediction at least 95% of the time when those conditions are met. This creates human-readable rules that users can trust as sufficient conditions for understanding why a particular decision was made.

example_use_cases.description: Explaining loan application decisions with rules like 'IF credit_score > 650 AND debt_ratio < 0.4 THEN approval = 95% likely', giving applicants clear, actionable conditions they can understand and potentially improve.

Generating diagnostic rules for medical predictions such as 'IF fever > 38.5°C AND white_blood_cells > 12,000 THEN infection = 92% likely', helping clinicians validate automated diagnoses with trusted clinical indicators.

Creating transparent hiring decisions with rules like 'IF experience >= 3_years AND degree = relevant THEN hire = 89% likely', providing clear justification for recruitment decisions that can be audited for fairness.

limitations.description: Limited to local explanations for individual instances, cannot provide global insights about overall model behaviour.
Requires discretisation of continuous features, which can lose important nuanced information and create arbitrary thresholds.
May fail to find suitable anchor rules if precision requirements are too strict or if the prediction space is highly complex.
Computationally expensive as it requires extensive sampling to validate rule precision, especially for high-dimensional data.

sample_claims.text: The model's individual predictions are supported by verifiable sufficient conditions with quantified confidence guarantees
The lending system provides loan applicants with specific, actionable conditions that guarantee approval with stated probability
The diagnostic system's recommendations are justified by minimal sets of clinical indicators that ensure the decision under specified conditions
The hiring decision criteria are documented as precise if-then rules with empirically validated confidence bounds
The fraud detection system identifies sufficient feature combinations that reliably predict flagged transactions with quantified precision

name: RuleFit
description: RuleFit creates interpretable surrogate models that can explain complex black-box models or serve as interpretable alternatives. It works by learning a sparse linear model that combines automatically extracted decision rules with original features. The technique first builds tree ensembles to generate candidate rules, then uses LASSO regression to select the most important rules and features. The resulting model provides global explanations through human-readable rules (e.g., 'IF age > 50 AND income < 30k THEN ...') combined with linear feature weights, making complex model behaviour transparent and auditable.

example_use_cases.description: Building customer churn prediction models with rules like 'IF contract_length < 12_months AND support_calls > 5 THEN churn_risk = high', allowing marketing teams to understand and act on the key drivers of customer attrition.

Creating credit scoring models that combine traditional linear factors (income, age) with interpretable rules (IF recent_missed_payments = 0 AND account_age > 2_years THEN creditworthy), providing transparent lending decisions.

Developing regulatory-compliant medical diagnosis models where treatment recommendations combine clinical measurements with clear decision rules (IF blood_pressure > 140 AND diabetes = true THEN high_risk), enabling audit trails for healthcare decisions.

limitations.description: Can generate large numbers of rules even with regularisation, potentially overwhelming users and reducing practical interpretability.
Performance may be inferior to complex ensemble methods when rule complexity is constrained for interpretability.
Rule extraction quality depends heavily on the underlying tree ensemble, which may miss important feature interactions if not properly configured.
Requires careful hyperparameter tuning to balance between model complexity and interpretability, with no universal optimal setting.

sample_claims.text: The credit risk model's decision logic is expressible as a sparse set of interpretable if-then rules combined with linear feature weights
The patient risk stratification system's predictions are traceable to explicit clinical decision rules that mirror diagnostic reasoning patterns
The fraud detection model identifies risk through comprehensible rules that stakeholders can validate against domain knowledge
The customer churn prediction system's global behavior is approximated by a small number of actionable business rules rather than opaque feature interactions
The regulatory compliance model combines human-readable decision boundaries with weighted factors in a single auditable representation

name: Monte Carlo Dropout
description: Monte Carlo dropout estimates how uncertain a neural network is about each prediction. Dropout randomly switches off some of the network's units and is normally used only in training, but here it stays on at prediction time. Each forward pass (one run of an input through the network) therefore uses a different random pattern of units, and the input is run through typically tens to a hundred times. The average gives the prediction, and the spread across runs is read as epistemic uncertainty, meaning uncertainty from the model's limited knowledge rather than noise in the data. The method approximates Bayesian inference, but the spread is an estimate whose reliability should be checked against held-out errors.

example_use_cases.description: Quantifying diagnostic uncertainty in medical imaging models by running 50+ Monte Carlo forward passes to detect when a chest X-ray classification is highly uncertain, prompting radiologist review for borderline cases.

An autonomous-driving team replays recorded camera footage through its object detector with dropout left on, and finds the scenes (night rain, unusual vehicles) where detections vary most between passes. It uses them to decide what data to collect and which scenarios to add to simulation testing.

A grid operator's demand-forecasting network, trained with dropout, is run 100 times each morning. Days on which the forecasts spread beyond the planners' tolerance are sent for human review before reserve capacity is booked.

limitations.description: The spread across passes reflects uncertainty about the model's parameters, not noise in the data that varies from input to input. An input in a very noisy region can still show a narrow spread, so a narrow spread does not mean the outcome is predictable.

Each prediction needs many forward passes, typically 50 to 100, so inference costs that many times more compute, and too few passes make the spread itself unstable. The passes can run in parallel, which limits added delay but not total compute, so real-time or edge deployments with tight budgets may not afford it.

The network must have been trained with dropout, and the derivation assumes it sits before every weight layer. A model trained without dropout has to be retrained, so the technique is often unavailable for models already built or bought in.

The size of the spread depends on the dropout probability and weight decay, which the developer sets or tunes on validation data rather than learns from the data. The uncertainty scale is partly a design choice and needs checking against held-out errors.

The spread is an approximation, and its behaviour depends on the architecture. In the original paper's regression experiments, uncertainty kept growing away from the training data with ReLU activations but stayed bounded with TanH, so a narrow spread on unfamiliar inputs is not proof of familiarity.

sample_claims.text: On held-out chest X-ray cases, the classifier's error rate among the 10% of cases with the highest Monte Carlo dropout uncertainty is at least double its error rate on the remaining cases.
The fraud model's Monte Carlo dropout variance is higher on transaction types held out of training than on types it was trained on, in a held-out check run before deployment.
Object detections flagged as high-uncertainty by Monte Carlo dropout are missed or mislabelled more often than unflagged detections when recorded driving scenes are replayed offline.

name: Out-of-Distribution Detector for Neural Networks
description: ODIN (Out-of-Distribution Detector for Neural Networks) flags inputs that look unlike the data a neural network classifier was trained on, and it works on an already trained network without retraining it. A classifier reports a confidence score, the highest probability it gives to any class, but that score is often high even for unfamiliar inputs. ODIN adjusts the score in two ways so that familiar and unfamiliar inputs separate better. It divides the classifier's raw output scores by a large constant, called the temperature, before turning them into probabilities, and it nudges the input slightly in the direction that raises the score, which lifts familiar inputs more than unfamiliar ones. An input whose adjusted score falls below a chosen threshold is flagged as out-of-distribution, so its prediction can be withheld or referred for review.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital screens each chest X-ray with ODIN before the diagnostic classifier's result is shown. Scans that are not chest X-rays, or that carry heavy artefacts, are flagged for human review instead of receiving a confident diagnosis, and the false positive rate is measured on a sample of such scans first.

An automated driving team scores each camera frame with ODIN and passes frames below the threshold to a fallback routine, such as slowing the vehicle and requesting remote assistance. The team measures how many unfamiliar frames, such as sensor faults or unusual scenes, are wrongly accepted before relying on the detector.

limitations.description: Temperature and perturbation size are tuned on a validation set that includes out-of-distribution examples, so some representative unfamiliar data is needed before deployment. The paper found settings transferred reasonably between validation sets, but only on image benchmarks.

Detection gets harder as unfamiliar inputs resemble the training data. In the original paper, at 95% acceptance of familiar images, the share of unfamiliar natural images wrongly accepted rose from at most about 11% with a 10-class training set to between 19% and 58% with a 100-class one, so performance must be measured on the deployment's own data.
Not designed to resist inputs deliberately crafted to look in-distribution, and the original paper does not evaluate adversarial evasion, so it gives no protection against a deliberate attacker.
Needs access to the network's gradients to compute the input perturbation, so it cannot be applied to a model that is reachable only through an API.
Each input needs at least one extra forward pass and one backward pass before the final scoring pass, which can matter for real-time or high-volume use.

sample_claims.text: Camera frames that fall outside the perception network's training distribution, such as those from a sensor fault, are flagged before the planner uses the network's output.
Scans that are not of the type the diagnostic classifier was trained on are rejected by the out-of-distribution detector instead of receiving a confident diagnosis.
The detector's threshold is set so that 95% of in-distribution validation inputs are accepted, and the share of out-of-distribution test inputs wrongly accepted at that threshold is reported.
Images of unfamiliar part types or from unfamiliar cameras are held for human inspection instead of passing through the automated quality-control classifier.

name: Permutation Tests
description: A permutation test asks how likely an observed result would be if there were no real relationship in the data. The tester shuffles the data many times in a way that breaks the relationship under test, recalculates the metric each time, and takes the p-value as the share of shuffled results at least as extreme as the real one. Shuffling the outcome labels and retraining tests whether a classifier's accuracy beats chance, and shuffling group membership tests whether a gap between groups in the rate of decisions, such as approvals, is larger than chance would produce. A restricted variant, Ojala and Garriga's second test, shuffles each feature's values separately within each class, which keeps every feature's own spread but breaks the relationships between features, so a classifier that makes significantly fewer errors on the real data than on the shuffled copies is using those relationships. The test needs no assumption about the shape of the data's distribution, but a small p-value does not show that an effect is large, important or causal.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital research group trains a classifier on 80 patients with thousands of gene-expression measurements. With so few cases, a good cross-validated accuracy could be luck, so it repeats the whole training and testing procedure on thousands of label-shuffled copies and reports the result only if it beats nearly all of them.

A council analytics team replacing a case-prioritisation model checks whether the new model's higher accuracy on the same test cases could be chance. It randomly swaps the two models' predictions case by case 10,000 times, recomputes the gap each time, and switches only if the real gap is larger than nearly all of the shuffled ones.

A bank's model-risk team sees a higher approval rate for one applicant group than another in a loan model's decisions. Before escalating, it shuffles group membership across applicants thousands of times and recomputes the gap, to test whether a gap this large could arise by chance. A significant gap prompts a fuller review but does not by itself show unlawful discrimination.

A cardiology team using a gradient-boosted model to flag high blood pressure expects height and weight to matter together, not only alone. It shuffles each feature within each outcome class 1,000 times and tests at the 5% level whether the model errs less on the real data, to decide if a simpler model treating features separately would do. A non-significant result means either the features are unrelated within classes or the model ignores the relationship.

limitations.description: Each permutation needs the metric recalculated, and a model may need retraining every time, so thousands of permutations of a large model can be expensive. Stricter thresholds need more permutations, because the smallest possible p-value is 1 divided by the number of permutations plus one, and repeated runs can disagree near the threshold.

Assumes exchangeability of observations under the null hypothesis, which may be violated in time series or hierarchical data structures, where simple shuffling gives p-values that are too small or too large.

A significant result shows that the data are unlikely under the stated null, such as 'features and labels are independent'. It does not show that the effect is large, important or causal, and shuffling cannot rule out a confounder or an artefact of how the data were collected.

Testing many features or groups at once produces some false positives by chance, so the p-values need correcting, for example with a false discovery rate procedure. Without that, a feature-by-feature test over many features will flag some that are only noise.

What is shuffled defines the question answered. Shuffling labels tests whether features and labels are related at all, while shuffling features within classes tests whether a classifier uses dependencies between features. The wrong scheme answers a different question from the one the assurance claim needs.

sample_claims.text: The classifier's accuracy on the patient cohort exceeds what label-shuffled copies of the same data produce, at the 1% significance level
The new case-prioritisation model's accuracy advantage over the current model is larger than random swapping of their predictions produces, at the 5% significance level

The gap in approval rates between the two applicant groups is larger than random reassignment of group membership produces, at the 5% significance level, and is reported as a disparity to investigate, not as evidence of discrimination
On the validation dataset, the blood-pressure model's accuracy depends on the relationship between height and weight, not only on each taken alone, at the 5% significance level

name: Demographic Parity Assessment
description: Demographic Parity Assessment evaluates whether a model produces equal positive prediction rates across different demographic groups, regardless of underlying differences in qualifications or base rates. It quantifies fairness using metrics like Statistical Parity Difference (the absolute difference in positive outcome rates between groups) or Disparate Impact ratio (the ratio of positive rates). Unlike techniques that modify data or models, this is purely a measurement approach that highlights when protected groups receive favourable outcomes at different rates, helping organisations identify and document potential discrimination.

example_use_cases.description: Evaluating credit approval algorithms by calculating that loan approval rates for different racial groups must be within 20% of each other (0.8 disparate impact ratio), ensuring compliance with anti-discrimination regulations.

Monitoring hiring platforms by measuring that job recommendation rates for male vs female candidates remain statistically equivalent (Statistical Parity Difference < 0.05), preventing systemic gender bias in career opportunities.
Auditing healthcare triage systems to verify that urgent care assignment rates are equal across ethnic groups, ensuring that automated medical prioritisation doesn't disadvantage minority patients.

limitations.description: Purely observational - identifies discrimination but doesn't provide solutions for remediation or bias mitigation.
May penalise models for legitimate differences in base rates between groups, potentially forcing artificial equality where none should exist.
Can conflict with individual fairness principles, where similarly qualified individuals might receive different treatment to achieve group parity.
Doesn't account for quality of outcomes or consider whether equal rates are actually desirable given different group needs or preferences.

sample_claims.text: The recruitment system's job offer rates are statistically equivalent across gender groups
The automated lending platform produces approval decisions at equal rates for all ethnic demographics
The medical referral system assigns specialist appointments at consistent rates across patient age groups
The benefits allocation system provides positive outcomes at equal rates across protected demographic categories
The admissions algorithm produces acceptance decisions at statistically indistinguishable rates for applicants from different socioeconomic backgrounds

name: Adversarial Debiasing
description: Adversarial debiasing reduces bias by training models using a competitive adversarial setup, similar to Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). The technique involves two neural networks: a predictor that learns to make accurate predictions on the main task, and an adversary (bias detector) that attempts to predict protected attributes (such as race, gender, or age) from the predictor's internal representations. Through adversarial training, the predictor learns to produce representations that retain predictive power for the main task whilst being uninformative about protected characteristics, thereby reducing discriminatory bias.

example_use_cases.description: Training a resume screening model for a technology company that evaluates candidates based on skills and experience whilst preventing the internal representations from encoding gender or ethnicity information, ensuring hiring decisions cannot be influenced by protected characteristics even indirectly through correlated features.

Developing a credit scoring model for loan approvals that accurately predicts default risk whilst ensuring the model's internal features cannot be used to infer applicants' race or age, thereby preventing discriminatory lending practices whilst maintaining predictive accuracy.

Creating a medical diagnosis model that makes accurate predictions about patient conditions whilst ensuring that the learned representations cannot reveal sensitive demographic information like gender or ethnicity, protecting patient privacy whilst maintaining clinical effectiveness.

limitations.description: Significantly more complex to implement than standard models, requiring expertise in adversarial training techniques and careful architecture design for both predictor and adversary networks.
Requires careful hyperparameter tuning to balance the competing objectives of task performance and bias mitigation, as overly strong adversarial training can harm predictive accuracy.

Effectiveness heavily depends on the quality and design of the adversary network - a weak adversary may fail to detect subtle biases, whilst an overly strong adversary may eliminate useful information.
Training can be unstable and may suffer from convergence issues common to adversarial training, requiring careful learning rate scheduling and regularisation techniques.
Provides no formal guarantees about bias elimination and may not prevent all forms of discrimination, particularly when protected attributes can be inferred from other available features.

sample_claims.text: The model's internal representations cannot be used to infer protected characteristics of individuals
The hiring system's learned features maintain predictive power for job suitability whilst being statistically independent of candidate gender
The credit scoring model's intermediate layers do not encode information about applicants' race or ethnicity
The diagnostic system achieves equitable performance across patient demographics without encoding sensitive attributes in its feature representations
The facial recognition model's hidden representations are uninformative about protected characteristics whilst preserving identification accuracy

name: Counterfactual Fairness Assessment
description: Counterfactual Fairness Assessment tests a model against the criterion of Kusner et al. (2017): a model is counterfactually fair if each individual's prediction would have had the same distribution had their protected attribute, such as race or sex, been different, with everything that attribute causes changed accordingly. The assessor first writes down a causal model, a graph of which variables cause which, covering the protected attribute, the model's inputs and unobserved background factors, and fits its equations to data. For each individual, the fitted model is used to infer the background factors from what was observed (abduction), set the protected attribute to another value (action) and recompute every input the attribute influences (prediction), giving a counterfactual version of that person. The model under test is run on the factual and counterfactual inputs, and the gap between the two predictions, per individual or as a distance between the two prediction distributions, is the evidence: distributions that lie on top of each other indicate counterfactual fairness under the assumed causal model. Every causal effect of the attribute counts as unfair, including effects that run through inputs it influences, such as test scores, which is what separates this criterion from versions that allow some pathways.

example_use_cases.description: A law school's admissions office uses a model to predict first-year grades from entrance-test scores and undergraduate grades. Its analysts build a causal model in which race and sex influence both inputs alongside an unobserved knowledge factor, fit it to past cohorts, and compare each applicant's predicted grade under actual and counterfactual race. A systematic shift shows that leaving race out of the inputs did not make the model counterfactually fair.

A credit risk team, working with economists, specifies a causal graph in which an applicant's ethnicity affects income and neighbourhood but not repayment behaviour directly, fits it to its applicant data, and checks whether the approval model's scores change for the counterfactual applicants. The result goes to the model risk committee together with the graph, because the conclusion holds only under that graph.

A public employment service reviewing a model that predicts job-seekers' risk of long-term unemployment from education and work history specifies, with labour-market researchers, how sex and migration background influence those inputs. It tests whether individual risk scores would change under counterfactual sex or migration background before the scores are used to allocate support.

limitations.description: The verdict rests on a causal model that cannot be checked against data: Kusner et al. note that counterfactual assumptions are generally unfalsifiable, even with experimental data, and should be treated as provisional. Different plausible graphs can give different verdicts, so a result is only as credible as the graph reported with it, and testing alternative graphs is part of the assessment.

A common cause left out of the graph, such as school quality affecting both test scores and later grades, biases the counterfactuals without any warning sign. Kilbertus et al. (2019) show that counterfactual fairness is sensitive to such unmeasured confounding and give tools to bound the effect for additive noise models, which adds a further analysis to do.

Every effect of the attribute counts as unfair, so a model that legitimately uses an input the attribute influences fails the test. Kusner et al. note that in practice few observed variables are unaffected by the attribute. Where some pathways are acceptable, for example where qualifications differ for reasons a decision may properly reflect, this criterion is stricter than the decision calls for.

Computing individual counterfactuals requires a fitted probabilistic model of the unobserved background factors; the original study fitted it in Stan, and DoWhy's counterfactual function needs mechanisms with additive noise and supports only continuous variables. With categorical inputs, many variables or unstructured data such as text and images, the assessment becomes hard to run or yields a spread of counterfactuals rather than one.

The counterfactual people are simulated by the fitted causal model, not observed. If its equations fit the data poorly or miss interactions, the counterfactual inputs are implausible and the measured gap reflects the causal model's errors as much as the predictor's; DoWhy's documentation notes counterfactual estimates are approximate for this reason.

sample_claims.text: Under the causal model agreed with the admissions committee, each applicant's predicted first-year grade has the same distribution under their actual and counterfactual race.
Under the documented causal graph linking ethnicity, income and neighbourhood, the credit model's approval scores do not change when applicants' ethnicity is counterfactually altered.

The unemployment-risk model's individual scores are unchanged under counterfactual sex and migration background, given the causal model reviewed by labour-market researchers, and the sensitivity of that result to unmeasured confounding has been bounded.

name: Causal Discrimination Testing
description: Causal discrimination testing checks whether a system gives different outputs to otherwise identical inputs because of a protected attribute, by changing only that attribute, or a name, term or other proxy that signals it, and measuring how often or how much the output changes. Galhotra, Brun and Meliou (2017), who called the approach fairness testing, generate inputs from a description of the valid input fields, make copies of each that differ only in the protected attribute (for example, recorded sex), run them all through the system as a black box, and report the causal discrimination score: the share of inputs whose decision changes, sampled until it is known within a chosen margin of error and confidence level. For text, the same test substitutes identity terms or names in otherwise unchanged sentences, such as one religion or ethnicity for another, and reports the average change in the model's score across the substitutions, which Garg et al. (2019) call the counterfactual token fairness gap. Because every other part of the input is held fixed, the test needs no model of how the attribute influences other variables: it measures whether the system itself responds to the attribute, or to the chosen proxy. The output is a score per attribute and, if the tester logs them, the input pairs whose outputs differed.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's model validation team tests a credit-approval model before release. For a sample of last year's applications it changes only the applicant's recorded sex, and separately their marital status, re-scores each pair, and reports the share of decisions that flip with a confidence interval, against a release threshold agreed with the compliance function.

A trust-and-safety team checks a toxicity classifier used to hold comments for review by substituting identity terms such as 'gay', 'Muslim' or 'Black' across a set of non-toxic comments. It measures the average change in toxicity score for each term and flags any term whose substitution pushes benign comments over the moderation threshold.

An HR technology supplier tests its CV-ranking service before a client deploys it, by submitting the same CVs under first names and surnames associated with different ethnicities and genders and reporting how often each candidate's rank or shortlisting changes.

A hospital's AI assurance lead tests a symptom-triage assistant with clinical vignettes that differ only in the patient's stated ethnicity. Clinicians first mark which vignettes should be unaffected by ethnicity, and only those pairs count as failures when the urgency rating changes.

limitations.description: Holding every other input fixed measures only the system's direct response to the attribute or proxy. It does not follow through the effects the attribute has on other inputs, such as career breaks on an employment history. Garg et al. note that token substitution is more limited than counterfactual fairness defined on a causal model. Where those downstream effects matter, a clean result does not show that individuals were treated fairly.

The test covers only what is perturbed. Unlisted identity terms, unperturbed proxies and multi-word references go undetected, as does discrimination that appears only when attributes change together: Galhotra et al. measured 11.2% for gender alone but 77.2% for gender, marital status and race together. Garg et al. found mitigation for listed terms generalised much less to held-out terms. A pass covers only the perturbations tried, and the list needs domain review.

Generated inputs may be unrealistic. Themis draws inputs uniformly from the input schema, so the score covers combinations that never occur in practice. Testing real inputs or an existing test suite avoids that, but the score is then only as representative as that set. Galhotra et al. note that Themis computes no confidence level for it, and an interval from a random sample of real cases covers sampling error only.

Not every substitution should leave the output unchanged. Garg et al. give 'That's so gay' versus 'That's so straight' as a pair a toxicity model may rightly score differently, and clinical risk can legitimately depend on sex. Without a judgement about which pairs must match, the test raises false alarms or, if such pairs are excluded wholesale, hides real failures.

A model can pass and still produce very different outcome or error rates across groups, because the test asks only whether changing the attribute changes the output, not whether outcomes are equal. Galhotra et al. distinguish this causal discrimination from group discrimination, and Garg et al. note that a text classifier can satisfy counterfactual fairness while completely failing equality of odds, so it does not replace group metrics.

sample_claims.text: Changing only an applicant's recorded sex changes the credit model's decision for fewer than 0.5% of last year's applications (upper limit of a 95% confidence interval from a random sample of them).
Substituting any listed identity term into non-toxic comments changes the moderation classifier's toxicity score by less than 0.05 on average.
Swapping names associated with different ethnicities and genders on otherwise identical CVs changes a CV's shortlisting outcome in fewer than 1% of the pairs tested.
The triage assistant's urgency rating changes in fewer than 1% of the vignette pairs that clinicians judged should be unaffected by the patient's stated ethnicity.

name: GAN-Based Tabular Synthetic Data
description: Generates synthetic tabular datasets using Generative Adversarial Networks, most commonly through architectures such as CTGAN (Conditional Tabular GAN) and TVAE (Triplet-based Variational Autoencoder). These models learn the joint distribution of mixed-type columns — continuous, discrete, and categorical — by training a generator and discriminator in an adversarial framework, with mode-specific normalisation to handle multimodal continuous distributions and training-by-sampling to address class imbalance. The resulting synthetic tables aim to preserve statistical relationships, correlations, and marginal distributions of the original data whilst containing no real records, supporting privacy-preserving data sharing, model development on sensitive datasets, and augmentation of limited training data.

example_use_cases.description: Generating synthetic patient records from hospital databases using CTGAN to enable multi-institution collaborative research on treatment outcomes without sharing identifiable health data across organisational boundaries.

Augmenting a limited fraud detection training set by generating synthetic fraudulent transaction records that preserve the statistical characteristics of rare fraud patterns, improving model recall on underrepresented fraud types.

Creating balanced synthetic datasets for credit scoring by generating additional records for underrepresented demographic groups, enabling fairness testing across protected characteristics without collecting new sensitive data.

limitations.description: Training instability inherent to GAN architectures (mode collapse, vanishing gradients) can result in synthetic data that fails to capture the full diversity of the original distribution, particularly for rare categories or tail distributions.
Requires substantial computational resources and hyperparameter tuning, with training times scaling poorly for datasets with many columns or complex inter-column dependencies.

Privacy guarantees are not inherent — without additional mechanisms like differential privacy, GAN-generated data may leak information about training records through memorisation or membership inference attacks.
Performance degrades significantly on datasets with high cardinality categorical columns, complex temporal dependencies, or relational structures across multiple tables.

sample_claims.text: The synthetic patient dataset generated by CTGAN preserves statistical correlations between clinical variables whilst containing no records traceable to real patients
The augmented training dataset includes GAN-generated records for underrepresented demographic groups, achieving balanced representation across all protected characteristics
The fraud detection model has been validated on GAN-generated synthetic transaction data that preserves the statistical distribution of rare fraud patterns from the original dataset

name: Statistical Oversampling Methods
description: A family of data augmentation techniques that generate synthetic minority-class examples through geometric interpolation in feature space, addressing class imbalance problems that degrade classifier performance on underrepresented groups. The foundational method, SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique), creates new instances by interpolating between existing minority samples and their k-nearest neighbours. Extensions include Borderline-SMOTE (focusing generation near decision boundaries), ADASYN (adaptively weighting harder-to-learn instances), and SVMSMOTE (using support vectors to guide generation). These methods operate directly on feature vectors without requiring neural network training, making them computationally lightweight and applicable to any tabular classification task.

example_use_cases.description: Applying SMOTE to oversample underrepresented ethnic groups in a loan approval training dataset, ensuring the classifier has sufficient examples from each demographic group to learn fair decision boundaries.
Using ADASYN to generate synthetic examples of rare manufacturing defect types, improving the reliability of quality control classifiers on edge cases that occur in fewer than 1% of production runs.

Applying Borderline-SMOTE to augment minority-class examples near the decision boundary in a medical diagnosis task, reducing false-negative rates for rare conditions without collecting additional patient data.

Oversampling underrepresented protected groups in a hiring dataset to enable equitable evaluation of candidates across gender and ethnicity, ensuring the model does not simply learn to predict the majority class.

limitations.description: Interpolation in feature space can generate synthetic instances that fall in regions of the feature space not occupied by the true data distribution, introducing noise or unrealistic combinations — particularly problematic for high-dimensional data.
Does not address the root cause of class imbalance (e.g. data collection bias, structural underrepresentation) and may mask rather than resolve underlying fairness issues in the data pipeline.
Performance degrades on high-dimensional datasets where the nearest-neighbour assumption breaks down, and oversampling in such spaces can amplify noise dimensions without improving classification.

Assumes the minority class forms coherent clusters in feature space; when minority examples are scattered or overlap heavily with majority-class regions, interpolation produces ambiguous or mislabelled synthetic samples.

sample_claims.text: The training dataset has been balanced using SMOTE oversampling to ensure the classifier has sufficient representation of all demographic groups for equitable decision-making
The rare defect classifier has been trained on an ADASYN-augmented dataset that maintains the original feature distributions whilst ensuring adequate representation of all defect categories

The diagnostic model performance on rare conditions has been improved through Borderline-SMOTE augmentation targeting samples near the decision boundary, without introducing fabricated clinical relationships

name: Sequential CART Synthesis
description: Sequential CART synthesis creates an artificial copy of a confidential microdata set (records about individual people or organisations) that can be released in place of the real data, in the form used by the synthpop package for R. Variables are synthesised one at a time in a chosen order: the first is generated by sampling with replacement from its observed values, and for each later variable a classification or regression tree (CART) is fitted on the real data to predict it from the variables earlier in the order. Each synthetic record is passed down that tree using its already-synthesised values, and the new value is copied from a randomly chosen real record in the leaf it reaches, so the joint distribution of the data is rebuilt as a chain of conditional distributions. Disclosure risk is limited by setting a minimum leaf size, smoothing synthesised continuous values and removing synthetic records that reproduce unique real ones, and several synthetic copies can be released so that analysts can allow for the extra uncertainty that synthesis adds.

example_use_cases.description: A national longitudinal study that links census returns to administrative records such as births, deaths and cancer registrations for a sample of the population cannot let approved researchers take the data off site. Its support team runs CART synthesis to produce a bespoke synthetic extract for each project, so researchers can explore the data and write and test their analysis code at their own institution before the final model is run on the real data in the secure setting.

A hospital trust wants a university team to develop a readmission model without receiving patient records. It releases a CART-synthesised copy of the admissions table with a minimum leaf size of ten and kernel smoothing of continuous values, removes any synthetic record that matches a unique real patient on age, sex and postcode district, and runs a disclosure-risk assessment before release.

A national statistics office publishes a synthetic teaching file of its labour force survey for university courses, generated by sequential CART synthesis with the variable order and minimum leaf sizes chosen with subject experts, and labels every record as synthetic so that no reader mistakes a row for a real respondent.

limitations.description: It gives no formal privacy guarantee. No synthetic record is a real person, but trees can reproduce rare combinations and extreme values, and an intruder who knows that a real record holds the largest value of a variable can bound it from the synthetic maximum. Risk must be measured for each release and reduced with larger leaves, smoothing and removal of unique matches, each of which costs analytical value.

Relationships the trees miss disappear from the synthetic data. A tree grown from few records may never split on a variable that matters, so the synthetic data show no association where the real data have one; in the method's original evaluation a regression coefficient for sex was attenuated to zero in this way. Small subgroups and weak effects are the most exposed.

Results depend on the order in which variables are synthesised and on which earlier variables predict each later one. A careless order can produce impossible combinations, such as a detailed category that contradicts the summary variable derived from it, so detailed variables should be synthesised before derived ones and the output checked for inconsistencies.

Synthetic data cannot reproduce every analysis of the real data. Analyses the synthesiser did not plan for may give different answers, so a release should state which analyses it supports, and users should confirm key findings on the real data, for example through a verification service or secure access.

sample_claims.text: The research extract released to the project team was generated by sequential CART synthesis with a minimum leaf size of ten and smoothing of continuous variables, and contains no record that reproduces a unique combination in the source data.

No confidential microdata left the secure environment during model development: external researchers wrote and tested their code on a synthetic extract, and only the final approved model was run on the real data.
A disclosure-risk assessment of the synthetic admissions table found no synthetic record matching a unique real patient on the agreed identifying variables.

name: Federated Learning
description: Federated learning enables collaborative model training across multiple distributed parties (devices, organisations, or data centres) without requiring centralised data sharing. Participants train models locally on their private datasets and only share model updates (gradients, weights, or aggregated statistics) with a central coordinator. This distributed approach serves multiple purposes: preserving data privacy and sovereignty, reducing communication costs, enabling learning from diverse data sources, improving model robustness through heterogeneous training, and facilitating compliance with data protection regulations whilst maintaining model performance comparable to centralised training.

example_use_cases.description: Developing a smartphone keyboard prediction model by learning from users' typing patterns without their text ever leaving their devices, enabling personalised predictions whilst maintaining complete data privacy.

Training a medical diagnosis model across multiple hospitals without sharing patient records, ensuring model robustness by learning from diverse patient populations and clinical practices across different institutions.

limitations.description: Communication overhead can be substantial, especially with frequent model updates and large models, potentially limiting scalability and increasing training time compared to centralised approaches.

Statistical heterogeneity across participants (non-IID data distributions) can lead to training instability, slower convergence, and reduced model performance compared to centralised training on pooled data.
System heterogeneity in computational capabilities, network connectivity, and availability of participating devices can create bottlenecks and introduce bias towards more capable participants.
Privacy vulnerabilities remain through gradient leakage attacks, model inversion, and membership inference attacks that can potentially reconstruct sensitive information from shared model updates.
Coordination complexity increases with the number of participants, requiring sophisticated aggregation protocols, fault tolerance mechanisms, and secure communication infrastructure.

sample_claims.text: The model training process does not require patient data to leave individual healthcare institutions
The diagnostic model performs reliably despite learning from patient populations with heterogeneous clinical characteristics across multiple sites
The keyboard prediction model learns from user typing patterns without transmitting personal text content to central servers

name: Differential Privacy
description: Differential privacy provides mathematically rigorous privacy protection by adding carefully calibrated random noise to data queries, statistical computations, or machine learning outputs. The technique works by ensuring that the presence or absence of any individual's data has minimal impact on the results - specifically, any query result should be nearly indistinguishable whether or not a particular person's data is included. This is achieved through controlled noise addition that scales with the query's sensitivity and a privacy budget (epsilon) that quantifies the privacy-utility trade-off. The smaller the epsilon, the more noise is added and the stronger the privacy guarantee, but at the cost of reduced accuracy.

example_use_cases.description: Protecting individual privacy in census data analysis by adding calibrated noise to demographic statistics, ensuring households cannot be re-identified whilst maintaining accurate population insights for policy planning.

Publishing differentially private aggregate statistics about model performance across different demographic groups, enabling transparent bias auditing without exposing sensitive individual prediction details or group membership.

limitations.description: Adding noise inherently reduces the accuracy and utility of results, with stronger privacy guarantees (smaller epsilon values) leading to more significant degradation in data quality.
Setting the privacy budget (epsilon) requires expertise and careful consideration of the privacy-utility trade-off, with no universal guidelines for appropriate values across different applications.
Sequential queries consume the privacy budget cumulatively, potentially requiring careful query planning and potentially prohibiting future analyses once the budget is exhausted.
Implementation complexity is high, requiring deep understanding of sensitivity analysis, noise mechanisms, and composition theorems to avoid inadvertent privacy violations.
May not protect against all privacy attacks, particularly sophisticated adversaries with auxiliary information or when combined with other data sources that could aid re-identification.

sample_claims.text: The census data analysis results remain statistically indistinguishable whether any single household's data is included or excluded
The medical research system's published statistics provide quantified privacy guarantees that bound the maximum disclosure risk for any individual patient
The model performance metrics across demographic groups are accompanied by documented privacy budget allocation and noise parameters
The system's privacy protection level is mathematically bounded and remains effective even under repeated queries within the allocated budget

name: Homomorphic Encryption
description: Homomorphic encryption allows computation on encrypted data without decrypting it first, producing encrypted results that, when decrypted, match the results of performing the same operations on the plaintext. This enables secure outsourced computation where sensitive data remains encrypted throughout processing. By allowing ML operations on encrypted data, it provides strong privacy guarantees for applications involving highly sensitive information.

example_use_cases.description: Enabling a cloud-based medical diagnosis service to process encrypted patient data and return encrypted results without the cloud provider ever accessing actual medical information, ensuring complete patient privacy during outsourced computation.

Protecting ML model intellectual property and confidential inference inputs during cloud deployment by running encrypted inference, ensuring that neither the client sensitive input data nor the server proprietary model weights and architecture are exposed to the cloud provider or the counterparty, enabling secure outsourced inference without requiring mutual trust assumptions.

limitations.description: Extremely computationally expensive, often 100-1000x slower than unencrypted computation, making it impractical for real-time applications or large-scale data processing.
Limited range of operations supported efficiently, with complex operations like divisions, comparisons, and non-polynomial functions being particularly challenging or impossible to implement.
Implementation requires deep cryptographic expertise to avoid security vulnerabilities, choose appropriate parameters, and optimise performance for specific use cases.
Memory and storage requirements are significantly higher than traditional computation, as encrypted data typically requires much more space than plaintext equivalents.
Current fully homomorphic encryption schemes have practical limitations on computation depth before noise accumulation requires expensive bootstrapping operations to refresh ciphertexts.

sample_claims.text: The cloud-based service processes patient data without the service provider ever accessing the underlying medical information
The financial analysis platform maintains data confidentiality throughout all computational operations performed by third-party infrastructure

name: Quantile Regression
description: Quantile regression predicts chosen percentiles of an outcome, such as the 10th, 50th and 90th, rather than only its average. In the classical method a separate model is fitted for each percentile, using a loss that penalises under-prediction and over-prediction unequally. For example, instead of predicting an average house price of £300,000, it can predict that a house of a given size and location has a 10% chance of selling below £250,000 and a 90% chance of selling below £380,000. Comparing the fitted percentiles shows how features affect different parts of the outcome, such as size mattering more for expensive homes than for cheap ones. A low and a high percentile together give a prediction interval (a range expected to contain a new outcome) without assuming the errors are normally distributed, though how often the interval actually contains new outcomes must be checked on held-out data.

example_use_cases.description: Predicting patient recovery times after surgery by fitting the 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles, so clinicians can say 'most patients recover within 2 to 4 weeks, but one in ten takes longer than 8' when planning follow-up care and bed use.

A grid operator extends its wind power forecast with 10th and 90th percentile forecasts, fitted on past forecast errors and weather conditions, and sizes reserve capacity to the 90th percentile of the next-day shortfall rather than to an average error.

A flood-forecasting agency fits high percentiles of river level on rainfall and soil moisture, giving an upper bound that does not assume symmetric errors, and uses it to decide when to issue warnings for extreme events.

limitations.description: Cost grows with the number of quantile levels fitted when, as in the classical method, each level is a separate optimisation, which adds up on large datasets or with complex models.

May produce crossing quantiles without proper constraints, where predicted 90th percentile values are lower than 50th percentile values, creating logically inconsistent and unusable prediction intervals.

Extreme quantiles (for example the 5th or 95th) rest on few observations and, with heavy-tailed outcomes, are noisy and unstable. With small datasets they cannot be estimated reliably, because too few points lie in the tails.

Gives no guarantee that an interval built from two quantiles contains the stated share of new outcomes. Coverage can fall short if the model form is wrong or the data shift, so check it on held-out data before relying on it.

In its classical form each conditional quantile is assumed to be linear in the features. If the true relationship is curved or has interactions, the fitted quantiles are biased, and flexible models that avoid this lose the readable coefficients.

sample_claims.text: The flood forecasting model estimates the specified lower and upper conditional quantiles of river level without imposing a symmetric error distribution, and how often observed levels fall inside them has been checked on held-out events.

The 90th percentile recovery-time forecast exceeds the observed recovery time for at least 90% of patients in the held-out audit sample, so the quoted longest timeframe is not systematically too short.
The wind power forecast's 10th to 90th percentile band contains observed output about 80% of the time on out-of-sample data, in each of the low, medium and high wind-speed ranges.

name: Conformal Prediction
description: Conformal prediction wraps any trained model so that, instead of a single answer, it returns a set of plausible answers (an interval, for a numeric prediction) that contains the true outcome at a chosen rate, such as at least 95% of the time. It first scores, on a calibration set of labelled data kept apart from training, how unusual each known outcome looks given the model's prediction, using a nonconformity score, and for a new case it keeps every candidate answer whose score falls below a threshold taken from those calibration scores. A diagnostic model might then return 'cancer or benign tumour' rather than 'likely cancer', and with a suitable score the sets grow larger where the model is less certain. The guarantee is distribution-free, meaning it assumes nothing about the shape of the data, but it does assume the calibration data and new cases are exchangeable, roughly that they come from the same source in no particular order. It holds on average over all cases, not within each subgroup, unless the calibration is done separately within each predefined group (Mondrian conformal prediction), which needs enough calibration cases in every group.

example_use_cases.description: A medicinal chemistry team screening compounds in silico builds prediction sets of the protein targets each compound may be active against, at 95% coverage. Compounds with a single-target set go to lab testing for that target, and those with several targets go to a wider panel, so costly experiments follow how uncertain the model is.

Providing transparent multi-class predictions in judicial risk assessment by showing all plausible risk categories at the stated coverage level, enabling judges to see the full range of possibilities rather than just a single point estimate.

A university predicts whether first-year students will complete their degree and offers early support when the 90% prediction set includes 'withdraws'. To keep that 90% true for every group, not only on average, the data team calibrates the sets separately within each demographic group, then checks coverage and average set size per group on held-out students. A group with too few calibration cases is reported as not covered by the guarantee.

limitations.description: Sets can be wide enough to be useless. A multi-class set holding most classes, or an interval spanning the plausible range, meets the coverage target but tells the decision-maker little, and sets containing opposing outcomes make decisions hard. Width depends on the model's quality and the scoring rule chosen, and the guarantee says nothing about it.

Needs labelled calibration data kept apart from training. On small datasets that means less data to train on, or a coarse and unstable coverage level, and variants that avoid a separate calibration set need several model fits.

The guarantee assumes calibration data and new cases are exchangeable, roughly that they come from the same source in no particular order. Drift, a changed population or strongly time-ordered data break it, and coverage then falls below target with no warning. In Shafer and Vovk's example, a nominal 5% error rate rose to 8% on a systematically different test set.

Coverage is guaranteed on average over all cases, not for each individual or subgroup, so a model can reach 95% overall while covering a minority group far less often. Mondrian calibration fixes this only for predefined, non-overlapping groups. It needs each new case's group at prediction time and is unstable when a group has few calibration cases (MAPIE's tutorial gives under 200 as an example).

Cost depends on the variant. Split conformal prediction adds little beyond scoring a held-out set, but full conformal prediction re-evaluates every candidate outcome and cross-conformal variants refit the model several times, which can be prohibitive for large models or real-time use.

sample_claims.text: On a held-out test set from the same patient population as the calibration data, the 95% prediction sets contained the true diagnosis in at least 95% of cases, within sampling error.
Prediction-set coverage on the latest quarter of live data stays within the agreed margin of its nominal level, so there is no sign that the exchangeability assumption has broken down in deployment.

For the perception model, the 95% prediction sets contained the true object class in at least 95% of held-out frames, and frames whose set holds more than one class trigger the cautious fallback behaviour.
Every credit-limit recommendation is shown with a set of plausible limit bands at 90% coverage, and any case whose set holds more than one band is routed to a human underwriter.

The 90% prediction sets are calibrated separately within each demographic group, and on held-out cases their coverage is within three percentage points of 90% in every group, with each group's number of calibration and test cases reported.

name: Platt Scaling
description: Platt scaling turns a classifier's raw scores into calibrated probabilities, meaning that among the cases given a probability of 0.3, about 30 per cent turn out to be positive. It was introduced for support vector machines, whose outputs are distances from a decision boundary rather than probabilities, and applies to any binary classifier that produces a real-valued score. After the classifier is trained, a two-parameter logistic (sigmoid) curve, P(y = 1 | f) = 1 / (1 + exp(A·f + B)), is fitted by maximum likelihood to map each score f to a probability, using labelled cases the classifier was not trained on, taken from a held-out set or from cross-validation folds. The fitted curve is strictly monotonic, so the order of cases and ranking measures such as the area under the ROC curve (how well the scores separate the two classes) are unchanged; only the probability attached to each case moves. The output is a recalibrated model, assessed before and after with a reliability diagram (predicted probability plotted against observed frequency) and with the Brier score or log loss (two measures of how far predicted probabilities fall from what happened).

example_use_cases.description: A retail bank's credit-risk team finds that its gradient-boosted default model ranks applicants well but squeezes predicted default probabilities towards the middle of the range. Before the probabilities feed expected-loss provisioning, the team fits Platt scaling on a held-out year of loan outcomes and checks on a reliability diagram that predicted and observed default rates agree in every score decile.

A benefits agency uses a linear support vector machine to flag claims for manual review, but its margin scores mean nothing to caseworkers. The team applies Platt scaling so the review screen can show the probability that a claim needs correcting, publishes the calibration curve in the caseworker guidance, and explains that the figure is a rate across similar claims rather than a verdict on the individual.

limitations.description: The sigmoid shape is an assumption. It corrects the S-shaped distortion typical of support vector machines and boosted trees, whose probabilities bunch towards the middle, but not the reverse distortion of overconfident models such as naive Bayes, whose probabilities pile up near 0 and 1. Where the reliability diagram shows that pattern, a flexible method such as isotonic regression is needed.

It works best when the classifier's scores for the two classes are spread in a similar way (roughly normal with equal variance). In highly imbalanced problems the scores of the two classes do not have equal spread, so the sigmoid can be a poor match for the data.

The curve should be fitted on labelled cases that played no part in training. The classifier separates its own training data better than new data, so a curve fitted to training scores overstates confidence in use; the cost is a held-out calibration set taken from scarce labelled data, or cross-validation with several model fits.

A single curve fitted across the whole population does not make the model calibrated within each subgroup. In a deployed malnutrition-risk model, recalibration improved calibration within each race and sex group, yet intercepts and slopes still differed significantly between Black and White patients. Fitting a curve per group needs group membership at prediction time, which may be unavailable or unlawful to use, and enough labelled cases in every group.

Recalibration changes every probability, so a decision threshold chosen on the raw scores no longer flags the same cases. After logistic recalibration of a deployed malnutrition-risk model, specificity rose from 0.74 to 0.93 and sensitivity fell from 0.75 to 0.35, so the cut-off has to be reset against the cost of each kind of error and the downstream process checked again.

sample_claims.text: After Platt scaling on a held-out year of loan outcomes, the default model's predicted probabilities agree with observed default rates in every score decile, within the tolerance set in the model risk policy.

After Platt scaling, the defect classifier's log loss on the held-out test set is lower than before, and its reliability diagram shows predicted defect rates within the tolerance set in the quality plan.

Each flagged claim is shown to caseworkers with a probability calibrated against held-out review outcomes, and the calibration curve and its meaning are published in the caseworker guidance, so a displayed 30 per cent corresponds to roughly 30 in 100 similar claims needing correction.

name: Temperature Scaling
description: Temperature scaling is a correction applied after training to a classifier that is more confident than it is accurate, a common problem in modern neural networks. It divides the model's raw scores (logits) by a single number, the temperature, before they are turned into probabilities, so a temperature above one lowers confidence and one below one raises it. The temperature is fitted on a labelled validation set kept apart from training by minimising negative log-likelihood, a measure that penalises confident wrong answers, and the model's own weights are not changed. Because dividing by one positive number never changes which class scores highest, predictions and accuracy stay the same. Stated confidence usually moves much closer to observed accuracy on data like the validation set, which a reliability diagram (a chart of stated confidence against how often the model was right) can show, but some miscalibration remains.

example_use_cases.description: A trust-and-safety team auto-removes posts only when its neural text classifier reports at least 95% confidence. The team fits a temperature on one labelled validation set, then checks on a second, unseen labelled set that posts scored near 95% really are abusive about 95% of the time, and adjusts the removal threshold if they are not.

An environmental agency's land-cover classifier was trained on summer satellite images and is now used on winter scenes, where it is overconfident. The team fits a fresh temperature on a small labelled winter sample and compares calibration error before and after on separate winter test scenes, rather than reusing the summer temperature.

A hospital radiology department displays the model's confidence beside each chest X-ray finding. Before display, the team fits a temperature on held-out scans from its own hospital and reports expected calibration error on a test set, so that clinicians can read a displayed 70% as roughly 70 correct findings in 100 similar cases.

limitations.description: A single temperature is fitted for the whole dataset, so it corrects average overconfidence but not differences between groups or regions of the input space. A minority group can stay overconfident while overall calibration looks good, and only a per-group calibration check shows it.

It leaves predicted classes unchanged, so accuracy and the model's mistakes stay as they were. A weak model remains weak and only becomes more honest about it, so calibration cannot substitute for improving the model.

The temperature is fitted on data resembling the training distribution, and calibration can degrade when deployment data shifts. In one large benchmark, error in stated confidence rose significantly as shift increased, even though it was low on unshifted data.

It needs labelled held-out data that resembles deployment, separate from the training data, and a further separate set to measure the result, because scoring calibration on the data used to fit the temperature flatters it. Small datasets may not leave enough for both.

Calibration is judged on the confidence of the predicted class only. The probabilities given to the other classes are not checked by that measure, so uses that read the whole probability list, such as ranking several likely diagnoses, need separate testing.

sample_claims.text: On a test set not used to fit the temperature, the diagnostic model's expected calibration error is below the agreed threshold, and observed accuracy in each confidence band is within tolerance of its stated confidence.

Calibrating the credit risk model with a single temperature left its predicted classes, and therefore its accuracy, unchanged, while its default probabilities now track the observed default rates on held-out data.
A displayed confidence of 80% corresponds to about 80 correct predictions in 100, as shown by a reliability diagram on data not used to fit the temperature.
After refitting the temperature on a labelled sample from the new region, the land-cover classifier's calibration error on that region's test data is no worse than on the original region.

name: Deep Ensembles
description: Deep ensembles estimate how uncertain a neural network's predictions are by training several copies of the same network independently and comparing what they predict. Each copy starts from different random initial weights, sees the training data in a different random order, and is trained to output a full predictive distribution, such as a probability for each class or a predicted value with its spread, rather than a single answer. The ensemble's prediction is the average of its members. Where members agree the prediction is usually more reliable, though agreement alone is no guarantee, and where they disagree the model is showing uncertainty about which answer is right, known as epistemic or model uncertainty. In the original study, ensembles of about five networks were better calibrated than single networks, meaning their stated confidence matched how often they were right, and expressed higher uncertainty on inputs from classes absent from the training data.
