example_use_cases.description: An autonomous vehicle team runs five independently trained obstacle-detection networks on each camera frame. When the members' outputs disagree beyond a set level, the vehicle slows and requests remote assistance instead of acting on the averaged detection.

A research team estimating body composition from MRI scans trains an ensemble of regression networks that each predict a measurement and its uncertainty, and flags scans where the ensemble is highly uncertain for manual checking before the values enter a population study.

A bank's underwriters see the spread of an ensemble's predicted default probabilities alongside each credit score. Scores with a wide spread are labelled low-confidence and sent for manual review, so staff can see where the model is unsure.

limitations.description: Training and running M networks multiplies compute, memory and latency by roughly M. A five-member ensemble costs about five times a single model, which can rule it out for very large models or for real-time and edge deployment.
Members trained on the same data share its blind spots. On inputs far from the training data they can agree on a confident wrong answer, so low disagreement is not evidence that an input is familiar.

Applies only where the networks can be trained from scratch, with access to the training data and the compute for several full training runs. It cannot be added to an existing pretrained or third-party model.

Disagreement among a small number of members is a noisy estimate, and members that end up too alike understate uncertainty. Calibration has to be checked on held-out data, not assumed from the ensemble.

Uncertainty depends on the training objective and what each member predicts. In regression, variance across member means alone omits the within-member variability included in the original probabilistic method.

sample_claims.text: On held-out scans, the imaging model's ensemble uncertainty is higher for cases it gets wrong than for cases it gets right, so scans above the uncertainty threshold can be sent for manual review.
The ensemble's predicted probabilities are calibrated on held-out data, so that predictions made with 90% confidence are correct about 90% of the time.
When shown inputs from a class absent from the training data, the ensemble's disagreement is measurably higher than on in-distribution inputs, as tested on a held-out set of unseen-class examples.

The driving system reports an uncertainty level with each detection, derived from disagreement between independently trained networks, and remote operators are alerted when it passes the documented limit.
Each credit score shown to underwriters carries an uncertainty range from the ensemble, and scores with a wide range are labelled as low-confidence.

name: Bootstrap Ensembles
description: Bootstrap ensembles estimate how much a model's predictions depend on the particular sample of data it was trained on. The training set is resampled with replacement many times, each resample (a bootstrap replicate) holding as many cases as the original so that some cases are repeated and others left out; one model is trained on each replicate with the same settings, and every new input is passed through all of the models. The spread of the models' predictions for an input, reported as a standard deviation or as a range between percentiles, estimates the uncertainty in the model's prediction for that input, and inputs where the models disagree are those the training data constrain least. The spread covers uncertainty in the fitted model only, not the random variation in individual outcomes, so an interval meant to contain a case's actual outcome must add an estimate of that noise, for example from the models' errors on held-out data. Putting a confidence interval around a measured performance score is a different procedure, which resamples the evaluation set and retrains nothing; see Bootstrap Confidence Intervals for Evaluation Metrics.

example_use_cases.description: An electricity network operator forecasting next-day demand at each substation trains 100 gradient-boosted models on bootstrap replicates of three years of meter readings, resampled in whole-week blocks because consecutive readings are correlated. Planners hold extra reserve at substations where the models' forecasts spread widely, because those are the sites whose forecasts the historical data settle least.

A hospital's readmission-risk tool shows clinicians, beside each patient's predicted risk, the range of risks given by models trained on bootstrap replicates of the training cohort, resampling patients rather than admissions so that one patient's admissions stay together, so that a clinician can see when an estimate rests on few comparable past patients and give it less weight in discharge planning.

A local authority reviewing a housing-need scoring model compares the average spread of bootstrap-ensemble scores across applicant groups and finds it widest for a group with few past applications, which shows that the model's scores for that group are least settled by the data; it collects more cases before letting the scores inform priority for that group.

limitations.description: Every member of the ensemble is a full training run, and every prediction must be made by every member, so training cost, storage and prediction time all grow in proportion to the number of replicates. For large neural networks this usually limits the ensemble to a handful of members, too few for stable percentiles of the spread.

The spread measures uncertainty in the fitted model, not the noise in outcomes. Presented as the range within which a case's actual outcome will fall, it understates the uncertainty, most of all where outcomes are noisy and training data plentiful, so the outcome noise has to be estimated separately, for example from held-out errors, and added.

The spread reflects only what the procedure lets vary: which cases are in each training set and, for models trained from a random start such as neural networks, each member's starting point. Fixed choices such as features, architecture and training settings add no spread. A model consistently wrong for a group the data under-represent can show little spread there, and members can agree closely on inputs unlike the training data, so a small spread is not evidence of reliability.

Each replicate contains on average only about 63 per cent of the distinct training cases, so each member learns from less information than a model trained on all the data. With small datasets or rare classes, some replicates may contain almost none of a rare class or subgroup, which inflates the spread for those cases and can leave individual members unusable.

Resampling single cases assumes they are independent. With repeated measurements of the same person, time series or other grouped data, case resampling spreads related cases across replicates and understates the uncertainty, unless whole groups or time blocks are resampled instead.

sample_claims.text: For each substation's next-day demand forecast, the spread across models trained on bootstrap replicates of the historical data, resampled in whole-week blocks, is reported, and forecasts whose spread exceeds the planning tolerance are flagged.
The flood model's uncertainty for each river gauge reflects how much its predictions change when it is retrained on versions of the gauge records resampled in blocks of consecutive days.
Each readmission-risk score shown to clinicians is accompanied by the range of scores produced by models trained on resampled versions of the training cohort.
The spread of the housing-need model's scores across bootstrap-trained models has been compared between applicant groups and is reported for each group.

name: Jackknife Resampling
description: Jackknife resampling, also called leave-one-out resampling, shows how much a result computed from a dataset depends on any single record. The result can be a model's coefficients, its predictions or a performance score; it is recomputed n times on a dataset of n records, leaving out a different record each time and refitting the model where the result depends on one. The spread of the recomputed results, after a standard rescaling, estimates the bias and variance of the original result, meaning how far it would move with a slightly different sample. Records whose removal moves the result most are flagged as influential, and may be outliers or data errors worth checking. The method assumes the records are independent and that no single record changes the result abruptly.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital data team fits a readmission-risk model on 600 patient records and refits it 600 times, leaving out one patient each time. The spread of the refitted coefficients shows which risk factors are stable enough to report, and the records whose removal shifts the fit most go back to clinicians to check for entry errors.

A water utility's analysts estimate how rainfall drives reservoir inflow from 40 annual observations. Leaving out each year in turn gives a variance estimate for the fitted slope and shows whether a single flood year drives the result, before the figure goes into a planning document.

A credit-risk team documents its scorecard's stability for model validators by refitting it with each of 800 sampled loan records left out. It reports the records whose removal changes any coefficient by more than a stated tolerance, so validators can see how much of the model rests on a few loans.

limitations.description: Computationally heavy when the result needs a model refit, since n records mean n refits, which is impractical for datasets with thousands or millions of records or for costly training. Simple statistics that are cheap to recompute do not have this problem.

Works only for statistics that change smoothly when one record is removed. For quantities that jump, such as the number of clusters in a mixture model, leave-one-out estimates are unreliable. Even for smooth statistics the variance estimate tends to run high, so intervals are conservative.

Assumes the records are independent. With repeated or clustered measurements, such as several visits per patient or neighbouring regions, leaving out one record leaves its close relatives in the data, so the refits barely change and the spread understates the true uncertainty.
Provides limited insight into model behaviour on truly novel data, as each jackknife sample is only minimally different from the full training set.

Measures how sensitive a result is to the sample in hand, not whether the model is right. A stable fit can still be systematically wrong, so a narrow spread across refits is no evidence of accuracy, or of performance on a different population.

sample_claims.text: The readmission model's coefficient estimates change by less than a stated tolerance when any single patient record is removed, so no individual record drives the reported risk factors.
The jackknife standard error of the fitted rainfall-to-inflow slope is reported with the estimate, and the planning threshold lies more than two standard errors away from it.
The scorecard's validation report lists the loan records whose removal most changes its coefficients, so reviewers can see how far the model depends on a handful of loans.

name: Cross-validation
description: Cross-validation estimates how well a model will perform on data it has not seen, and how much that estimate depends on the particular data used. The dataset is divided into k parts called folds, the model is trained on all but one fold and scored on the held-out fold, and this repeats until every fold has served as the held-out set once. The scores are averaged to give a performance estimate, and their spread gives a rough indication of how much the result depends on which data the model was trained on. Common variants are stratified cross-validation, where each fold keeps the overall class proportions, and leave-one-out, where each fold is a single example. A large gap between training scores and held-out scores points to overfitting, where a model has learned quirks of its training data that do not carry over to new data.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital data-science team has records for about 900 patients and is building a readmission-risk model. It runs 10-fold cross-validation with each patient's admissions kept in the same fold, then reports the mean and spread of held-out scores. A wide spread, or a large gap to the training score, tells the team the model is not yet stable enough to take to a prospective trial.

A bank's fraud team compares three candidate classifiers by running the same stratified 10-fold cross-validation on a year of labelled transactions, so every candidate is scored on identical folds and the rare fraud cases are spread evenly across them. They select the model with the best mean recall at a fixed false-alarm rate and drop any candidate whose fold-to-fold scores vary widely.

A materials-science group has only 120 labelled samples from costly experiments. Instead of trusting one train-test split, it repeats 5-fold cross-validation with different random splits and reports the spread of the accuracy estimate, which decides whether the model is reliable enough to guide the next round of experiments.

limitations.description: The number of folds trades cost against bias and variance. Each fold is another training run. Few folds (2 to 5) train on less data and tend to understate performance, whereas leave-one-out has little bias but unstable estimates and the highest cost. Ten folds is a common compromise, not a rule.

Assumes records are independent. If the same patient, customer or site appears in several records, a fold can be trained on records nearly identical to those it is tested on, and the score is optimistic. Folds must then be built by group, not drawn at random.

Ignores time order. Training on later records and testing on earlier ones lets future information leak into the estimate and flatters the model. For time-ordered data, use an evaluation that always tests on data later than the training data, such as rolling-origin evaluation.

Anything learned from the data must be fitted inside each training fold, including scaling, feature selection and hyperparameter tuning. Done once on the full dataset beforehand, it leaks test-fold information and inflates the scores. Tuning and reporting on the same folds is also optimistic, so nested cross-validation is needed for both.

A score from a small sample is imprecise, and the spread across folds understates the true uncertainty. In one neuroimaging study, error bars on a cross-validated score were roughly plus or minus 10% with 100 samples, so a small gain between two models can be noise.

sample_claims.text: Across ten stratified folds, the model's AUC varied by no more than 0.03 around its mean, so the reported performance does not depend on which records were held out.
The fraud detection model's recall on fraudulent transactions stays within the agreed band in every fold of the historical data, with no fold below the minimum acceptable recall.

With all preprocessing and feature selection fitted inside each training fold, repeated cross-validation shows the readmission model's performance estimate is not inflated by information from the test folds.
The readmission-risk model shows no sign of overfitting, with held-out scores on every fold within the agreed margin of its training score.

name: Area Under Precision-Recall Curve
description: Area Under Precision-Recall Curve (AUPRC) summarises how well a classifier finds the cases that matter when those cases are rare. Precision is the share of positive predictions that are correct, and recall is the share of actual positives that are found. Plotting one against the other at every classification threshold gives a curve, and AUPRC is the area under it, from 0 to 1. Neither precision nor recall uses true negatives, so a large majority class does not flatter the score as it can flatter accuracy and AUC-ROC. A model with no skill scores about the proportion of positives in the data, so the score is only meaningful next to that baseline.

example_use_cases.description: A payments team compares candidate fraud models on a held-out month of transactions in which about 1 in 500 is fraudulent. It ranks them by AUPRC against the 0.2% no-skill baseline, then reads the best model's curve to choose a threshold that keeps false alarms within what the investigation team can review.

A hospital evaluates a model that screens for a rare condition affecting about 1 in 200 patients. ROC AUC can look high even when most flagged patients are healthy, so the team reports AUPRC against the 0.5% baseline and reads the precision at the recall clinicians require, to decide whether the follow-up workload is manageable.

A manufacturer compares two defect-detection models for a production line where about 1 in 1,000 parts is faulty. It uses AUPRC on a labelled validation batch to choose between them, so that a model is not preferred simply for labelling nearly every good part correctly.

limitations.description: AUPRC depends on the share of positives in the data, so scores from datasets or groups with different proportions cannot be compared directly, and no universal pass mark can be set. Each score has to be read against its own no-skill baseline, which is about the positive proportion.

It treats one class as the positive class and ignores true negatives, so it says nothing about how reliably the model clears the majority class. That matters where certifying a case as negative or safe is as important as catching positives.

A single area averages over every threshold, including ones no deployment would use, and can hide poor precision at the recall the application needs. Choosing the operating point needs a look at that part of the curve and the cost of each kind of error.

The area can be computed in different ways. Trapezoidal linear interpolation between points gives an overly optimistic value, whereas step-wise average precision does not, so scores from different libraries or settings may not match.
Few positive test cases make precision-recall estimates unstable, so a high score from a small sample may not hold on a larger, representative evaluation set.

sample_claims.text: On the held-out transactions, the fraud model's AUPRC is above the agreed acceptance value and well above the no-skill baseline set by the fraud rate
At the recall that clinicians require, the screening model's precision on the validation set stays above the level that keeps follow-up workload manageable
The updated defect-detection model's AUPRC on the labelled validation batch is higher than the current model's, with the no-skill baseline reported alongside

name: Safety Envelope Testing
description: Safety envelope testing checks how an AI system performs at and beyond the edges of the conditions it was designed for, so that failure modes are found before deployment. Testers first write down those conditions, called the operational design domain, such as the road types, weather, lighting and speeds a vehicle is built for. They then build scenarios that push each condition towards its limit and past it, and measure how performance degrades as conditions get harder, repeating runs where the system does not behave the same way twice. The results show where, within the conditions tested, the system moves from acceptable to unsafe behaviour. They support operating limits, safety margins and a point at which the system should hand over to a person or stop.

example_use_cases.description: Testing autonomous vehicle perception systems at the limits of weather conditions, lighting, and sensor coverage to establish safe operational boundaries and determine when human intervention is required.

A radiology team tests a chest X-ray triage model on scans at the edge of its intended use, such as the poorest image quality and the oldest scanner models it was approved for, and records where sensitivity falls below the agreed floor, so that scans beyond that point are referred to a radiologist.

A trading firm replays historical crash periods and synthetic shocks with volatility pushed beyond the range its trading model was developed on, to check that position limits and the automatic trading halt trigger before losses reach the agreed ceiling.

limitations.description: Results are only as good as the operational design domain used. If the specification omits a condition the system meets in service, such as a road type or a market regime, the tests probe the wrong edge and a clean result gives false confidence.

Coverage is incomplete by construction. Conditions interact across many dimensions, so the number of boundary combinations grows quickly, and failures that appear only when several factors reach their limits together can be missed.
Performance of a learned system need not fall smoothly towards the boundary. Failures can sit inside the envelope, so good results at the edge do not show that the interior is safe.

Results describe one system version in one test setting, and a single pass proves little for a system that behaves differently on successive runs, which needs repeated trials. Retraining, new sensors or a gap between simulation and the real world can move the boundary, so the tests need repeating after each material change.
The technique shows where the system stops performing acceptably. It does not keep the system inside that envelope in service, which needs a separate runtime monitor or out-of-distribution detector.

sample_claims.text: The perception system has been tested at and beyond the limits of its operational design domain in weather, lighting and sensor-coverage conditions, and the point at which it hands control to a human driver is documented.

The diagnostic model's sensitivity has been measured across graded levels of image quality and case complexity up to the edge of its intended use, and the level at which cases are referred to a specialist is set from those results.

The forecasting model's error has been measured under progressively more extreme weather inputs up to the documented operating limits, with the point at which accuracy falls below the agreed bound recorded.
The trading algorithm's automatic suspension has been shown to trigger in stress scenarios when volatility passes the documented limit, before position losses exceed the agreed ceiling.

The inspection system's defect-detection rate has been tested at the edges of the lighting, part-orientation and surface-finish ranges expected in production, and the range in which it meets the required rate is documented.

name: Algorithm Review Boards
description: An algorithm review board is a standing, multidisciplinary body inside an organisation that examines proposed AI systems or AI research projects at set points and decides whether, and on what conditions, they may proceed. The literature also calls these bodies AI ethics boards or AI review boards. They differ from an Institutional Review Board (IRB), which protects the human subjects of research, because they also weigh harms to the people a system will affect and to society. A risk-based triage decides which projects need full review; the project team then submits a written account of the system's purpose, data, foreseeable harms and planned mitigations, and members drawn from technical, legal, ethical and domain backgrounds, sometimes with people from affected communities, question the team and iterate on that account with them. The board approves, approves with conditions such as a monitoring plan or a re-review date, or rejects, and the output is a dated decision record with its reasons and conditions that later reviews and audits can check against what was built.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital group's algorithm review board examines a sepsis early-warning model before a ward pilot. It approves the pilot on condition of a monitoring plan for alert rates and missed cases, names who may switch the model off, and sets a re-review once six months of local performance data are in, before any wider roll-out.

A bank's board reviews a proposed credit-limit model before launch. It asks the team for its disparate-impact analysis by protected group and for evidence that applicants can contest a decision, and withholds approval until both are supplied, so the decision to deploy rests with a body outside the development team.

A university AI research programme releases grant funding only after each project has passed an ethics and society review, in which researchers state the risks their work poses to society and to particular groups, commit to mitigations, and revise them with an interdisciplinary faculty panel.

A government department publishes the board's decision record for a benefits-triage tool, giving the reasons for approval, the conditions attached and the re-review date, so that its oversight committee and the public can see what was examined, by whom and when, and check later that the conditions were met.

limitations.description: Review adds time and cost to every project that goes through it, and organisations under commercial pressure may route work around the board or narrow its remit, so the board's coverage, not just its existence, needs to be shown.

Its judgements are only as good as its membership. A board without the relevant technical, domain or community expertise will miss harms that fall outside what its members know, and a board drawn mainly from inside the team's own reporting line is open to group-think.

Independence is hard to keep inside an organisation. Practitioners report tension between profit and the cost of responsible-AI review, and a board can come under pressure to approve projects that leadership has already committed to, which weakens it most where review matters most.

Without authority to stop or delay a project, and a way to check that its conditions are met, a board's recommendations can be ignored. Evidence from a board is strong only when its decision record shows what it could block and what happened to its conditions.

There is no agreed measure of whether a board works, and review can become box-ticking. A record that a project was reviewed shows that a process ran, not that the review was substantive or that its concerns were addressed.

sample_claims.text: Every high-risk AI system was reviewed and approved by the organisation's algorithm review board before operational use, and the board could have blocked deployment
The conditions the review board attached to the credit-limit model's approval, including a disparate-impact analysis by protected group and a re-review date, were met before and after launch
The clinical decision-support model was deployed under a monitoring plan and re-review schedule set by a multidisciplinary review board independent of the development team
The diagnostic AI system's development and deployment decisions are traceable to dated board decision records that state the risks assessed, the reasons for approval and the conditions attached
The review board's decision record for the risk assessment tool, with its reasons and conditions, is available to the oversight body and the public

name: Red Teaming
description: Red teaming is a structured adversarial evaluation process in which a dedicated team systematically probes an AI/ML system to discover vulnerabilities and failure modes. Unlike individual testing techniques (such as prompt injection testing, jailbreak resistance testing, or safety envelope testing), red teaming defines the organisational methodology: team composition, campaign planning, attack taxonomy, and reporting structure. The red team coordinates diverse attack vectors — including prompt manipulation, adversarial examples, edge case exploitation, and social engineering scenarios — into a coherent assessment programme. Results feed into risk registers and remediation plans rather than pass/fail metrics.

example_use_cases.description: Testing a content moderation AI by attempting to make it generate harmful outputs through creative prompt injection, jailbreaking techniques, and edge case scenarios to identify safety vulnerabilities before deployment.

Probing a medical diagnosis AI system with adversarial examples and edge cases to identify failure modes that could lead to incorrect diagnoses, ensuring the system fails gracefully rather than confidently providing wrong information.

Systematically testing a hiring algorithm with inputs designed to reveal hidden biases, using adversarial examples to check if the system can be manipulated to discriminate against protected groups or favour certain demographics unfairly.

Systematically testing AI systems for security vulnerabilities including prompt injection, data exfiltration, jailbreaking, and model manipulation by simulating adversarial attacks. This helps identify security weaknesses before deployment and provides documented evidence for compliance with regulatory requirements such as EU AI Act Article 55 and ISO 42001 adversarial testing mandates.

limitations.description: Requires highly specialized expertise in both AI/ML systems and adversarial attack methods, making it expensive and difficult to scale across organizations.
Limited by the creativity and knowledge of red team members - can only discover vulnerabilities that testers think to explore, potentially missing novel attack vectors.
Time-intensive process that may not be feasible for rapid development cycles or resource-constrained projects, potentially delaying beneficial system deployments.
May not generalize to real-world adversarial scenarios, as red team attacks may differ significantly from actual malicious use patterns or user behaviours.
Risk of false confidence if red teaming is incomplete or superficial, leading organizations to believe systems are safer than they actually are.

sample_claims.text: The medical AI system maintains safe behavior when subjected to edge case scenarios and adversarial inputs designed to elicit harmful clinical recommendations
The financial advisory system resists attempts to extract confidential client information through social engineering scenarios and multi-turn manipulation strategies
The public benefits allocation system withstands systematic probing designed to reveal exploitable pathways for discriminatory outcomes against protected groups
The autonomous vehicle control system fails gracefully rather than catastrophically when exposed to creative adversarial scenarios that exploit edge cases in perception and decision-making
The conversational AI assistant resists goal misalignment attacks and jailbreak attempts that probe for ways to circumvent safety constraints through iterative prompt refinement

name: Human-in-the-Loop Safeguards
description: Human-in-the-loop safeguards establish systematic checkpoints where human experts review, validate, or override AI/ML system decisions before they take effect. This governance approach combines automated efficiency with human judgement by defining clear intervention criteria (such as uncertainty thresholds, risk levels, or sensitive contexts) that trigger mandatory human oversight. By incorporating domain expertise, ethical considerations, and contextual understanding that machines may lack, these safeguards help ensure that critical decisions maintain appropriate human accountability whilst preserving the benefits of automated processing for routine cases.

example_use_cases.description: Implementing mandatory human physician review for any medical AI diagnostic recommendation before treatment decisions are made, especially for complex cases or when the system confidence is below established thresholds, ensuring patient safety through expert oversight.

Requiring human review of automated loan approval decisions when applicants request explanations or appeal rejections, allowing human underwriters to provide clear reasoning and ensure customers understand the decision-making process behind their application outcomes.

Mandating human oversight when hiring algorithms flag candidates from underrepresented groups for rejection, enabling recruiters to verify that decisions are based on legitimate job-relevant criteria rather than potential algorithmic bias, and providing fair recourse mechanisms.

limitations.description: Scales poorly with high request volumes, creating bottlenecks that can delay critical decisions and potentially overwhelm human reviewers with excessive workload.
Introduces significant latency into automated processes, potentially making time-sensitive applications impractical or reducing user satisfaction with slower response times.
Human reviewers may experience decision fatigue, leading to decreased attention quality over time and potential inconsistency in review standards across different cases or time periods.
Risk of automation bias where humans defer too readily to AI recommendations rather than providing meaningful independent review, undermining the safeguard's effectiveness.
Requires significant ongoing investment in human resources, training, and expertise maintenance, making it expensive to implement and sustain across large-scale systems.

sample_claims.text: The autonomous vehicle system requires qualified driver intervention before executing maneuvers flagged as high-risk by safety criteria
All loan denial decisions are subject to review by qualified underwriters who can access the reasoning behind algorithmic recommendations
The hiring system routes candidates from underrepresented groups to human reviewers when automated scores fall within a defined uncertainty range
The diagnostic support system prevents treatment recommendations from being actioned until reviewed by a licensed physician
The content moderation system escalates borderline cases to human moderators based on defined criteria rather than relying solely on automated classification

name: Confidence Thresholding
description: Confidence thresholding creates decision boundaries based on model uncertainty scores, routing predictions into different handling workflows depending on their confidence levels. High-confidence predictions (e.g., above 95%) proceed automatically, whilst medium-confidence cases (e.g., 70-95%) may trigger additional validation or human review, and low-confidence predictions (below 70%) receive extensive oversight or default to conservative fallback actions. This technique enables organisations to maintain automated efficiency for clear-cut cases whilst ensuring appropriate human intervention for uncertain decisions, balancing operational speed with risk management across safety-critical applications.

example_use_cases.description: Implementing tiered confidence thresholds in autonomous vehicle decision-making where high-confidence lane changes (>98%) execute automatically, medium-confidence decisions (85-98%) trigger additional sensor verification, and low-confidence situations (<85%) engage conservative defensive driving modes or request human takeover.

Deploying confidence thresholding in fraud detection systems where high-confidence legitimate transactions (>90%) process immediately, medium-confidence cases (70-90%) undergo additional automated checks, and low-confidence transactions (<70%) require human analyst review, ensuring system reliability through graduated response mechanisms.

Using confidence thresholds in automated loan decisions to provide clear explanations to applicants, where high-confidence approvals include simple explanations, medium-confidence decisions provide detailed reasoning about key factors, and low-confidence cases receive comprehensive explanations with guidance on potential improvements.

limitations.description: Many models produce poorly calibrated confidence scores that don't accurately reflect true prediction uncertainty, leading to overconfident predictions for incorrect outputs or underconfident scores for correct predictions.

Threshold selection requires careful calibration and domain expertise, as inappropriate thresholds can either overwhelm human reviewers with too many cases or miss genuinely uncertain decisions that need oversight.

High-confidence predictions may still be incorrect or harmful, particularly when models encounter adversarial inputs, out-of-distribution data, or systematic biases that the confidence mechanism doesn't detect.
Static thresholds may become inappropriate over time as model performance degrades, data distribution shifts occur, or operational contexts change, requiring ongoing monitoring and adjustment.

Implementation complexity increases significantly when managing multiple confidence levels and routing mechanisms, potentially introducing system failures or inconsistencies in how different confidence ranges are handled.

sample_claims.text: The autonomous system transitions to conservative fallback modes when prediction confidence falls below established operational thresholds
The system routes low-confidence predictions to human review while processing high-confidence cases automatically
The fraud detection system applies graduated verification steps based on transaction confidence levels
The diagnostic system communicates the level of certainty alongside each prediction to support clinical decision-making
The automated decision system engages additional safeguards when operating in regions of high uncertainty

name: Runtime Monitoring and Circuit Breakers
description: Runtime monitoring and circuit breakers observe a deployed AI service and restrict model calls when configured signals breach specified limits. In the closed state, requests pass through and recent failures are counted, while an open breaker rejects requests or provides a configured fallback, such as a cached answer, a simpler model, a rule-based default or referral to a person. After a waiting period, the half-open state permits a few trial calls and closes again only if they succeed. Model-related triggers can include immediately available signals such as input-drift scores (how far incoming data has moved from the training data) or low prediction confidence, since accuracy usually needs later outcome labels. Logs record state changes and triggering signals, supporting review of why the service was restricted without guaranteeing that the fallback is safe.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital's diagnostic-support service stops showing model suggestions to clinicians when the share of low-confidence predictions or the input drift score passes preset limits, for example after a scanner software update changes the images. A notice tells staff the standard workflow applies until engineers reset the breaker.

Deploying runtime monitoring for a recommendation engine that tracks recommendation diversity, click-through rates, and user engagement patterns, automatically switching to simpler algorithms when complex models show signs of performance degradation or unusual behaviour patterns.

A bank's credit-scoring service records every breaker state change, the metric that triggered it and the fallback used in an audit log. Model risk reviewers read the log each month to see how often, when and why the model was restricted, and whether the thresholds need revisiting.

An airline's customer-service assistant is wrapped in a circuit breaker that counts timeouts, blocked outputs and refusals. When they pass a limit after a faulty release, traffic switches to a scripted menu and the on-call engineer is paged, so the faulty version is stopped quickly without waiting for a manual decision.

limitations.description: Thresholds are hard to set. Too tight and the breaker trips on normal variation and withdraws a working service. Too loose and it stays closed through a real failure. Good settings need historical data from the live system, which is scarce at launch.

Model-level triggers are proxies for correctness. Drift scores and confidence can look normal while the model is confidently wrong, so a breaker that never trips is not evidence that predictions are right.

Gradual degradation and slow attacks can stay inside the limits, because each reading is acceptable while the cumulative effect is harmful. Catching them needs separate trend analysis or delayed accuracy checks alongside the breaker.

The breaker only moves the risk to the fallback. A cached answer, a simpler model or a human referral must itself be tested, and referral fails if reviewers cannot absorb a sudden diversion of traffic.

Tripping has a cost. A false trip withdraws a working service from users who may depend on it in time-critical settings, and reopening after a fixed cooldown, or on a few easy trial requests, can restore traffic before the underlying fault is fixed.

sample_claims.text: The diagnostic-support service stops showing model suggestions to clinicians when the share of low-confidence predictions or the input drift score passes its preset limit, and the standard clinical workflow applies until the breaker is reset.
The fraud-scoring service keeps answering requests during a model fault because the breaker diverts traffic to a rules-based fallback once the failure rate passes its threshold.
The forecasting service falls back to a simple baseline forecast when its inputs leave their historical ranges, so downstream users do not receive out-of-range forecasts.
Every breaker state change is recorded with its time, the metric that triggered it and the fallback used, and the log is available to system owners and auditors.
The platform records when its configured runtime restrictions activate and when normal calls resume.

name: Model Cards
description: Model cards are standardised documentation frameworks that systematically document machine learning models through structured templates. The templates cover intended use cases, performance metrics across different demographic groups and operating conditions, training data characteristics, evaluation procedures, limitations, and ethical considerations. They serve as comprehensive technical specifications that enable informed model selection, prevent inappropriate deployment, support regulatory compliance, and facilitate fair assessment by providing transparent reporting of model capabilities and constraints across diverse populations and scenarios.

example_use_cases.description: Documenting a medical diagnosis AI with detailed performance metrics across different patient demographics, age groups, and clinical conditions, enabling healthcare providers to understand when the model should be trusted and when additional expert consultation is needed for patient safety.

Creating comprehensive model cards for hiring algorithms that transparently report performance differences across demographic groups, helping HR departments identify potential bias issues and ensure equitable candidate evaluation processes.

Publishing detailed model documentation for a credit scoring API that clearly describes training data sources, evaluation methodologies, and performance limitations, enabling financial institutions to make informed decisions about model deployment and regulatory compliance.

limitations.description: Creating comprehensive model cards requires substantial time, expertise, and resources to gather performance data across diverse conditions and demographic groups, potentially delaying model deployment timelines.
Information can become outdated quickly as models are retrained, updated, or deployed in new contexts, requiring ongoing maintenance and version control to remain accurate and useful.
Organisations may provide incomplete or superficial documentation to avoid revealing competitive advantages or potential liabilities, undermining the transparency goals of model cards.
Lack of standardised formats and enforcement mechanisms means model card quality and completeness vary significantly across different organisations and use cases.
Technical complexity of documenting model behaviour across all relevant dimensions may exceed the expertise of some development teams, leading to gaps in critical information.

sample_claims.text: The model's performance characteristics are documented across all relevant demographic groups and operating conditions
The diagnostic system's accuracy and error rates are reported separately for each patient subpopulation
The model's intended use cases and known limitations are clearly communicated to decision-makers
The lending model's approval rates and error distributions are transparently reported for all applicant demographics
The system's training data characteristics, evaluation procedures, and ethical considerations are comprehensively documented

name: Datasheets for Datasets
description: Datasheets for datasets establish comprehensive documentation standards for datasets, systematically recording creation methodology, data composition, collection procedures, preprocessing transformations, intended applications, potential biases, privacy considerations, and maintenance protocols. These structured documents enhance dataset transparency by providing essential context for appropriate usage, enabling informed decisions about dataset suitability for specific tasks, supporting bias detection and mitigation efforts, ensuring compliance with data protection regulations, and promoting responsible data stewardship throughout the entire data lifecycle from collection to disposal.

example_use_cases.description: Documenting a medical imaging dataset with detailed information about patient privacy protections, anonymisation procedures, and data sharing constraints to ensure sensitive health information is handled appropriately and regulatory compliance is maintained.

Creating comprehensive datasheets for recruitment datasets that document demographic representation across different job categories, helping developers identify potential bias in training data and develop more equitable hiring algorithms.

Establishing transparent documentation for financial transaction datasets that clearly describes data collection methodology, preprocessing steps, and intended use cases, enabling researchers to make informed decisions about dataset appropriateness for their specific applications.

Documenting a safety-critical autonomous vehicle perception dataset with records of sensor calibration procedures, environmental conditions during collection, edge-case scenario coverage, and known distributional gaps, enabling safety engineers to assess whether training data adequately represents the operating conditions required for safe deployment and to support regulatory type-approval submissions.

Documenting the statistical distributions, temporal coverage, and known quality characteristics of training datasets to support model monitoring pipelines, enabling operations teams to detect data drift and assess whether production data remains within the documented training distribution for informed decisions about model retraining or recalibration.

limitations.description: Creating thorough datasheets requires significant time investment and domain expertise to properly document collection methods, biases, and ethical considerations, potentially delaying dataset release or publication.
Information may become outdated as datasets undergo preprocessing, cleaning, or augmentation, requiring ongoing maintenance to ensure documentation accuracy throughout the data lifecycle.
Absence of standardised templates and enforcement mechanisms leads to inconsistent documentation quality and completeness across different organisations and research communities.
Dataset creators may intentionally omit sensitive information about collection methods, participant consent, or potential biases to avoid legal liability or competitive disadvantage.
Limited adoption and awareness means many existing datasets lack proper documentation, creating gaps in the historical record and making legacy dataset assessment difficult.

sample_claims.text: The training dataset's collection methodology, participant consent procedures, and intended use constraints are documented and accessible to model developers
The dataset composition across demographic groups and protected characteristics is documented to enable bias detection during model development
The dataset's privacy protections, anonymisation procedures, and re-identification risks are documented before data sharing
The data provenance from original sources through preprocessing transformations is traceable for regulatory review
The environmental sensing dataset documents geographic coverage, temporal distribution, and known measurement biases across different operating conditions

name: MLflow Experiment Tracking
description: MLflow is an open-source platform that tracks machine learning experiments by automatically logging parameters, metrics, models, and artifacts throughout the ML lifecycle. It provides a centralised repository for comparing different experimental runs, reproducing results, and managing model versions. Teams can track hyperparameters, evaluation metrics, model files, and execution environment details, creating a comprehensive audit trail that supports collaboration, reproducibility, and regulatory compliance across the entire machine learning development process.

example_use_cases.description: Tracking medical diagnosis model experiments across different hospitals, logging hyperparameters, performance metrics, and model artifacts to ensure reproducible research and enable regulatory audits of model development processes.

Managing fraud detection model versions in production, tracking which specific model configuration and training data version is deployed, enabling quick rollback and performance comparison when system reliability issues arise.

Documenting loan approval model experiments with complete parameter tracking and performance logging across demographic groups, supporting fair lending compliance by providing transparent records of model development and validation processes.

limitations.description: Requires teams to adopt disciplined logging practices and may introduce overhead to development workflows if not properly integrated into existing processes.
Storage costs can grow substantially with extensive artifact logging, especially for large models or high-frequency experimentation.
Tracking quality depends on developers consistently logging relevant information, with incomplete logging leading to gaps in experimental records.
Complex multi-stage pipelines may require custom instrumentation to capture dependencies and data flow relationships effectively.
Security and access control configurations require careful setup to protect sensitive model information and experimental data in shared environments.

sample_claims.text: All experimental configurations and hyperparameters tested during model development are centrally logged with their corresponding performance outcomes
The deployed clinical model is reproducible from logged training parameters, data versions, and execution environment specifications
The fraud detection model's performance evolution across successive training runs is traceable through logged metrics and artifact histories
The production model version can be systematically compared against alternative experimental configurations evaluated during development
Model training artifacts and evaluation metrics are accessible to authorized team members through a centralized repository supporting collaborative review

name: Data Version Control
description: Data Version Control (DVC) is a Git-like version control system specifically designed for machine learning data, models, and experiments. It tracks changes to large data files, maintains reproducible ML pipelines, and creates a complete audit trail of data transformations, model training, and evaluation processes. DVC works alongside Git to provide end-to-end lineage tracking from raw data through preprocessing, training, and deployment, enabling teams to reproduce any model version and understand exactly how datasets evolved throughout the ML lifecycle.

example_use_cases.description: Tracking medical imaging dataset versions and model training pipelines to ensure reproducible research results, enabling hospitals to verify which specific data version and preprocessing steps were used for regulatory submissions.

Managing credit scoring model data pipelines with complete version control of training datasets, feature engineering steps, and model artifacts, ensuring reliable model reproduction and rollback capabilities when performance issues arise.

Maintaining pharmaceutical drug discovery data lineage across multiple research teams, tracking compound datasets, feature extraction processes, and model versions to support FDA submissions with complete experimental provenance.

limitations.description: Requires learning Git-like workflows and CLI commands, which may have a steep learning curve for teams unfamiliar with version control systems.
Storage costs can be substantial for large datasets with frequent changes, especially when maintaining multiple versions and branches of data.
Complex data pipelines with many interdependencies may require significant setup time and careful configuration to track properly.
Performance can degrade with very large files or datasets due to checksumming and synchronisation overhead during operations.
Team coordination becomes essential as improper branch management or merge conflicts can disrupt collaborative workflows.

sample_claims.text: The training dataset's lineage is traceable from original data sources through all preprocessing transformations to the deployed model
The model's performance can be recreated using the exact dataset version and pipeline configuration from any prior release
All modifications to sensor calibration data and feature extraction steps are documented with timestamps and author attribution
The system can be rolled back to any previous data processing pipeline version when performance degradation is detected
The complete history of dataset changes is preserved and queryable across the model's development lifecycle

name: Monotonicity Constraints
description: Monotonicity constraints require a model's prediction to move only one way as a chosen input rises, with the other inputs held fixed, so that, for example, predicted salary never falls as years of experience increase. The direction for each constrained feature is set from domain knowledge before training, and the learning algorithm or model structure then rules out any fit that breaks it, so the model cannot learn reversals that come from noise or sampling quirks in the data. Boosted-tree libraries apply the constraint when they choose splits and monotonic neural networks build it into their structure, while penalty-based methods only discourage violations. Because a penalty, a constraint set on the wrong column or a later processing step can still let a reversal through, testers then vary each constrained input across its range over many generated or real cases, with the other inputs fixed, and count any prediction that moves the wrong way. The evidence is that violation count, expected to be zero, together with a comparison of held-out accuracy with and without the constraint.

example_use_cases.description: A mortgage lender constrains its approval model so that higher income, longer employment and a higher credit score can only raise the approval score. Loan officers can then tell an applicant that improving any of these factors can only help the application, and the lender can state each factor's direction to its regulator.

A water utility's pipe-burst risk model is constrained so that risk rises with pipe age and operating pressure and falls with the quality of recent maintenance. Asset managers can then explain the ranked inspection list to the regulator through three directional rules, instead of an opaque score.

A hospital analytics team builds a tree-based model that predicts the cost of care for each patient and constrains the prediction never to fall as age or number of chronic conditions rises. Before release they sweep each constrained feature across its range for thousands of generated patient records, with the other features held fixed, and confirm that no prediction moves the wrong way. They also compare held-out accuracy with and without the constraints.

A utility's day-ahead demand forecast for office buildings is constrained so that predicted demand never falls as occupancy or floor area rises. The validation team writes this as an automated test that draws random building profiles, raises one constrained input at a time and fails the build if any forecast drops, so a retrained model that breaks the rule is caught before deployment.

limitations.description: Forces a one-way relationship even where the real one reverses, such as an inverted U between experience and performance. The model then fits that feature worse and cannot show the turning point, so held-out accuracy should be compared with and without the constraint.

Choosing which features to constrain, and in which direction, needs domain expertise. A wrong constraint builds a false belief into the model, and the check on the trained model will still pass, because it shows only that the constraint holds, not that it is right.

The rule covers one feature with the others held fixed, and says nothing about the size of the effect. A model can meet it by ignoring the feature, and when correlated inputs move together a person's overall score can still fall as one favourable input rises, so the constraint does not make the whole model easy to explain.

Support differs by model family. Tree-boosting libraries such as XGBoost accept constraints directly, while neural networks need a special architecture or a penalty term. With histogram-based tree methods, constraints can remove every candidate split and leave shallow trees that underfit.

A sweep or property-based test samples the input space. It can find a violation but cannot prove there is none, and a pass depends on how well the generated inputs cover realistic and rare combinations of features.

sample_claims.text: Every constrained input in the mortgage model has a documented direction of effect, so loan officers can tell an applicant that, other details being equal, higher income never lowers the approval score.
The clinical risk score is documented as never falling when a vital-sign measure worsens, other measures being equal, and clinicians are given that rule before they use the score.
In property-based testing over generated patient records, raising age or the number of chronic conditions on its own never lowered the cost model's prediction, and the test is rerun on every release
In sweeps of each constrained input across its full range, the building demand forecast recorded no case where predicted demand fell as occupancy rose.
Across 100,000 generated applicant records, raising income alone never lowered the lending model's predicted approval probability.

name: Generalized Additive Models
description: An intrinsically interpretable modelling technique that extends linear models by allowing flexible, nonlinear relationships between individual features and the target whilst maintaining the additive structure that preserves transparency. Each feature's effect is modelled separately as a smooth function, visualised as a curve showing how the feature influences predictions across its range. GAMs achieve this through spline functions or other smoothing techniques that capture complex patterns in individual variables without interactions, making them particularly valuable for domains requiring both predictive accuracy and model interpretability.

example_use_cases.description: Predicting hospital readmission risk with a GAM that provides transparent, auditable risk assessments by showing how readmission probability varies nonlinearly with patient age, blood pressure, and medication adherence, enabling clinicians to understand and trust the model's reasoning for regulatory compliance.

Building a credit scoring model that explains loan decisions to applicants by visualising how income, credit history, and debt-to-income ratio individually affect approval likelihood, providing clear feature attributions that satisfy fair lending requirements and regulatory explainability mandates.

limitations.description: Cannot capture complex interactions between features unless explicitly modelled, limiting their ability to represent relationships where variables influence each other.
Setup requires domain expertise to decide which features need nonlinear treatment and appropriate smoothing parameters, making model specification more challenging than linear models.
Fitting process is computationally more expensive than linear models, particularly for large datasets with many features requiring smoothing.
Risk of overfitting individual feature relationships if smoothing parameters are not properly regularised, potentially reducing generalisation performance.
Interpretation complexity increases with the number of nonlinear features, as understanding multiple smooth curves simultaneously becomes cognitively demanding.

sample_claims.text: The clinical decision model's predictions are decomposable into individual feature contributions that can be visualized as smooth curves
The lending model reveals how each applicant attribute nonlinearly influences approval likelihood whilst maintaining an additive structure
The model's decision logic is directly inspectable without requiring separate explanation methods
The resource allocation model documents how each policy-relevant factor shapes outcomes through interpretable functional relationships

name: Neuron Activation Analysis
description: Neuron activation analysis examines the firing patterns of individual neurons in neural networks by probing them with diverse inputs and analysing their activation responses. This technique helps understand what concepts, features, or patterns different neurons have learned to recognise, providing insights into the model's internal representations. For large language models, this can reveal neurons specialised for linguistic concepts, semantic categories, or even potentially harmful patterns, enabling targeted interventions and deeper model understanding.

example_use_cases.description: Analysing GPT-based models to identify specific neurons that activate on toxic or harmful content, enabling targeted interventions to reduce model toxicity whilst preserving general language capabilities for safer AI deployment.

Examining activation patterns in multilingual language models to detect neurons that exhibit systematic biases when processing text from different linguistic communities, revealing implicit representation inequalities that could affect downstream applications.

Investigating individual neurons in medical language models to understand which clinical concepts and medical knowledge representations drive diagnostic suggestions, enabling healthcare professionals to validate the model's medical reasoning pathways.

limitations.description: Many neurons exhibit polysemantic behaviour, representing multiple unrelated concepts simultaneously, making it difficult to assign clear interpretable meanings to individual neural units.
Important model behaviours are often distributed across many neurons rather than localised in single units, requiring analysis of neural circuits and interactions that can be exponentially complex.

Computational costs scale dramatically with modern large language models containing billions of parameters, making comprehensive neuron-by-neuron analysis prohibitively expensive for complete model understanding.

Neuron activation patterns are highly context-dependent, with the same neuron potentially serving different roles based on surrounding input context, complicating consistent interpretation across diverse scenarios.
Interpretation of activation patterns often relies on subjective human analysis without rigorous validation methods, potentially leading to confirmation bias or misattribution of neural functions.

sample_claims.text: The language model's internal representations reveal which individual computational units respond to specific semantic concepts relevant to clinical diagnosis
The content moderation system's harmful output patterns are attributable to identifiable neurons that can be selectively modified without degrading general language capabilities
The multilingual model's neurons do not exhibit systematic activation biases when processing text from different linguistic communities
The financial risk assessment model's internal computational units encode interpretable market concepts rather than opaque statistical artifacts
The model's specialized neurons for toxic content detection activate consistently across diverse phrasings and contexts of harmful patterns

name: Prompt Robustness Testing
description: Prompt robustness testing measures how much a language model's answers, or its performance on a task, change when the prompt is varied in ways that should not matter, such as rewording, formatting, capitalisation, reordering, or the typos and synonym swaps real users make. The tester starts from task prompts with known correct answers, writes variants that keep the meaning from templates or generates them with perturbation tools such as PromptBench, and runs the model on every variant. Some tools search for the variant that does the most damage, so a drop under that kind of attack is a worst case, not a typical failure rate. The result is reported as the spread of performance across variants, for example the gap between the best and worst format, together with the variants that changed the answer. On one widely used open model, accuracy differed by up to 76 points across formatting changes that kept the meaning, which is why one prompt template is not enough.

example_use_cases.description: A digital health provider testing a symptom-triage chatbot rewrites each benchmark scenario as a brief layperson message, a detailed account, a clinician's summary and an anxious message, and checks that the urgency category stays the same across all four, treating any change as a failure to investigate before release.

A public-sector team choosing between candidate language models for classifying citizen enquiries evaluates each across a set of plausible prompt formats and instruction paraphrases, and compares models on worst-format and average accuracy rather than on a single prompt, because the ranking of models can change with the template.

A bank validating a model that summarises suspicious-transaction reports checks that the risk category it extracts does not change when the same activity is described with different terminology, abbreviations or layout, as reports from different branches would be.

limitations.description: The space of possible prompt variants is unbounded, so a test samples it. A model can pass on every variant tried and still fail on a phrasing nobody generated, and the conclusion holds only for the kinds of variation the test set covers.

Whether a variant keeps the meaning of the original is a judgement. Automated perturbations can change meaning or produce text no user would write, and attack-based tools search for the most damaging variant, so their drops are worst cases. Variant sets need checking by someone who knows the domain.

Results do not transfer between models: which formats work well correlated only weakly across models in a large study, and robustness to one domain's phrasing says little about another's. The test has to be rerun for each model version, each prompt template change and each domain.

Every variant multiplies the number of model calls, and for open-ended answers each response may need scoring by a domain expert rather than against a fixed label. Testing many formats across many examples and candidate models quickly becomes costly.

It shows that outputs are brittle, not why. Choosing the best-scoring template on the same variants used to test it gives an optimistic estimate of how that template will perform on new inputs, so template selection and the final robustness measurement need separate data.

sample_claims.text: The triage assistant assigns the same urgency category to each benchmark scenario whether the patient's description is brief, detailed, clinical or anxious in style
The enquiry-classification model's accuracy stays within a stated margin of its mean across every prompt template and instruction paraphrase in the evaluation set
The risk category extracted from suspicious-transaction reports does not change when the same activity is described with different terminology or layout

name: Causal Mediation Analysis in Language Models
description: Causal mediation analysis traces which internal components of a language model carry the effect of a change in the input to the output. The analyst makes a controlled change to the input, such as swapping 'nurse' for 'man' in a prompt, and measures how the model's next-word probabilities shift. To find the indirect effect through one component (a single neuron, or an attention head, which is the part of the model that chooses which earlier words to focus on), they feed the model the original input but give that component the value it took on the changed input. To find the direct effect, they feed the changed input but hold that component at its original value. Repeating this across many components shows where in the network a behaviour is carried.

example_use_cases.description: A safety team finds that a language model gives unsafe medical advice when a request is phrased as an instruction rather than a question. They compare outputs for the two phrasings and use mediation analysis to find which attention heads carry most of the shift in the probability of the unsafe reply, so a fix can target those heads and the analysis can be rerun to check it worked.

A research team studying why a language model sometimes gets subject-verb agreement wrong in sentences with an intervening clause changes the number of the subject noun and measures the shift in the verb's probability. Mediation analysis then shows which neurons carry the number information, and whether the same neurons are used across sentence structures.

limitations.description: Needs white-box access and knowledge of the architecture. The analyst must read and overwrite activations at chosen points inside the model, so it cannot be used on a model offered only through an API, and a poorly chosen intervention point can give misleading conclusions.

Conclusions hold for the contrast tested. Swapping 'nurse' for 'man' and tracking one probability ratio tests a single contrast, and a different prompt set or outcome measure can point to different components. Effects also differ between models: larger GPT-2 models showed larger effects, and masked language models matched less well.

Every component and every prompt needs its own forward passes, so testing all the neurons or heads of a large model on many prompts is expensive. Analysts often test a subset or groups of components, which can miss effects elsewhere in the network.

Single-component effects do not simply add up. Vig et al. found that intervening on all neurons together produced an effect far larger than the sum of the single-neuron effects, so ranking components one at a time can understate or misplace where a behaviour is carried.

The split into direct and indirect effects is not guaranteed to be exact. In a non-linear network the total effect need not equal their sum, and Vig et al. report only an approximate match for GPT-2, so the split should be checked rather than assumed.

sample_claims.text: On the tested prompts, most of the effect of the input change on the language model's output is carried by a small number of attention heads, each with a measured indirect effect.
The model's subject-verb agreement behaviour is carried by identifiable neurons that are reused across sentences of similar structure.
The shift in the probability of the unsafe reply caused by the instruction phrasing is mediated mainly by identified components, and the finding is reproduced on held-out prompts.
After mitigation is applied to the components identified as carrying the unsafe behaviour, rerunning the same analysis shows a reduced indirect effect.

name: Concept Activation Vectors
description: A concept activation vector (CAV) is a direction inside a neural network that stands for a human idea such as 'stripes'. The analyst supplies example inputs showing the concept and random counter-examples, and trains a simple linear classifier to separate the network's activations (the values a chosen layer produces) for the two sets. The CAV is the direction at right angles to that classifier's dividing boundary, pointing towards the concept examples. Testing with CAVs (TCAV) then reports, for one output class, the share of its inputs whose class score would rise if the activations moved in the concept's direction, and repeating this with many random counter-example sets and applying a significance test guards against a meaningless direction. Concept sets built from examples of a protected characteristic, such as gender or ethnicity, turn the test into a check of whether a class is sensitive to that characteristic, as the original paper demonstrates.

example_use_cases.description: Auditing a medical imaging model to check whether its chest X-ray classifications are sensitive to diagnostic concepts (like 'tumour characteristics') or to irrelevant ones (like 'scanner type' or 'patient positioning'), so the clinical team can judge whether the model relies on medically relevant information.

A team auditing an image classifier used for content tagging builds concept sets from photographs of people of different ethnicities and genders, with random photographs as the comparison, and tests each output class for significant sensitivity to those concepts, as the original paper did. Classes with significant sensitivity to an ethnicity or gender concept are listed for retraining with balanced data; a low score is not taken as clearance.

A developer of a driver-assistance system documents, for a type-approval authority, how its traffic-sign classifier responds to visual concepts. The report gives significance-tested TCAV scores for the 'stop sign' class against concepts such as graffiti, snow cover and low sun glare, so the authority can see what the classifier's predictions are sensitive to.

limitations.description: Requires clearly defined concept examples and non-concept examples, which can be hard to obtain for abstract or subjective concepts. If the examples differ from the random counter-examples in other ways, such as image source or lighting, the CAV mixes those differences in with the concept.

Assumes the concept is represented as a direction that a linear classifier can pick out at the chosen layer. If the concept is not linearly separable there, the CAV is unreliable, so check that the classifier separates the two sets well before reading any scores.

Results depend heavily on which layer is examined, because layers capture different levels of abstraction. A concept can be invisible at one layer and strong at another, so a single-layer result should not be generalised.

The significance test trains hundreds of classifiers per concept and layer (the paper uses about 500), so cost multiplies with the number of concepts and layers tested. FastCAV, a 2025 preprint, reports speed-ups of up to 63.6 times.

Scores are class-level and describe sensitivity, not cause. A TCAV score is the share of a class's inputs whose score rises along the concept direction, so it does not explain an individual decision, and a high score does not show that the concept causes the prediction.

sample_claims.text: The chest X-ray classifier's 'pneumonia' predictions are significantly sensitive to clinically recognised findings and not significantly sensitive to scanner type or patient positioning, at the layers tested.

The content-tagging classifier's TCAV scores for the ethnicity and gender concept sets are recorded for every output class at the tested layers, and the classes with significant sensitivity are listed for review.
The traffic-sign classifier's sensitivity to graffiti, snow cover and glare concepts is documented with significance-tested TCAV scores for each sign class the approval authority has requested.
The object recogniser's class predictions depend mainly on concepts that domain experts regard as meaningful for that class, such as shape and texture, rather than on background concepts.

name: Reweighing
description: Reweighing is a pre-processing method, from Kamiran and Calders (2012), that removes the statistical association between a protected attribute and the outcome label in training data by giving each training example a weight, without changing any feature values or labels. For every combination of group and label (for example, women who were hired), the weight is the number of examples that combination would have if group and label were independent, divided by the number it actually has: the group's share of the data times the label's share, over the combination's observed share. Combinations rarer than independence predicts, such as positive outcomes in a disadvantaged group, are weighted up and over-represented ones are weighted down, so that in the weighted data every group has the same rate of positive labels. A model is then trained on the original data using these weights; the outputs are the weighted training set and a small table of weights that records exactly how each group-label combination was adjusted.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's model team finds that in the historical loan decisions used as training labels, applicants from one ethnic group were approved far less often than others. Before retraining its approval model it computes reweighing weights, so that approved applicants from that group count for more and refused ones for less, trains with them as sample weights, and compares the approval-rate gap and accuracy on held-out data against the unweighted model.

A health insurer's analytics team building a model to target postpartum depression outreach from Medicaid claims compares reweighing by race with simply removing race from the inputs. It reports each option's disparate impact ratio (the ratio of positive-prediction rates between groups) and predictive performance to its clinical governance group before choosing one.

A recruitment platform training a shortlisting model on past hiring outcomes, in which women were hired into senior engineering roles less often than men, applies reweighing by sex before training so that the weighted history shows equal hiring rates, then checks shortlisting rates by sex on a held-out set of applications.

An auditor reviewing a benefits-fraud model asks for the table of reweighing weights kept with the training run. A weight of 1.8 on one nationality group's not-fraud cases shows how far that group's historical labels departed from independence, and the table records exactly how the training data were adjusted, so the auditor can reconstruct the intervention without rerunning it.

limitations.description: Its target is fixed: equal rates of positive labels across groups in the weighted training data (statistical parity).
