Scores are averaged over many cases, are in the units of the forecast quantity with lower values better, and are often reported as a skill score relative to a reference forecast such as climatology (the long-run historical distribution), giving evidence for claims about the accuracy of a forecaster's probabilities by variable, location and lead time.

example_use_cases.description: A national weather service deciding whether to run a machine-learning ensemble alongside its physics-based ensemble scores both against a year of station observations, computing the fair CRPS (the two ensembles differ in size) for 2-metre temperature and 10-metre wind at every station and lead time. It adopts the new system only for the variables and lead times where its CRPS skill relative to the existing ensemble is positive.

A wind-farm operator choosing between two vendors of probabilistic power forecasts for day-ahead trading receives 19 quantiles per hour from each. It approximates each forecast's CRPS by averaging the quantile scores across those levels and compares the vendors over a full winter against metered output. Because high-output hours drive balancing costs, it also compares them on a version of the score weighted towards the upper quantiles, averaged over all hours, not only those with high output.

A hospital group's capacity team plans elective admissions with a probabilistic forecast of bed occupancy one week ahead. Each week it computes the forecast's CRPS against the occupancy that followed and its skill score against a seasonal naive forecast, and a rolling eight-week skill score below zero triggers a review of the model before it is used for the next planning cycle.

limitations.description: One CRPS value combines calibration (whether outcomes behave like draws from the forecast distribution) and sharpness (how narrow the forecast is), so a better score does not show which improved, and an average over many cases can hide conditions in which forecasts are consistently too narrow or too wide. A claim about calibration needs Hersbach's decomposition of the score into reliability and resolution parts, a rank histogram or a spread-skill check as well.

Every threshold carries equal weight and extreme outcomes are rare, so the average score says little about how well extremes are forecast; WeatherBench 2 notes that the CRPS does not specifically focus on extreme weather. Averaging only over cases in which an extreme occurred does not repair this and can discredit skilful forecasters (Lerch et al. 2017); claims about warnings of extremes need a threshold-weighted CRPS that emphasises the tails.

It scores one quantity at one place and lead time at a time, so it does not test whether a forecast gets the relationships between places, times or variables right. WeatherBench 2 notes that its CRPS results ignore spatial and temporal correlation, and found models trained on each wind component separately biased in wind speed; claims about joint quantities, such as rainfall totalled over a catchment, need a multivariate score such as the energy score.

The score is in the units of the forecast quantity and grows with how variable that quantity is, so raw values cannot be compared or pooled across variables, locations or seasons with different variability, and averages are dominated by the most variable cases. Comparisons across these need a skill score relative to a stated reference forecast, and the choice of reference, such as climatology or persistence, changes the result.

For an ensemble, the usual estimate treats the members as the whole forecast distribution, which penalises small ensembles: if two systems draw members from the same distribution, the one with fewer members scores worse on average. Ferro (2014) showed the usual ensemble CRPS is unfair in this sense and gave an adjusted fair version, which libraries such as scoringrules provide; it should be used whenever ensembles of different sizes are compared.

sample_claims.text: Over the 2025 verification year, the machine-learning ensemble has a lower mean fair CRPS for 2-metre temperature than the operational ensemble at every lead time from one to ten days, averaged over all stations in the service area.
The one-week-ahead bed-occupancy forecast has had a positive CRPS skill score relative to a seasonal naive forecast in every rolling eight-week window since it entered use.

Scored against metered output over the winter season, the selected vendor's probabilistic wind-power forecasts have a lower mean CRPS than the alternative vendor's, and also a lower mean when the score is weighted towards high output, with both averages taken over all hours.
The comparison between the 20-member and 50-member ensemble systems used the fair version of the CRPS, so the reported difference does not reflect ensemble size.

name: Explainer Latency Benchmarking
description: Explainer latency benchmarking measures how long an explanation method takes to produce an explanation for a single prediction, on the hardware, software and settings it will run with, and compares the result with the time that the decision it supports allows. The evaluator first sets the time budget, the share of the time the decision allows that is left for the explanation once the prediction is ready, then runs the explainer exactly as it will be deployed (the same model, background data, number of samples and batch size) on a representative set of real inputs, timing each explanation from request to a result ready to display, after warm-up runs and with one-off set-up costs, such as building the explainer, recorded separately. Because the time varies with the model, the data, the hardware and the load on the system, each configuration is timed many times, as machine-learning inference benchmarks such as MLPerf Inference time a model, under realistic concurrent demand where the explainer runs as a shared service, and the result is reported as a distribution: the median, high percentiles such as the 95th or 99th, the slowest case and the share of explanations over budget. Canha et al.'s benchmark framework for explanation methods, which scores methods on properties measurable without human participants, includes this property under the name speed and rates it on a five-level scale with cut-offs at 0.1, 1, 5 and 10 seconds aligned with human response-time limits; the scale suits comparisons between methods, while a claim about a deployment needs the measured percentiles set against that deployment's own budget. The output is a latency profile for each explainer configuration, recorded with its hardware, software versions and load, which shows whether explanations will arrive in time and lets a team choose between explainers and settings on speed alongside the explanation quality measured by other tests.

example_use_cases.description: A card issuer shows its fraud analysts a feature attribution beside each held transaction and needs it within the two seconds before the review queue refreshes. Benchmarking on the production server at peak queue load, it finds that a sampling-based explainer misses the budget for about one explanation in twenty while an explainer specific to its tree ensemble stays well inside it, and adopts the second once its attributions pass the same faithfulness tests.

A hospital adding an explanation panel to a sepsis-risk alert in its electronic health record agrees with clinicians that the panel must load within one second of a nurse opening the alert. The informatics team times explanations on the hospital's own servers with a week of real alerts at typical volume, reports the 95th percentile and the slowest case against that limit, and repeats the measurement after each model or software update.

An online marketplace shows each seller the main reasons its moderation model held a new listing for review, and the page must update within three seconds. Before launch, the team times the service on its production servers with a week of recorded traffic replayed at its real pace; the first request after each quiet period is far slower because the explainer and its background data load on demand. It keeps a loaded explainer running, re-measures, and reports the slowest case.

limitations.description: Speed and explanation quality trade off through the explainer's settings. Sampling-based explainers run faster with fewer samples or a smaller background dataset, but SHAP's documentation notes that more samples give lower-variance estimates, so a faster setting gives noisier explanations. A latency result holds only for the settings tested, and must be measured at the settings whose faithfulness and stability were checked, or a configuration may meet the budget with untested explanations.

Times depend on the hardware, the implementation and the load at the moment of measurement, which Canha et al. single out as the main caveat on their speed metric, so a figure from a developer's workstation does not carry over to a shared production server or an edge device. Any change to the model, the explainer version, the hardware or the traffic pattern calls for re-measurement, and the configuration must be recorded with the result for it to be checked or repeated.

Claims about the slowest cases need many timed explanations. MLPerf Inference, which sets tail-latency bounds for model inference in the same way, sizes its runs so that a 99th-percentile bound holds with 99 per cent confidence, which at its chosen margin takes about 263,000 queries. A few hundred timings can support a claim about the median but not about the 99th percentile, and a single timed run supports neither.

A fast explanation is not necessarily a good one. Latency says nothing about whether an explanation reflects what the model did or whether people can use it, and it leaves out the time a person needs to read it. It supports a claim about explanations only alongside tests of faithfulness and stability and, where people act on the explanations, a study of whether they can use them within the time available.

The budget has to come from the decision, not from a generic scale. Canha et al.'s cut-offs reflect general limits on human response time, which may be looser or tighter than a particular workflow allows, and a budget that leaves out the time to run the model, move the data and display the result will be met in the benchmark and missed in use; MLPerf likewise derives its server-scenario latency bounds from the user's overall time target.

sample_claims.text: On the production review server at peak queue load, 99 per cent of feature attributions for held transactions were delivered within the two-second budget set by the fraud-review workflow, measured over more than 300,000 explanations.
The explainer configuration whose latency was benchmarked, including its background data and number of samples, is the same configuration whose faithfulness and stability were evaluated.

After the latest model update, explanation latency was re-measured on the hospital's production servers at typical alert volume, and both the 95th percentile and the slowest case remained within the one-second limit agreed with clinical users.

On the listing-review service's production servers, with a week of recorded traffic replayed at its real pace, both the 95th-percentile and the slowest explanation times, including requests after quiet periods, were within the three-second budget.

name: Kernel Two-Sample Test (Maximum Mean Discrepancy)
description: A kernel two-sample test checks whether two sets of data could have come from the same distribution; in assurance it is used to check whether the inputs a deployed model now receives still resemble the data on which it was validated, and to detect when they stop doing so. Its statistic, the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), is built from a kernel, a function that scores how similar two data points are (commonly a Gaussian function of the distance between them), and in its usual squared form it is the average similarity among points in the reference sample, plus the average similarity among points in the new sample, minus twice the average similarity between points from different samples. With a characteristic kernel such as the Gaussian, the population value is zero only when the two distributions are identical, so the test can respond to any kind of difference, including a change in how features vary together that tests applied to one feature at a time cannot see, and kernels exist for strings and graphs as well as numerical vectors. To obtain a p-value, the two samples are pooled and repeatedly divided at random into groups of the original sizes, the statistic is recomputed for each division, and the p-value is the share of divisions giving a value at least as large as the one observed; high-dimensional inputs such as images are usually first reduced to a short vector, for example the code of an autoencoder or the model's predicted class probabilities. The output, for each window of new data, is the MMD value and its p-value at a stated significance level, which shows whether that window differs detectably from the reference, but not whether the difference affects the model's accuracy.

example_use_cases.description: A card issuer's model-risk team tests a random sample of each night's transactions, at most one per customer, against a fixed sample from the fraud model's validation period, after standardising the input features. It set the significance level so that, with nothing changed, it expects about one false alarm a quarter, and a significant result triggers a check of the model's accuracy on newly labelled cases before its alert thresholds are relied on the next day.

Before switching on a chest X-ray triage model at a second hospital that uses a different make of scanner, the deploying team compares 500 recent images from the new site with 500 from the validation set. Each image is first reduced to a short vector by an autoencoder trained on validation images. A significant difference sends the model for local validation on labelled cases from the new site instead of relying on its original results.

A customer-service team whose question-answering assistant was evaluated on a fixed test set compares the sentence embeddings of each week's user questions with those of the test set. When a week is flagged, it computes the MMD witness function, which scores each question by how much more it resembles the new week's questions than the test set, reads the top-scoring questions, finds queries about a new product, and adds such questions to the test set.

limitations.description: A significant result shows that inputs differ from the reference, not that the model has got worse: Rabanser et al. note that distributions shift constantly and often harmlessly, and with large windows the test can flag differences too small to matter. A drift alarm becomes evidence about performance only when followed by an accuracy check on labelled cases, and an absence of alarms reassures only if the test was shown beforehand to detect the shifts that harm the model.

On raw high-dimensional inputs the test has little power: in Rabanser et al.'s comparison on image data the multivariate test performed poorly without first reducing the dimension. The reduction then decides what can be seen, since a change that leaves the autoencoder code or predicted probabilities unchanged goes undetected. The kernel's width matters too: it is usually set to the median distance between points, which Gretton et al. call a heuristic, the best width being an open question.

The statistic compares every pair of points, so its cost grows with the square of the combined sample size, and the permutation test repeats it many times; Rabanser et al. ran kernel tests only up to 1,000 new samples for this reason. Gretton et al.'s linear-time version is far cheaper but needs much more data for the same power, so high-volume monitoring has to trade window size, detection delay and computing cost against each other.

The permutation p-value assumes that observations within each sample are independent. Consecutive sensor readings, transactions from one customer or successive time steps are correlated, and shuffling them breaks that dependence, so the test signals a difference far more often than its stated level: in Chwialkowski et al.'s experiments on autocorrelated signals the permutation test almost always rejected when nothing had changed. Such data need thinning or a wild bootstrap.

Run on every new window at the conventional 5 per cent level, the test flags about one window in twenty even when nothing has changed, which for daily windows means around 18 false alarms a year. Continuous monitoring needs a stricter level, a correction for repeated testing, or an online version of the test whose threshold is set for an expected run time between false alarms.

sample_claims.text: Applied to autoencoder representations of 500 images from each source, the kernel two-sample test found no significant difference at the 1 per cent level between the new hospital's chest X-rays and the validation images, and the same test detected the simulated scanner changes that had reduced the model's accuracy in validation.

Every alarm raised by the nightly kernel two-sample test on the fraud model's inputs in the past six months was followed within two working days by an accuracy check on newly labelled cases, and each check either met the accuracy requirement or led to retraining.

In each weekly window since deployment, the loan-application model's production inputs showed no difference from its validation sample detectable by the agreed kernel two-sample test, at a significance level corrected for weekly repetition, and the same test detected the input shifts that had reduced the model's accuracy in pre-deployment trials.
Replayed on reference data alone, the drift monitor's kernel two-sample test raised false alarms at no more than the configured rate of one per quarter.

name: Rolling-Origin Evaluation
description: Rolling-origin evaluation, also called time-series cross-validation or backtesting, estimates how accurately a forecasting model will predict the future by repeatedly recreating the position it will be in when used: trained only on data up to a point in time, it forecasts the period that follows. The evaluator chooses a first forecast origin (the last time point the model may see) late enough to leave adequate training data, fits the model on the data up to that origin, forecasts every step of a fixed horizon ahead, for example one to seven days, and records the error at each lead time against the values later observed. The origin then moves forward by one step or a block of steps and the process repeats, with the model either refitted at each origin on all the data so far or on a window of fixed length (recalibration, in Tashman's terms), or kept unchanged and simply given the new observations as inputs (updating), whichever matches how it will be maintained in service. Because every forecast uses only data from before its origin, the method avoids the leakage of future information that randomly shuffled cross-validation can cause on time-ordered data, and because it uses many test periods rather than the single one of a fixed train-test split, its result depends less on which period happened to be held out. The output is the forecast error, under whatever error measure suits the forecast, broken down by lead time and by origin date for each candidate model, which supports claims about expected accuracy on unseen future data over a stated horizon and shows how that accuracy varies across seasons and conditions.

example_use_cases.description: A regional electricity distributor deciding whether to replace its regression model for day-ahead substation demand with a gradient-boosted model evaluates both over the last two years, with an origin each day at the time forecasts are issued, a horizon of the next 48 half-hours and weekly refitting, as planned for operation. It compares error at each lead time and in each season, and switches only after finding the new model better in winter peaks as well as on average.

A national weather service's post-processing team testing a machine-learning correction for station temperature forecasts places origins every day over three years, with lead times of one to ten days, and refits the correction monthly as it would in service. Error by lead time and by month shows whether the correction still helps at the longest lead times and whether its gain in winter holds in all three winters rather than one.

A hospital's operations analysts choosing a model to forecast emergency admissions one to fourteen days ahead for staff rotas compare a seasonal statistical model with a neural network, using weekly origins over two years that include two winter peaks. They report error at the seven-day lead time the rota planners use, and keep the simpler model because the neural network's advantage disappears at that horizon.

limitations.description: Refitting at every origin multiplies training cost by the number of origins: daily origins over two years means more than 700 fits. Machine-learning forecasters are often refitted only now and then and otherwise just fed new data, which Hewamalage et al. describe as common practice; that is cheaper but measures something different, so the refit schedule in the evaluation must match the one planned for deployment or the errors do not describe the deployed system.

The time-ordered split prevents leakage only through the split itself. Scaling, smoothing, decomposition, feature selection or tuning done on the whole series before splitting, or features summarising a period not yet over at the forecast time, still let future information in. Hewamalage et al. show a model beating the best possible forecast of a random walk only because a decomposition was fitted to the whole series; every such step must be redone within each origin.

Errors from neighbouring origins share most of their training data and, for multi-step horizons, overlapping test periods, so they are correlated: an average over hundreds of origins is less precise than the count suggests, and the spread across origins is not a confidence interval. Deciding whether one model beats another needs a test designed for serially correlated forecast errors, such as the Diebold-Mariano test, not a plain comparison of average errors.

The first origins have little training data, so their errors can overstate those of a model trained on the full history, and a short series leaves few test periods and a noisy average. For purely autoregressive models (past values as the only inputs) on stationary series, whose errors show no remaining autocorrelation, Bergmeir et al. show that standard k-fold cross-validation remains valid, and Hewamalage et al. recommend it for short series as it uses the data more efficiently.

It measures how the model would have performed over the history available, not how it will perform after a change that history does not contain, such as a new tariff, a replaced sensor or an abrupt structural break; Hewamalage et al. note that no evaluation design can anticipate a break that lies only in the future. Results should be stated for the periods and conditions they cover and repeated as new data arrive.

sample_claims.text: Across daily forecast origins over the two most recent years, the new day-ahead demand model has a lower mean absolute error than the current model at every lead time from one to 48 half-hours, and the difference is significant under a test designed for serially correlated forecast errors.

With weekly refitting matching the planned retraining schedule, the seven-day-ahead admissions forecast stayed within the agreed error limit in every month of the two-year rolling-origin evaluation, including both winters.
Every scaling, feature-selection and tuning step behind the reported forecast errors used only data available before each forecast origin.
The temperature correction reduces ten-day-ahead forecast error in each of the three winters covered by the rolling-origin evaluation, not only on average across them.

name: Deletion and Insertion Curves
description: Deletion and insertion curves test whether a feature-attribution explanation, such as a heatmap over an image or highlighted words in a text, puts first the input features the model actually relies on. For the deletion curve, the evaluator removes features in the order the explanation ranks them, most important first, replacing each with a neutral value such as zero, the dataset mean, random noise or a blurred copy, and records the model's score for the explained class after each step; a faithful ranking makes the score fall quickly, so a smaller area under the curve is better (equivalently, a larger area over it, the AOPC score Samek et al. report). The insertion curve runs the other way: it starts from an input with every feature removed or blurred, restores features in ranked order, and rewards a fast rise. For text, the same procedure is often reported as comprehensiveness (how far the predicted-class probability drops when the top-ranked words are deleted) and sufficiency (how far it drops when only those words are kept), either at one cut-off or averaged over cut-offs from the top 1% to the top 50% of words. Explanation methods are compared on the same model, inputs and replacement value, against a random ranking as a baseline, and the result shows how well the ranking tracks the model's behaviour, not whether the highlighted features make sense to a person.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital's cardiology informatics team has a deep network that measures intervals and amplitudes from 12-lead ECGs and must choose which heatmap method to show cardiologists. It perturbs the highest-ranked sample points first, one per step, tracks the rise in measurement error over several thousand ECGs, and compares each method's area under the error curve with that of random heatmaps. Because expert preferences and the curves can disagree, it reports both before choosing.

A regulator's data team routes consumer complaints with a fine-tuned transformer classifier and wants to highlight for caseworkers the words behind each routing decision. Before choosing between two word-attribution methods, it computes comprehensiveness and sufficiency on a validation sample at the 1, 5, 10, 20 and 50% cut-offs and adopts a method only if it clearly beats randomly ranked words on both measures.

A rail operator's engineering team uses an image classifier to flag defects in track inspection photographs and wants heatmaps that point inspectors to the defect. It runs deletion with pixels set to a constant and insertion from a blurred image for three heatmap methods, then repeats the deletion run with a second replacement value, and adopts a method only if it ranks first under both.

limitations.description: Removing pixels or words produces inputs unlike anything the model was trained on, so part of the drop in score can be the model reacting to an unfamiliar input rather than to the loss of the information the explanation pointed to, and the shape of the removed region can itself carry class information. Results are least trustworthy when large parts of the input are removed; variants that retrain the model or fill removed pixels from their neighbours reduce the effect.

The score depends on how features are removed and in what order. On one image classifier, the best-ranked method changed when removed pixels were set to the dataset mean instead of random colours, removing the least relevant pixels first ranked the methods roughly in reverse of removing the most relevant first, and rankings varied from image to image. A comparison holds only for the stated replacement value, order, step size and fraction removed, and should be checked under a second replacement.

Only the order of the attribution scores counts, not their size, so explanations with very different magnitudes can receive the same score. Taking absolute values of signed attributions changes the order and hence the result. The curves cannot tell an explanation that ranks the right features but gives them misleading magnitudes from one that gets both right; that needs a measure that uses the attribution values.

The curves show whether the ranking tracks the model, not whether the explanation is useful or correct for the domain: a model that relies on a spurious cue receives a faithful explanation of that cue. In a study of ECG models, ECG experts' choice of the best heatmap method disagreed considerably with the perturbation ranking, so a good curve does not show that experts will find the explanation helpful.

Each curve needs one model evaluation per step, for every input and method compared, so fine-grained curves over large images, long documents or big test sets are expensive. In the original region-perturbation study, two settings over 5,040 images each, with 100 steps repeated ten times because the replacement values were random, took roughly 36 hours on a workstation with 20 hyper-threaded Xeon cores in 2015. Coarser steps cut the cost but make the curve less able to separate methods.

sample_claims.text: Across a held-out set of ECGs, perturbing the sample points ranked highest by the selected heatmap method raises the interval-measurement error faster than perturbing points ranked by random heatmaps, by at least the margin set in the validation plan, measured by the area under the error curve over the first 15 perturbation steps.

The word highlights shown to complaint caseworkers exceed randomly ranked words by at least the margin set in the validation plan on both comprehensiveness and sufficiency (higher comprehensiveness, lower sufficiency) on the validation sample, averaged over the 1, 5, 10, 20 and 50% cut-offs.

The heatmap method used in the track-inspection tool has a smaller deletion area and a larger insertion area than the other candidate methods on the validation images, under both replacement values tested.

name: Explanation Infidelity
description: Explanation infidelity scores a feature-attribution explanation (one importance score per input feature) by how well it predicts what the model does when the input is changed. The evaluator chooses a distribution of meaningful perturbations, for example small random noise around a reference input, or setting random subsets of features or square patches of an image to a reference value, and draws many perturbations from it. For each one it compares the change in output that the explanation predicts, the sum over features of each feature's perturbation multiplied by its attribution score, with the change the model actually shows, its output on the original input minus its output on the perturbed one. Infidelity is the average squared difference between the two, estimated by random sampling, so lower is better; Yeh et al. (2019), who proposed it, showed that several common explanation methods each have the lowest infidelity for one particular perturbation distribution, so the distribution chosen defines what counts as faithful in a given test. Scores are averaged over a set of inputs and compared across explanation methods, or across settings of one method, under the same perturbations; unlike a deletion curve, the score uses the size of each attribution as well as its rank.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's model-risk team must choose which attribution method supplies the reason scores shown to credit analysts for a neural-network default model. It computes infidelity on held-out applications for three candidate methods, with perturbations that set random subsets of features to a documented reference applicant and with rescaling switched on, and records the perturbation distribution in the validation report beside the method it selects.

A manufacturer's quality team uses a convolutional network to flag defects in weld radiographs and smooths its gradient heatmaps by averaging them over noisy copies of each image. It sets the amount of noise by computing infidelity under square-patch perturbations sized to typical defects on validation radiographs and choosing the level with the lowest score, since in the original study infidelity first fell and then rose as smoothing increased.

A hospital's clinical AI team retrains its deterioration-risk model each quarter and shows ward staff the attribution scores behind each alert. After every retraining it recomputes rescaled infidelity on the latest validation data, with the perturbations fixed at first validation, for the deployed attribution settings and two alternatives, and holds the release for review if the deployed settings are no longer the lowest, since the absolute score also moves with the retrained model.

limitations.description: What counts as faithful is set by the perturbation distribution. Yeh et al. show that several common explanations each have the lowest possible infidelity for one particular distribution (for example, Shapley values for the feature-subset scheme that SHAP uses), so a comparison can be won by choosing matching perturbations. The distribution should be fixed in advance and justified by the question the explanation is meant to answer.

The score is a squared error between predicted and actual changes in output, so it depends on the scale of the attribution scores: two methods that rank features identically but on different scales get different infidelity. Yeh et al. rescale each explanation optimally before scoring, and Captum offers this rescaling as an option that is off by default; without it, comparisons across methods mislead.

Some attribution methods multiply each feature's sensitivity by the input's distance from a reference and others do not, and the perturbation term has to be computed to match. Yeh et al. compare the two kinds separately, and Captum asks the user to state which kind is being scored; getting this wrong produces a score that reflects the mismatch rather than the explanation.

It follows from the definition, though Yeh et al. do not discuss it, that the predicted change is a sum of per-feature effects. Where the model's response to the chosen perturbations is not additive, as when pixels within an object or words within a phrase interact, no attribution can reach zero infidelity. The floor is the same for every method scored on the same model and perturbations, so rankings stand, but the score is not the explanation's error alone and cannot be compared across models.

The score is an average over random perturbations, each needing a model evaluation. Yeh et al. used 1,000 perturbations per input; Captum's default is 10. Few samples give noisy scores, so small differences between methods need repeated runs, while many samples multiply the cost by the inputs, methods and settings compared. Quantus's built-in version perturbs square patches and so handles image data only.

sample_claims.text: Under the documented perturbation distribution, the attribution method that supplies credit analysts' reason scores has the lowest rescaled infidelity of the candidate methods on the held-out applications.
The smoothing level used for weld-radiograph heatmaps gives lower mean infidelity under square-patch perturbations than the unsmoothed heatmaps on the validation radiographs.

After each quarterly retraining, the deployed attribution settings have the lowest rescaled infidelity of the settings compared on current validation data, under the perturbation distribution fixed when the explainer was first validated.

name: Explanation Max-Sensitivity
description: Explanation max-sensitivity measures how stable an explanation is: whether inputs that differ only slightly, in ways that should not change the answer, receive very different explanations. For each input, the evaluator samples many nearby points within a small radius (for example, no feature moved by more than 0.02 on a 0 to 1 scale), recomputes the explanation at each with the same explanation method, and records the largest distance between a recomputed explanation and the original; Yeh et al. (2019) defined the measure and estimated it by random sampling. Dividing each change in the explanation by the distance the input moved, and taking the largest ratio, gives the closely related local Lipschitz estimate of Alvarez-Melis and Jaakkola (2018), which they maximised with an optimiser rather than by sampling; the two are not interchangeable, because the ratio is dominated by the smallest input changes and can be unbounded where max-sensitivity is finite, so they can rank methods differently. Lower scores mean a more stable explanation, and scores are compared across explanation methods, or across settings of one method, on the same inputs, radius and distance measure. The test treats the explanation method as a black box, so it applies to attribution scores from any method, but on its own it says nothing about faithfulness: a constant explanation that ignores the model is perfectly stable.

example_use_cases.description: A consumer lender tells declined applicants the main reasons for each decision, taken from Shapley-value attributions of its credit model. Its model-risk team measures max-sensitivity on a sample of declined applications, perturbing features only within bounds the lending policy treats as immaterial, to choose between two sampling budgets for the explainer, because applicants who differ trivially should not be given different main reasons.

An Earth-observation team comparing attribution methods for a multi-label land-cover classifier on satellite image patches computes max-sensitivity for each method together with a most-relevant-first deletion curve, and short-lists methods that do well on both. Pairing the two matters because smoothing an explanation lowers its sensitivity, and a stable method is worth choosing only if it also tracks the model.

A vehicle perception team averages gradient heatmaps over noisy copies of each camera frame to steady them for safety reviewers. It sets the noise level by tracking max-sensitivity and infidelity together on validation frames as the level rises, and picks the point where sensitivity has levelled off before infidelity starts to increase, since too much smoothing produces stable maps that no longer reflect the detector.

limitations.description: A low score does not mean the explanation is right. The most stable explanation possible is a constant one that ignores the model, and heavy smoothing keeps lowering sensitivity while eventually making the explanation less faithful. Max-sensitivity should be reported with a measure of faithfulness on the same inputs, and a method should not be chosen for stability alone.

The sampled maximum is a lower bound on the true worst case: with a handful of random samples per input (Captum's default is 10), the largest change found can be far below the largest that exists. Deliberately chosen perturbations that leave the prediction unchanged can alter explanations dramatically, so a low score does not show that explanations resist manipulation.

The number depends on settings that differ between tools: the radius, the distance measure for inputs and explanations, the number of samples and whether explanations are normalised first. By default Captum samples 10 points within a radius of 0.02 and Quantus 200 points within 0.2, ten times wider, while Yeh et al. used 50 points within 0.1 and normalised explanations to unit length. Scores are comparable only under identical settings and identically scaled inputs.

A high score can come from the model rather than the explanation method. Near a decision boundary, or where the model's output changes quickly, a faithful explanation should change, and Yeh et al. note that explanations built from the model's own sensitivity can be more sensitive than the model. Perturbations that change the prediction should be excluded or reported separately.

The test assumes inputs can be nudged by small continuous amounts. For words, categories or other discrete inputs no such small change exists, and the fallback of comparing explanations of similar examples already in the test data is weaker and depends on how many close neighbours the data contain. The per-unit Lipschitz form can be unbounded for gradient explanations of ReLU networks, one reason Yeh et al. prefer the undivided maximum, which stays finite.

sample_claims.text: On a held-out sample of declined applications, the largest change in normalised attribution scores under perturbations within the lending policy's immaterial bounds stays below the agreed threshold for at least 95% of applications.

The attribution method used for land-cover analysts has the lowest mean max-sensitivity of the candidate methods on the validation patches at the stated radius and sample count, and a steeper deletion curve than a random ranking.

At the noise level used to smooth the perception system's heatmaps, mean infidelity on validation frames is no higher than at any lower level tested, and mean max-sensitivity is within the tolerance stated in the test plan of the lowest value reached across the levels tested.

name: Sanity Checks for Saliency Maps
description: Sanity checks for saliency maps are two randomisation tests that show whether an explanation method's output depends on what a neural network has learned, or would look much the same for a network that had learned nothing. In the model parameter randomisation test, the evaluator recomputes explanations for a fixed set of inputs after replacing the trained weights with random ones, either cumulatively from the output layer down towards the input (cascading randomisation) or one layer at a time with the others left trained (independent randomisation). In the data randomisation test, the evaluator trains a copy of the same architecture on the training data with the labels shuffled, until it has memorised them, and compares its explanations with those of the model trained on the true labels. Similarity between original and randomised explanations is measured with rank correlation, with and without absolute values, and with image similarity scores such as the structural similarity index; a method whose maps stay similar fails, because its output cannot reflect the learned weights or the relationship between inputs and labels, as Guided Backpropagation and Guided GradCAM failed in the original study when the upper layers were randomised, while plain gradients and GradCAM passed. Passing is a necessary condition, not proof of a good explanation: it shows a method responds to the model, not that its explanations are faithful or useful.

example_use_cases.description: A radiology AI group considering saliency maps as a guide to where a chest-radiograph model sees a pneumothorax runs cascading randomisation on the trained network, measuring structural similarity between original and randomised maps after each block. It sets aside methods whose maps stay similar, as several common methods did in a published study of this task, unless a deletion test shows they still track the model, and uses the rest only alongside a separately validated localisation model.

An insurer's fraud analytics team shows investigators attribution scores for each claim flagged by a neural-network model. Before rollout it runs independent layer randomisation, one layer at a time, and checks that rank correlation without absolute values falls for every layer, so that the scores investigators see depend on the trained weights throughout the network rather than mostly on the claim's raw feature values.

A wind-farm operator's reliability team uses a one-dimensional convolutional network on gearbox vibration signals and gives maintenance engineers heatmaps over each signal. It runs the data randomisation test by training the same architecture on shuffled fault labels until it fits them, and keeps only heatmap methods whose maps differ clearly between the two networks, since a map that survives shuffled labels cannot show what the network learned about faults.

limitations.description: Passing is easy for an explanation that carries no information. Binder et al. show that attribution maps with no correlation between neighbouring pixels score well in model randomisation tests, and that top-down randomisation tends to preserve the scale of forward-pass activations, so even a good explanation can change only so much. They argue the test should not alone decide whether a method is kept: two methods that score poorly on it beat several gradient methods in occlusion-based tests.

The verdict depends on how similarity is measured. In the original study, rank correlation with absolute values and structural similarity stayed high for some methods after randomisation while rank correlation without absolute values fell to near zero, because randomisation flipped signs but kept the input's outline. There is no agreed pass threshold and libraries set their own defaults, so the measure, absolute-value setting and threshold must be reported with the result.

The similarity measures are sensitive to noise, so a method with noisy maps looks changed by randomisation partly because of its own noise, and its score is overstated. Later work proposes repairs: averaging each explanation over noisy copies of the input before comparing (Smooth MPRT), or comparing how much more complex the explanation becomes after full randomisation (Efficient MPRT); its authors report more reliable results with both.

The model parameter test needs the weights and a layered network, so it cannot be run on a model reached only through an interface. The data randomisation test needs the training data and pipeline and a network able to memorise shuffled labels; the original study trained to over 95% training accuracy, which for a large model costs a full training run.

Most evidence for the tests comes from image classifiers. Passing says nothing about whether the highlighted regions match what matters in the domain: in a chest-radiograph study, every saliency method, including those that passed the randomisation test, localised abnormalities worse than a dedicated detection or segmentation network.

sample_claims.text: Every saliency method used in the chest-radiograph review tool produced maps whose structural similarity to the original fell below the agreed threshold once the top blocks of the network were randomised, on a held-out sample of radiographs.

For the fraud model's attribution scores, rank correlation without absolute values between original and layer-randomised attributions is below the threshold set in the validation plan for every layer tested.

Heatmaps from the methods kept for the gearbox dashboard differ between the network trained on true fault labels and the same architecture trained on shuffled labels, by more than the threshold stated in the test report.

name: Diverse Counterfactual Explanations
description: Diverse Counterfactual Explanations (DiCE) explains one decision of a classifier by generating several altered versions of the input, called counterfactuals, each changed just enough that the model would have given the other outcome, and chosen to differ from one another so that a person sees several distinct ways the result could have been different. Where the contrastive explanation method returns, for one input, a minimal set of features that must be present and a minimal set that must stay absent, DiCE returns several complete alternative inputs at once, within limits the user sets on which features may change and over what range. In the original method all the counterfactuals are optimised together by gradient descent on a loss with three parts: a hinge loss that pushes each across the model's decision threshold, a distance term (each continuous feature's change divided by its median absolute deviation in the training data, plus the share of categorical features changed) that keeps each close to the original, and a diversity term, the determinant of a similarity matrix between them, that rewards them for differing. Afterwards, small changes are reset to their original values for as long as the counterfactual still gets the other outcome, to make it sparser, and counterfactuals that break causal rules supplied by the user, such as gaining a degree without growing older, can be filtered out. The method as published needs a differentiable model such as a neural network; the reference library adds random-sampling, genetic-algorithm and nearest-training-example searches that need only the model's predictions.

example_use_cases.description: A credit-risk validation team at a lender generates five counterfactuals for each of 500 sampled refused applications with every feature free to change, to see what the model treats as enough for approval. Counterfactuals that reach approval by changing only the postcode, or another likely proxy for a protected characteristic, are logged as findings and passed to the fairness testing team.

A hospital team piloting a classifier that places patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in low, moderate or high cardiovascular risk generates counterfactuals restricted to modifiable factors such as blood pressure, cholesterol and smoking. Clinicians check whether the changes the model links to a lower risk category agree with clinical knowledge before the tool is shown to patients.

A consumer lender puts up to three counterfactuals in each refusal letter, generated against the model version that made the decision and limited to features the applicant can change (income, balances, loan amount and term), each shown as an application that would have been approved. Before rollout it tests a draft letter with applicants, checking that they can name a change that would have worked and understand that the options are not a promise of approval if they reapply.

limitations.description: A counterfactual is only valid for the model version that produced it. The method assumes the model does not change, and after retraining a previously suggested change can stop flipping the decision, so a person who acts on it may still be refused. Counterfactuals shown to people should be dated, tied to a model version and re-checked whenever the model is updated.

Feasibility depends on constraints the user supplies. Without them, counterfactuals can change attributes a person cannot change, such as race or sex, or propose impossible combinations: in the original experiments over a third of the counterfactuals that changed education were infeasible, most raising the degree without raising age. Causal rules can only be applied afterwards, as a filter.

The set returned is not unique. It depends on the weights on distance and diversity, per-feature weights, the number requested and random starting points, and with the library's random-sampling method a different seed gives a different set. The authors note that showing people counterfactuals produced with different settings is a problem, so fix and record settings and seeds.

Distance is measured feature by feature (scaled change for numbers, changed or not for categories), so it ignores how features move together, treats every category change as equally hard, and can place counterfactuals where there is little real data. In a study of 9,613 patient records, DiCE's counterfactuals were closer and sparser but less plausible than those of a sampling-based alternative.

The original paper tests no people. Its stand-in for understanding, a nearest-neighbour model trained on the counterfactuals, is in the authors' words a best case of rational extrapolation, and they leave a behavioural study and the cost of choosing among more options to future work. A counterfactual also does not say which features must stay as they are, so a person who raises income by changing job may still be refused. Test the wording with recipients before relying on it.

sample_claims.text: For 500 sampled refused applications, no counterfactual reached approval by changing only the postcode or another field on the agreed list of proxies for protected characteristics.

Every refusal letter issued since the model release contains at least two counterfactuals that change only features on the agreed list of applicant-changeable features, each re-scored against the model version in use on the day the letter was sent and confirmed to reach approval.

For 100 sampled patients, clinicians found no case in which the cardiovascular-risk classifier's counterfactuals, restricted to modifiable risk factors, reached a lower risk category through a change contrary to clinical guidance.
Re-running counterfactual generation with the recorded settings and seed reproduces the counterfactual sets given to applicants for all audited cases.

In a comprehension test of the draft refusal letter with 50 recent applicants, at least 80% named a change that would have led to approval, and at least 80% correctly said that the options do not guarantee approval if they reapply.

name: GNNExplainer
description: GNNExplainer explains one prediction of a graph neural network, a model that passes information along the edges of a graph such as a molecule, a payment network or a mesh of weather grid points, by finding a small subgraph and a small set of input features that most support that prediction. Explanation methods for flat inputs, such as SHAP and LIME, give each input feature its own score and have no built-in notion of a connection between two nodes; this method scores the connections themselves, restricted to the part of the graph the model actually reads for the prediction (its computation graph, the neighbourhood within as many hops as the model has message-passing layers). It learns a mask with a value between 0 and 1 for each edge of that computation graph and for each node-feature dimension by gradient descent: the masked graph is fed to the model, and the masks are adjusted to keep the predicted label as likely as possible while penalties keep the total mask small and push values towards 0 or 1. Edges and features whose mask values fall below a threshold are then dropped, leaving a compact subgraph and feature subset that can be drawn over the input graph; the same procedure explains node labels, predicted links and whole-graph labels, and the original paper also aligns the explanations of many nodes of one class into a summary pattern. It needs gradient access to the model, and each explanation is a separate optimisation.

example_use_cases.description: A pharmaceutical company's computational toxicology team uses a graph neural network to flag candidate molecules as likely mutagenic. For each flagged compound it reviews the substructure and atom features GNNExplainer selects and checks them against known structural alerts such as nitro groups, to decide whether a flag rests on chemistry the team recognises before the compound is deprioritised.

A bank's financial-crime unit scores accounts with a graph neural network over its payment network to flag likely money-mule accounts. Investigators receive with each flag the explanation subgraph of counterparties and transfers and the account features it selected, and use them to decide whether to escalate; model validators sample explanations to check that flags do not rest mainly on features such as branch or account-opening channel.

A weather service's model evaluation team runs the regression mode of the PyTorch Geometric implementation on a small set of high-impact forecasts from a graph-based forecasting model, such as the predicted rainfall total at one location. Forecasters check whether the connections and input variables selected, for example humidity upwind, are physically plausible, and the team deletes the selected connections to confirm the forecast changes, before such forecasts feed a warning service.

limitations.description: Each explanation is a separate optimisation, run for a set number of steps (100 by default in the PyTorch Geometric implementation), so explaining many nodes or graphs is slow and explanations of similar cases are not required to agree. A view of the model as a whole needs an extra step, such as the class-level summary in the original paper, or a method that trains one explainer for all instances.

The masks are soft during optimisation, so the model is run on graphs whose edges and features are scaled by fractions it never saw in training, and these values can add meaning or noise of their own. The objective is not convex and the masks start at random: in a 2024 benchmark, the ten-edge explanations from runs with different seeds overlapped by a Jaccard index of only 0.18 to 0.80 across six datasets. The final subgraph also depends on the threshold used to cut the mask.

The size of the explanation is set by the user, not found. The original experiments fixed it at the known size of the planted pattern on synthetic graphs and at 10 edges and 5 features on real ones, and the PyTorch Geometric implementation advises tuning the size penalty to the graph's average degree. A compact explanation can therefore leave out structure the model uses.

Most evidence that it finds the right structure comes from synthetic graphs with planted patterns, and a trained model need not use the planted edges, so agreement with them can mislead. A 2023 benchmark found graph explainers, this one included, less faithful when linked nodes tend to differ and when the deciding structure is large. Check fidelity on your own model, for example by deleting the explanation and measuring the change.

It assumes the computation graph is small. The computation graph grows with every message-passing layer, so in a mesh-based forecasting model that passes messages many times along long-range edges (GraphCast uses 16 such layers) it probably spans most of the mesh: the mask then covers most edges and compactness comes from the size penalty, not the model. This has not been tested. PyTorch Geometric applies the mask inside its own message-passing layers, so the model must use them or be adapted.

sample_claims.text: For at least 90% of the validation molecules the toxicity model flags as mutagenic, the explanation subgraph contains a recognised structural alert, and deleting the explanation subgraph removes the flag for at least 80% of them.
Across 300 sampled money-mule flags, branch and account-opening channel are never among the three node features with the highest mask values in the explanation.

For each of the 20 high-impact rainfall forecasts reviewed, forecasters judged the selected connections and input variables physically plausible, and removing the selected connections changed the forecast total by more than the agreed tolerance.
Repeating each reviewed explanation from five random starting masks gives ten highest-weighted edge sets whose pairwise Jaccard index is at least 0.8.

name: Sparse Autoencoder Feature Analysis
description: Sparse autoencoder feature analysis looks for human-interpretable units inside a neural network, usually a language model, by learning from the activations at one layer a large dictionary of directions, called features, such that each activation vector can be rebuilt from only a few of them. Unlike neuron activation analysis it does not take the network's own neurons as the units, since single neurons often respond to several unrelated things, and unlike concept activation vectors it needs no labelled examples of a concept chosen in advance, because the features are found without supervision. The analyst records activations at the chosen layer over a large body of ordinary text and trains an autoencoder, a network with one hidden layer usually several times wider than the layer studied, to reconstruct them while a sparsity penalty keeps most hidden units at zero; the decoder weights of each hidden unit then give one feature direction. Each feature is labelled from the inputs on which it fires most strongly, by a person or by a language model that writes a description, which is then scored on how well it predicts the feature's activations on other text, and the label is tested by removing or amplifying the feature inside the running model and checking the change in output. The output is a catalogue of labelled features with example activations, interpretability scores and measured effects, plus a reconstruction score saying how much of the layer's behaviour the dictionary accounts for; the features can then serve as units for causal mediation analysis, which traces pathways, while this method finds and checks the units themselves.

example_use_cases.description: Before deploying an open-weights language model as a customer-service assistant, a bank's AI assurance team uses sparse autoencoders published for that model to find features active on prompts where the assistant should refuse to give investment advice. It tests each candidate by suppressing it and measuring the change in refusal rate, and records which labelled features the refusal behaviour depends on in the model's assurance file.

A bioinformatics group using a protein language model to annotate newly sequenced proteins trains sparse autoencoders on its embeddings and compares the features with database annotations of binding sites, structural motifs and domains. Features that match known biology are used to propose candidate annotations for curators to verify, features that fire widely with no clear meaning are flagged for review, and the model's own annotation accuracy is still tested on held-out proteins.

A team that fine-tuned a language model to triage clinical referral letters lists the sparse autoencoder features that most change the 'urgent' score on a validation set, and checks whether they describe clinical content or properties of the letter, such as the referring practice's template. A template feature among the leading drivers is recorded as a finding and leads to retraining on reformatted letters.

limitations.description: The dictionary does not capture everything the layer carries, and what it misses cannot be inspected. In the originating study, replacing one layer of a small language model with its reconstruction raised perplexity from 25 to 40; a concurrent study recovered 79% of a layer's contribution to the loss in its main run. Not finding a feature for a concept does not show that the model lacks it.

The features found are not unique. Larger dictionaries split a feature into narrower ones (one base64 feature at 512 features became three at 4,096), and for a 131,000-feature autoencoder on one layer of Llama 3 8B only about 30% of features were shared by two runs differing only in random seed. A conclusion resting on one feature should name the autoencoder used and be checked on a second run.

Labels are hypotheses drawn from the top-activating examples, and automated scores are modest: the first five features reported in the originating study scored between -0.11 and 0.57, and the advantage over simpler decompositions faded in later layers. Back a label with an intervention that changes the output as the label predicts before citing it as evidence.

It needs the model's internal activations, plus storage and compute to train an autoencoder for each layer studied (one concurrent study trained on 8 billion activation vectors from a single layer). For large models practitioners often rely on autoencoders released for particular open-weights models, so the method is not available for a model reached only through an API.

Being interpretable does not make the features better for a given task. In a 2025 study of detecting concepts from model activations, probes built on autoencoder features did not beat logistic regression on the raw activations on average, and the spurious correlations and data problems they exposed could also be found with simpler baselines. Where detection is the goal, compare against such baselines.

sample_claims.text: Substituting the sparse autoencoder's reconstruction for the audited layer recovers at least 90% of that layer's contribution to next-token loss on the audit prompts.

Each feature cited in the refusal analysis has a description that predicts its activations on held-out prompts with a correlation of at least 0.5, and suppressing it lowers the refusal rate on the investment-advice test set by at least 20 percentage points.
None of the 50 features with the largest effect on the triage model's 'urgent' score on the validation set responds mainly to the referring practice's letter template.

Features in the protein model labelled as binding-site detectors activate on annotated binding-site residues of held-out proteins with a precision of at least 0.8, and the same features appear in a second autoencoder trained with a different seed.

name: TimeSHAP
description: TimeSHAP explains one prediction of a model that reads a sequence of events, such as a recurrent neural network that scores a bank transaction using the account's history, by giving each past event, each input feature and selected event-feature cells a Shapley value: a share of the score, taken from cooperative game theory, such that all the shares add up to the difference between the model's score and its score with every event and feature removed. It adapts KernelSHAP, the sampling estimator in SHAP, which explains a single input vector and so, applied to the latest event of a recurrent model, gives earlier events no credit; TimeSHAP instead switches off whole rows or columns of the event-by-feature input matrix, replacing them with a background value (the training-data average in the original paper), queries the model on many such perturbed sequences, and fits a weighted linear model whose coefficients are the attributions. Because the number of event combinations doubles with every event, a pruning step first walks back from the most recent event and merges all older events into a single player once their combined attribution falls below a chosen tolerance, and cell-level values are computed only where the most important events and features intersect, with the other cells grouped. The model is treated as a black box that takes a batch of sequences and returns one score per sequence, and the output is event, feature and cell attributions for each explained sequence, plus plots that aggregate them across many sequences into a global view.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's fraud operations team runs TimeSHAP on each alert from its recurrent account-takeover model, so the analyst reviewing an alert sees which earlier events (for example a password change, then a login from a new device) and which features carried the score, not only the payment being held. The analyst uses this to decide whether to release the payment or contact the customer, and the model team samples the explanations to check that the drivers match known fraud patterns.

A hospital data-science team validating a recurrent model that predicts next-day escalation of treatment for patients in intensive care computes event- and feature-level TimeSHAP values for test-set patients and reviews them with clinicians. Drivers the clinicians judge implausible, such as an indicator that a measurement is missing outweighing the measurements themselves, are investigated before the model is used in a prospective study.

An airport's forecasting team using a recurrent model to warn of fog in the next six hours from the past 48 hours of station observations uses the pruning statistics and global event plots to find how far back the model actually draws on, and the feature attributions to check that humidity, temperature and wind lead each warning. The findings set the input window for the next retraining and go into the model's validation report.

limitations.description: Every attribution is measured against the background chosen to stand for a removed event or feature, the training-data average in the original paper. A sequence containing averaged events may be unlike anything the model has seen, and another background gives other attributions; the original authors note that a feature scoring zero for every sequence may reflect the background rather than the model. Report the background with the results.

Exact values need every combination of events, which doubles with each event. On the original fraud data (median sequence about 138 events), exact values were possible for only 10% of sequences with 32,000 sampled combinations, and repeated runs disagreed (relative standard deviation 1.71 without pruning, 0.98 at the chosen tolerance). With tens of thousands of model calls per explanation, explaining every scored event in real time is impractical; the alerts people review are the usual scope.

Pruning trades detail on older events for speed and stability. All events before the cut-off share one attribution. The cut-off test compares the older block's net, signed attribution with a user-set tolerance, so by construction an early event that pushed the score up can pass unseen if others pushed it down; the original paper does not measure how often this happens. Results change with the tolerance, so fix it in advance and report it.

It explains one score per sequence: the reference implementation expects the model to return a single value for each sequence. A model with many outputs, such as a forecast for several lead times or locations, needs a separate run or a chosen summary for each. The attributions show what the model relies on, not causes in the world: in the original study a high attribution to customer age led to a bias audit, which was needed to establish the disparity.

Each event and feature receives one number, so an effect that arises only from a combination, such as a settings change followed by a login from a new device, is shared out among its parts: an analyst sees each part with some credit but cannot tell that they matter only together. Cell-level values are computed only where the top-ranked events and features intersect. A clinical study using the method found escalation effects hard to see and suggested interactions as the cause.

sample_claims.text: On a sample of 1,000 alerts from the account-takeover model, the five features with the largest mean absolute TimeSHAP attribution are all on the fraud team's list of recognised account-takeover indicators.

Clinicians reviewing the event- and feature-level attributions for 200 test-set patients judged the leading drivers of the escalation model clinically plausible in at least 90% of cases, and each implausible case was traced to a documented data or model issue.
For 95% of the fog warnings explained in validation, observations more than 12 hours before the forecast time carry less than 10% of the summed absolute event attribution.
With the background and pruning tolerance fixed in the validation plan, ten repeated TimeSHAP runs on the validation sample give event attributions whose relative standard deviation is below 0.5.

name: Appropriate Reliance Measurement
description: Appropriate reliance measurement tests whether people who receive an AI system's advice follow it when it is right and keep their own judgement when it is wrong, and whether an explanation, or another aid such as a confidence score, moves them towards that pattern. It uses a two-step decision study on a classification task, the only kind Schemmer et al. define it for: for each task item the participant first decides alone, then sees the AI's advice, with or without the explanation, and makes a final decision, on a set of items with known correct answers drawn so that the AI is wrong on a known share of them. Only items on which the first decision and the advice disagree are counted, because when they agree the final decision cannot show which source the person relied on. Schemmer et al. define two rates over these items: relative AI reliance, the share of items with a wrong first decision and correct advice on which the person switched to the advice, and relative self-reliance, the share of items with a correct first decision and wrong advice on which the person kept their own answer. Comparing the two rates between an explanation condition and a control condition shows whether the explanation reduces under-reliance (rejecting correct advice), reduces over-reliance (accepting wrong advice) or merely raises agreement with the AI, which overall accuracy or agreement with the AI does not show on its own.

example_use_cases.description: An insurer considering highlighted claim features as an explanation for its fraud-flagging model runs a two-step study with its claims handlers on 40 past claims, with the model wrong on a quarter of them, comparing handlers who see the flag alone with handlers who also see the highlights. It adopts the highlights only if relative AI reliance rises without relative self-reliance falling, since higher acceptance of all advice, right and wrong, would show deference rather than better judgement.

A conservation charity whose volunteers identify bird species with help from an image classifier measures relative AI reliance and relative self-reliance separately for experienced birders and beginners, and for example-based and written explanations. It chooses which explanation to show each group from the results, because a volunteer's expertise changes how an explanation, especially a wrong one, shifts their reliance on the classifier.

A hospital whose safety case for a sepsis alert relies on ward doctors overriding wrong alerts, and whose workflow has doctors record their own escalation decision before the alert appears, runs a vignette study in that workflow, with and without the alert's explanation panel. Before switching the panel on, it reports relative self-reliance, and the share of wrong-alert cases that ended in a wrong decision, against the oversight requirement in the safety case.

limitations.description: The rates describe behaviour on a task set built to contain many AI errors: Schemmer et al. drew equal numbers of items from each cell of the confusion matrix, which put the AI's accuracy on their 16 items at 50%. The study does not show how people rely on advice when errors are rarer, as they usually are in service, so it supports a claim about the conditions tested, not a direct estimate of over-reliance in deployment.

Only items on which the first decision and the advice disagree enter the two rates, so each rate can rest on a handful of items per person, and items on which the person and the AI are wrong together, the errors that oversight cannot catch, enter neither rate. Plan the sample around the expected number of disagreements, and report beside the rates the share of wrong-advice items that ended in a wrong final decision.

Asking for a decision before the advice is shown is itself an intervention. Guo et al.'s reanalysis of an earlier study found reliance closer to the appropriate level when people decided first than when they saw the AI's advice first, so a two-step study may show better reliance than a deployed system that presents the advice straight away.

The rates judge each decision by whether the advice turned out to be right, not by whether following it was the better bet given what the person could see. Guo et al. argue that this outcome-based definition mixes two failures, wrong beliefs about how often the AI is right and poor use of those beliefs, and treats a close call the same as an obvious one, so a low rate does not say which to fix.

Results depend on who takes part and on how good the explanations are. Morrison et al. found that participants' expertise changed how incorrect explanations affected their reliance, and that example-based explanations misled participants more than written ones, so a result from novices, or from explanations that were always correct, does not carry over to expert users or to explanations that are sometimes wrong.

sample_claims.text: Claims handlers shown the highlighted features switched to the fraud model's correct advice on a higher share of disagreement cases than handlers shown the flag alone, and the share in which they kept a correct decision against wrong advice was no more than five percentage points lower, the margin set in the study plan.

In a vignette study using the decide-first workflow, ward doctors shown the explanation panel kept their correct escalation decision against an incorrect sepsis alert in at least 80% of disagreement cases, and fewer than 10% of all incorrect alerts led to a wrong final decision.

For both experienced and beginner volunteers, the share of disagreement cases in which they rejected the classifier's incorrect species identification was no more than five percentage points lower with the chosen explanation format than without it, the margin set in advance.

name: Explanation Satisfaction Scale
description: The Explanation Satisfaction Scale is a short questionnaire on which people who have used an AI system's explanations rate how satisfying and sufficient they found them; Hoffman, Mueller, Klein and Litman developed it in the DARPA Explainable AI programme to capture the user's judgement of an explanation, as distinct from a researcher's judgement of its quality. Each item is a statement about the explanation, for example that from it the user understands how the system works, or that it is satisfying, has sufficient detail, seems complete, tells the user how to use the system, is useful to their goals or shows how accurate the system is, and each is rated on a five-point scale from 'I agree strongly' to 'I disagree strongly'. Participants complete it after they have worked with the system and received explanations, usually once for each explanation condition in a study that compares conditions; the published form sets no scoring rule or threshold, and the implementation by one of its authors in the OpenScales library scores it as the mean of the item ratings. Versions differ: the authors' 2018 report gives eight items, their 2023 journal article seven (it drops the item on knowing when to trust the system), and the form on the XAITK site nine (it adds an item on reliability), with a note that researchers may use a subset. The score measures how users judge an explanation, not whether they understood it or decide better with it, and the authors present it beside separate measures of mental models, trust and task performance.

example_use_cases.description: A research team comparing counterfactual images with saliency heatmaps (LIME and layer-wise relevance propagation) for a chest X-ray pneumonia classifier gives lay participants the scale after they have predicted the classifier's decision on a set of images. It chooses which explanation to develop on prediction accuracy and uses the ratings only as a second check, so that the explanation people prefer is not assumed to be the one they understand better.

A team deciding whether causal explanations of a reinforcement-learning agent's strategy in a real-time strategy game are worth the extra modelling gives participants the scale after each explained gameplay video. It compares the causal explanations with a simpler explanation and with no explanation on four items (understanding, satisfaction, sufficient detail and completeness), and pairs the ratings with a test of whether participants can predict the agent's next action.

A lender piloting a new letter that explains which factors led to a credit refusal asks pilot applicants to complete the scale after reading either the new letter or the current one.
