It uses the items on sufficient detail and usefulness to decide whether to add the sentence, held back so far, that says what change would have led to approval.

limitations.description: A high rating does not show that people understand the system or decide better with it. Hase and Bansal found no evidence that participants' ratings of explanation quality predicted whether the explanations helped them predict the model, Buçinca et al. found that subjective measures did not predict performance on the real decision task, and the scale's authors note that people can feel satisfied while their understanding is piecemeal or wrong.

The published evidence for the scale is small: content-validity ratings by 35 attendees of a DARPA programme meeting, an internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha) of 0.86, and eight volunteers rating good and bad explanations of everyday technologies, where the difference was large but only marginally significant. The 2018 report's mean for good explanations (42.75) exceeds what eight items scored 1 to 5 can sum to, so the form tested is unclear, and the XAITK page asks for reliability data.

There are no norms or thresholds, so a score means something only against another condition in the same study, such as the current explanation or no explanation. A mean rating reported on its own, such as 4 out of 5, cannot support a claim that an explanation is satisfactory.

Versions with seven, eight and nine items are in circulation, item wording differs between them, and the form invites researchers to use a subset; Madumal et al., for example, report four items. Scores from different studies are therefore not comparable unless the same items and wording were used, and each study should report exactly which it used.

sample_claims.text: Participants rated the counterfactual explanations higher on the Explanation Satisfaction Scale than the heatmap explanations, and their accuracy in predicting the classifier's decisions was no more than five percentage points below that of the heatmap group, the margin set in the study plan.

Participants rated the causal explanations of the game agent higher than both the simpler explanations and no explanation on the satisfaction, sufficient-detail and completeness items of the Explanation Satisfaction Scale.
Pilot applicants who received the new refusal letter rated its explanation higher on the 'sufficient detail' and 'useful to my goals' items than applicants who received the current letter.

name: Forward Simulation Test
description: A forward simulation test checks whether people who have studied a model's explanations can predict the model's output for inputs they have not seen, so it tests with people the understanding an explanation method is assumed to give, where fidelity checks only compare the explanation with the model by computation. Doshi-Velez and Kim proposed it as a human-grounded evaluation of interpretability: participants are given an explanation and an input and must state what the model will output, whether or not that output is correct. In the controlled design of Hase and Bansal, participants study a set of examples with the model's outputs, predict the outputs for a separate set of test inputs, then study the same examples with explanations added and predict the same test inputs again, and the gain in accuracy is credited to the explanations (a separate group that studies the examples without explanations guards against a practice gain); the test inputs are kept apart from the explained examples so that explanations cannot give the answers away, and are chosen so that the model is right and wrong equally often, so that predicting the true label scores no better than chance. A counterfactual variant, in Hase and Bansal's form, shows an input, the model's output and its explanation, and asks what the model will output for an edited version of that input, with edits chosen so that half change the output. The result is the change in the share of correct predictions, with a confidence interval, for each explanation method or design compared; it is evidence that people can anticipate the model on the kind of input tested, not that they make better decisions with it.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's model validation team must choose between feature-attribution bar charts and a short rule list as the explanation shown to credit analysts for a loan-default model. It runs a forward simulation test with 30 credit analysts on past applications, balanced between correct and incorrect model predictions, and adopts the rule list only if its gain over the no-explanation baseline is clearly larger than that of the bar charts; otherwise it treats the two as equal.

An online platform's trust and safety team uses the counterfactual variant to test whether moderators who see which words a toxicity classifier weighted can predict whether it will still flag a comment after one of those words is replaced. A score no better than the baseline tells the team that the highlights do not show how the classifier responds to edits, before it writes moderation guidance that relies on them.

A research team choosing between counterfactual images and saliency heatmaps for a chest X-ray pneumonia classifier shows each group of participants explained example images, then asks them to predict the classifier's decision on 12 other images, three from each cell of its confusion matrix, without explanations. It takes forward to a study with clinicians the explanation whose group predicts best, measured against a group that saw the examples without explanations.

A local authority plans to show caseworkers, who are outside the team that built it, the reasons behind a housing-benefit fraud-risk score. Before releasing the reasons in that form, it runs a forward simulation test with caseworkers on unseen cases, half of them cases the score got wrong, using the reasons exactly as they will appear, and revises them if caseworkers who studied them predict the flag no better than caseworkers who did not.

limitations.description: A pass shows that people can anticipate the model, not that they decide better with it. Buçinca et al. found that results on a task of predicting an AI's decisions did not predict results on the real decision task, and Poursabzi-Sangdeh et al. found that people who could better simulate a simple, clear model did not follow it more when that helped, and in some experiments were less able to correct its large mistakes. A claim about decisions needs a decision study.

The test is easily made trivial. If the explained examples are reused as test items, explanations that show the predicted class or a probability give the answer away, and if the model is mostly right, participants can score well by predicting the true label. Hase and Bansal found earlier studies that reused the same items for explanation and prediction; results from such designs overstate what the explanation conveys.

Effects are often small against the variation between people and items. With 32 trained undergraduates and about 180 to 320 responses per condition, Hase and Bansal's 95% confidence intervals on the change in accuracy were about 8 to 13 percentage points either side, and only LIME on tabular data clearly improved both forward and counterfactual simulation. A study must be sized for the difference it needs to detect, with a bootstrap over both participants and items.

The score holds for the people tested. Many studies use students or crowd workers because domain experts are costly to recruit, which Doshi-Velez and Kim give as the reason this kind of evaluation is cheaper; a result from lay participants does not show that the clinicians, analysts or caseworkers who will use the explanation can predict the model.

The before-and-after design credits any gain to the explanations, but participants see the same examples and test items twice, and Hase and Bansal had no group that repeated both phases without explanations, so a practice gain is not ruled out. Their participants also found it hard to remember the explained examples while predicting, so the number of examples and the time allowed must be fixed and reported when methods are compared.

sample_claims.text: Credit analysts who studied the rule-list explanations predicted the loan-default model's output on unseen applications more accurately than at their no-explanation baseline, on a test set balanced between correct and incorrect model predictions.

Caseworkers who studied the fraud-risk reasons predicted the score's flag on unseen cases, half of them cases the score got wrong, more accurately than caseworkers who studied the same cases without the reasons, and above the accuracy threshold set in the evaluation plan.

Moderators shown the toxicity classifier's word weightings predicted whether an edited comment would still be flagged more accurately than before they saw the weightings, on a set of edits half of which changed the classifier's decision.

Participants who studied the counterfactual images predicted the pneumonia classifier's decisions on separate, unexplained images more accurately than participants who studied the saliency heatmaps, on a test set in which the classifier was wrong as often as it was right.

name: Think-Aloud Study of Explanation Use
description: A think-aloud study of explanation use asks a small number of participants to say what they are thinking while they use an AI system's explanations to do a realistic task, so that the design team can see how the explanation is read, used, ignored or misread. It applies the think-aloud method from cognitive psychology, which rests on Ericsson and Simon's account of verbal reports: people can voice what they are attending to as they work without changing their thinking, provided they are not asked to report things they would not otherwise attend to, such as the reasons for their actions. In a session, a facilitator gives a short practice task, then sets tasks in which the participant sees the model's output and explanation and makes a decision, and while the participant works gives only neutral reminders, such as 'what are you thinking?', when they fall silent; audio and screen are recorded. The recordings are transcribed and coded, often by thematic analysis, into findings such as parts of the explanation that were misread, parts never looked at and questions it left unanswered, and the team changes the design and tests it again. The output is qualitative, design-stage evidence about how an explanation is understood: it can show that a misreading occurs, but not how often it occurs among users or whether their decisions improve.

example_use_cases.description: A team building a nurse-facing explanation for a patient deterioration score runs think-aloud sessions with six ward nurses on a clickable prototype using past patient records. It finds that nurses read a factor that lowered the score as a sign that the patient was improving, relabels the chart, and re-tests the new labels in a second round before fixing the design for a quantitative evaluation.

The developer of a vocal emotion-recognition app that highlights which parts of a recording drove each prediction runs remote think-aloud sessions with a dozen users. One participant reads the highlight colour bar as a trace of the speaker's tone of voice, a misreading that no rating of the explanation would have revealed, and the team changes how the highlight is drawn.

A bank's model risk team preparing to give loan officers counterfactual explanations (for example, the income at which a refused application would have been approved) runs think-aloud sessions with five officers on past applications, including some the model got wrong. It learns which suggestions officers would pass on to applicants and which they reject as implausible, and decides whether to filter the suggestions before release.

limitations.description: How participants are asked to talk changes what is observed. A meta-analysis of 94 studies by Fox, Ericsson and Best found that plain thinking aloud left accuracy unchanged, but that asking people to explain or describe their thinking changed performance, and that verbal reports of every kind tended to make tasks take longer. Facilitators must avoid 'why' prompts, and task times from these sessions cannot serve as performance measures.

Talking through a task can make people attend to an explanation more than they would at work. In Buçinca et al.'s think-aloud study, participants' preferences between two explanation types matched the results of a proxy task rather than those of the realistic task, and the authors suggest thinking aloud pushed people into analytical thinking, so these sessions may overstate how closely users read explanations in normal use.

Studies use few participants (between 4 and 14 in the sources for this record), so a finding shows that a problem exists, not how common it is, and cannot support a claim about the share of users who understand an explanation or about decision quality. The sessions also show only the situations their tasks include: tasks need some wrong model outputs if the team wants to see how people use an explanation when the model errs.

Not everything people do with an explanation gets said. Quick, perceptual uses leave little trace: in Zhang and Lim's study, participants called the audio examples intuitive but did not say why they found them simple. People also tend to say what they think the right answer is, the social desirability bias the GOV.UK guidance warns of. Silence about part of an explanation does not mean it went unused or was understood, and a screen recording or gaze data is needed to tell these apart.

Findings depend on the analyst: coding transcripts into themes is interpretive, so a study meant to support an assurance claim needs a stated coding scheme and a second coder. The voice and screen recordings are personal data that need participants' consent and controlled storage, and recordings made on real cases may also hold personal data about the people those cases concern.

sample_claims.text: Each misreading of the deterioration-score explanation found in think-aloud sessions with ward nurses is recorded in the design log with the change made and the result of re-testing it.

The explanation interface for loan officers was tested in think-aloud sessions with intended users, including cases where the model's recommendation was wrong, before the design was fixed for quantitative evaluation.

The misreading of the highlight colour bar as a trace of the speaker's tone, found in the first round of think-aloud sessions, led to a redrawn highlight that was re-tested with new participants before release.

name: Conditional Demographic Disparity
description: Conditional demographic disparity (CDD) measures whether members of a protected group make up a larger share of the people a system turns down than of the people it accepts, after taking into account a factor that differs between groups and that the assessor treats as a legitimate explanation of outcomes; Wachter, Mittelstadt and Russell (2021) propose it as baseline statistical evidence for assessing possible discrimination under EU non-discrimination law. Demographic disparity is the group's share of the unfavourable outcomes minus its share of the favourable ones: in the Berkeley graduate admissions data the paper revisits, women were 46 per cent of rejected applicants but 32 per cent of admitted ones, a disparity of 0.14. CDD computes the same difference separately within each stratum of the conditioning attribute (there, the department applied to) and averages the strata, weighting each by its number of people, so a gap that arises only because groups apply in different proportions to strata with different acceptance rates (an instance of Simpson's paradox) drops out, while a gap within strata remains. Conditioning on department turns the Berkeley figure to about -0.02, a slight disparity in women's favour: within departments, women were on average 40 per cent of rejected and 42 per cent of admitted applicants. The output is the disparity in each stratum and their weighted average, computed on the outcomes recorded in a dataset before training or on a model's decisions after it; the authors present it as a descriptive magnitude to support a contextual judgement, not a pass-or-fail test, and the choice of conditioning attribute is a judgement the measure does not make.

example_use_cases.description: An employer's HR analytics team audits a CV-screening model used across job families. Women make up a larger share of screened-out applicants than of shortlisted ones overall, but apply in greater numbers to the families with the fewest vacancies per applicant, so the team reports CDD conditioned on job family, with each family's own disparity, letting the recruitment board see whether a gap remains within families before it decides whether to keep using the model.

A consumer lender's compliance team computes CDD on its credit model's decisions for applicants of different ethnic origins, recorded for equality monitoring, conditioned first on the loan product applied for and then on income band. It reports both results with the per-stratum figures and a written reason for treating each factor as a legitimate explanation, as the starting point for its assessment of possible indirect discrimination.

A local authority planning to train a model on past housing allocation decisions measures CDD in those decisions, conditioned on assessed band of housing need, before any training. A positive disparity for one ethnic group within need bands, larger than chance would explain, indicates that the labels carry a pattern a model could learn, and the project board uses the finding to decide whether those decisions can serve as training labels at all.

limitations.description: The result depends on which attribute is conditioned on, and the measure cannot tell whether that attribute is a legitimate explanation. If the attribute is itself shaped by discrimination, for instance if one group was deterred from applying to some departments, conditioning on it removes the very disparity a claimant would point to. Wachter et al. leave the choice of factors to courts and context, so each choice needs a recorded justification that a reviewer can contest.

The weighted average can hide large disparities of opposite sign in different strata. In the Berkeley data the per-department disparities run from about -0.09 to +0.05 around a summary of -0.02, and Wachter et al. note that the largest swings come from the department where few women applied, which chance alone could produce. A claim should rest on the per-stratum figures, with their counts, as well as on the summary.

Searching many conditioning attributes or their combinations will find disparities by chance, as the authors warn, and choosing among them after seeing the results can equally make a real one disappear. The authors also offer a descriptive magnitude rather than a statistical test, and set no threshold for how much disparity is too much, so the conditioning attributes need fixing before the data are examined, and a claim that a gap is real needs an interval or test added.

CDD compares shares of outcomes, not rates, so the same gap in acceptance rates gives a smaller value where the group is a small part of a stratum: accepted at 20 per cent against 50 per cent for others, a group scores about 0.33 where it is half the stratum but 0.02 where it is 2 per cent. A fixed threshold therefore tolerates larger rate gaps for smaller groups. Scores and graded outcomes must also first be cut into favourable and unfavourable, and the result changes with the cut.

In the open-source SageMaker Clarify code, a stratum where everyone gets the same outcome is counted rather than skipped: an all-rejected stratum adds a disparity equal to the group's share of it, though no one there was treated differently, so such strata need removing first. AWS has closed Clarify to new customers. The calculation is easy to reimplement, but published applications to deployed AI systems are scarce; the paper's worked example is the 1975 Berkeley admissions study.

sample_claims.text: Conditioned on job family, the CV-screening model's conditional demographic disparity for women in the last hiring round is below 0.02, and no job family with at least 100 applicants shows a disparity above 0.05.

The conditioning factors for the credit model's disparity analysis were fixed, with written reasons, before the decision data were examined, and the disparity in each stratum is reported with its count alongside the weighted summary.

In the historical housing allocation decisions proposed as training labels, each ethnic group's share of refused applicants exceeds its share of successful applicants by no more than 0.03 within any band of assessed housing need, and each group's acceptance rate in each band is reported beside the disparity.

name: Disaggregated Evaluation
description: Disaggregated evaluation assesses and reports a system's performance separately for each group of people a claim covers, and for combinations of groups (intersectional groups, such as darker-skinned women), so that a good overall score cannot hide a group for whom the system works badly. Following Barocas et al. (2021), the evaluator first fixes the design choices that change what the evaluation can show: which groups and combinations to report; how other factors that affect performance, such as lighting or recording conditions, are handled (held constant, varied deliberately, or left as they occur); which metrics to use, for a classifier often false positive and false negative rates reported separately, because each can harm different people; and whether the evaluation is exploratory, or confirmatory, meaning that it tests hypotheses stated in advance on data built to hold enough cases in every group. Each metric is then computed on a labelled evaluation set for every group and combination, together with the number of cases behind it and an interval showing how far the estimate could move through sampling alone, obtained for example by resampling the evaluation set. Groups are compared by absolute and by relative gaps, which can tell different stories: false negative rates of 1 and 10 per cent differ by nine points but tenfold. The output is a table or chart of per-group and per-combination results with their case counts and intervals, and a record of the design choices needed to interpret them; it is this design, more than any one metric or interval method, that decides which comparisons the evaluation can support and how conclusive each is.

example_use_cases.description: Before a hospital trust adopts a supplier's skin-lesion classifier, its clinical safety team reports sensitivity and specificity on locally labelled images for each skin-tone group, sex and age band, and for skin tone crossed with sex. Cells holding fewer melanoma cases than the evaluation protocol requires are marked as too small to estimate rather than reported, and the trust collects more images for them before deciding whether the tool may be used for all patients.

A consumer organisation evaluating the speech-to-text services behind automated phone lines has speakers from several regional and ethnic groups, matched on age and gender, read identical scripted passages, and reports word error rate per group with intervals. Because everyone says the same words, a gap can be attributed to how each service recognises speech rather than to what was said, the evidence the organisation needs for a complaint to the providers.

A bank's model risk team runs a confirmatory evaluation of its fraud model each quarter. The groups (age band, sex and their combinations), the metrics (false positive rate, which drives blocked legitimate payments, and false negative rate), the sample and the largest acceptable gap are fixed in a protocol before the data are drawn, and the model stays in service only if every interval for a gap lies inside that margin.

An exam board piloting an automated essay-scoring model runs an exploratory evaluation of its agreement with human markers, split by first language, school type and their combinations. It finds one weak cell, candidates with English as an additional language at small schools, too small to be conclusive, and commissions a confirmatory study with a sample built to fill that cell before deciding whether the scores can count towards grades.

limitations.description: Each attribute added multiplies the number of cells and shrinks each one, so combinations of attributes soon hold too few cases for a stable estimate, and where a cell holds only a few errors, intervals from resampling come out too narrow. Comparing many cells also throws up some large gaps by chance. A confirmatory claim needs enough cases in every cell, which Barocas et al. note existing datasets rarely provide, so the data available limit which comparisons can be tested.

A gap between groups shows that performance differs, not why. Another factor that affects performance may differ between the groups, as with the time between paired images that NIST suggested could explain a higher false negative rate for Asian people in face recognition. Holding such a factor constant hides gaps at its other values, varying it needs the factor labelled for every case, and strongly correlated factors are hard to separate, or impossible when they always occur together.

The result is only as good as two sets of labels. Where ground-truth outcomes are wrong, or recorded differently for different groups, and the extent of the error cannot be identified, Barocas et al. note the results are meaningless however careful the design. Group membership is often ascribed by an institution or inferred from appearance, adding errors and possible harm to those labelled, and datasets may hold few of some groups (darker-skinned women were 4.4 per cent of one benchmark).

It measures differences in performance and nothing else. Equal error rates say nothing about whether outputs stereotype or demean people, or whether favourable decisions are shared in proportion, and narrowing a gap under one metric can open a gap under another. A clean result supports a claim about the performance gaps measured, for the groups and conditions tested, and no wider fairness claim.

Results on a laboratory dataset may not carry over to the system in use, where lighting, recording conditions and operators' decisions differ, and Barocas et al. note that a component's performance alone may say little about the whole system around it. Evaluating in the setting of use captures this but is costly, and is often impossible for an outside evaluator, who usually sees the system only as a black box.

sample_claims.text: On the trust's locally labelled images, the skin-lesion classifier's sensitivity for each skin-tone group, and for skin tone crossed with sex, is within 5 percentage points of its overall sensitivity, with the 95 per cent interval for each gap and the number of melanoma cases in each cell reported.

The groups, combinations, metrics and acceptable gaps for the fairness evaluation were fixed in a protocol before the evaluation data were drawn, and every cell with too few cases to estimate its gap to the agreed precision is reported as untested rather than as passed.

In each of the last four quarters, the upper bound of the 95 per cent interval for the difference in false positive rate between each age-and-sex group and the best-served group was below the 1 percentage point margin set in the model risk policy.

On identical scripted passages read by speakers matched on age and gender, the upper bound of the 95 per cent interval for each speaker group's gap in word error rate to the best-served group is below the agreed margin.

name: Predictive Parity and Calibration Within Groups
description: This test checks whether a model's output means the same for every group: among people who receive the same score or the same decision, the share who turn out to have the outcome (or its average, for an outcome such as a cost or a count of illnesses) should not depend on their group, a requirement the fairness literature calls sufficiency. For a model that outputs a risk score, cases with known outcomes are grouped into score bins and, for each group, the observed outcome rate in each bin is plotted against the score, giving one calibration curve per group (a score is calibrated when, of the cases scored 0.3, about 30 per cent have the outcome); calibration within groups (Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan) holds when each group's curve matches the scores, and the weaker condition that the curves coincide holds when a given score corresponds to the same outcome rate in every group. For a yes/no decision the same comparison is made in the two cells of the decision: predictive parity (Chouldechova) holds when the positive predictive value, the share of people flagged positive who turn out positive, is equal across groups, and the negative predictive value can be compared in the same way for those not flagged. The two read-outs can disagree, because a score that means the same for every group can still give unequal positive predictive values at a threshold when the groups' scores are spread differently above it, so the test reports the read-out matching the output on which decisions are taken, with intervals and the gaps between groups. Where comparisons of error rates condition on the true outcome and ask whether people who turn out the same are treated the same, this test conditions on the model's output and asks whether people treated the same turn out the same; when the outcome is more common in one group, the two cannot both hold except in special cases.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital's clinical informatics team checks a deterioration-risk score before it is shown to ward staff. On a year of admissions with recorded outcomes it plots a calibration curve, with intervals, for each ethnic group and each sex, and approves the score for use with every patient only if, across the scores that trigger escalation, each group's curve stays within a band agreed with clinicians.

A lender's model validation team compares the repayment rate among approved applicants across age bands, using two years of outcomes, to check whether approval means the same for each band. Because a difference among the approved can come from how scores are spread above the cut-off rather than from a different bar for one band, it also compares the calibration curves of the underlying score before raising any finding with the credit risk committee.

A probation service assessing a supplier's reoffending-risk tool is shown evidence that its positive predictive value is equal across ethnic groups. Its analysts reproduce the figures on local data and set them beside the groups' false positive and false negative rates, which differ because reconviction rates differ, so that the oversight board chooses which criterion the tool will be held to with both sets of figures in front of it.

A health insurer auditing a score that selects members for a care-management programme checks twice whether the score means the same for every racial group: against next year's costs, the label the model was trained on, and against a measure of illness such as the number of active chronic conditions. A score calibrated for cost but not for illness, with one group sicker than another at the same score, would lead the insurer to retrain on a different label.

limitations.description: When the outcome is more common in one group, a score or decision that satisfies predictive parity cannot also give the groups both equal false positive and equal false negative rates, and calibration within groups cannot coexist with equal average scores for each group's positives and negatives except with perfect prediction or equal base rates (Chouldechova; Kleinberg et al.). Passing this test therefore means accepting unequal error rates, a choice the test informs but cannot make.

Passing says little about how accurately the model predicts for each group. A well-fitted model usually comes close to calibration within groups without any fairness intervention when group membership can be inferred from its inputs, and a model that predicts accurately for one group while giving everyone in another group that group's average rate is still perfectly calibrated (Barocas, Hardt and Narayanan). The result needs pairing with performance measured for each group.

The test uses recorded outcomes, so it inherits any difference between groups in how the outcome is recorded. Rearrest stands in for reoffending, and a care-management score was calibrated by race for health costs while, at the 97th percentile of the score, Black patients had 26 per cent more chronic illnesses than white patients (Obermeyer et al.). A model can pass while scoring one group's need too low, so the outcome tested must be the one the claim is about.

A gap in positive predictive value is not by itself evidence that the score treats groups differently: the value averages over everyone above the threshold, so it depends on how each group's scores are spread there and moves when the threshold moves. Chouldechova notes that well-calibrated scores can fail predictive parity, and the converse also holds. Where scores are available the calibration curves should be reported, and the threshold stated.

Per-group calibration curves need labelled cases across the score range in every group; in a small group the high-score bins may hold a handful of people, so their rates swing widely, and the choice of bin widths changes the picture. An outside auditor who sees only decisions, not scores, can test predictive parity but not calibration, so access determines which claim the evidence can support.

sample_claims.text: Across the deterioration-risk scores that trigger escalation, each ethnic group's observed deterioration rate lies within 3 percentage points of the rate for all patients with the same score, with the 95 per cent interval for each gap inside that band, on twelve months of admissions held out from model development.

Among applicants approved by the credit model in the evaluation period, the repayment rate for each age band is within 2 percentage points of the rate for all approved applicants, and the calibration curves of the underlying score for each band are reported alongside.

At the deployed threshold, the reoffending-risk tool's positive predictive value differs between ethnic groups by less than 5 percentage points on local data, and the corresponding differences in false positive and false negative rates are reported with it.

At each decile of the care-management score, the mean number of active chronic conditions differs between racial groups by less than the tolerance agreed with the clinical lead, so the score indicates the same level of illness in every group, not only the same expected cost.

name: Bias Benchmark for Question Answering
description: The Bias Benchmark for Question Answering (BBQ) is a fixed set of about 58,500 multiple-choice reading questions that tests whether a language model's answers rely on social stereotypes, across nine social dimensions (age, disability status, gender identity, nationality, physical appearance, race and ethnicity, religion, socio-economic status and sexual orientation) and two combinations of them, using stereotypes documented as harmful in US English-speaking contexts (Parrish et al., 2022). Each item describes two people from different groups and asks a question that points at a stereotype, such as who is bad at maths, with three answers to choose from: either person, or an answer such as 'cannot be determined'; in the ambiguous version the passage does not say which person the question is about, so 'cannot be determined' is correct, and in the disambiguated version an added sentence settles it. Items come in balanced sets that swap the two groups and their order and pair each negative question with a non-negative one, so that a model which simply prefers one group whatever the question is not counted as stereotyping. From the model's chosen answers (generated, or picked by comparing the probabilities it gives the three options) the test reports accuracy in each version and a bias score per category from -100% to 100%: the share of answers naming a person that follow the stereotype, rescaled so that 0 means no consistent direction and a negative score leans against the stereotype, and in the ambiguous version multiplied by the error rate, so that stereotyped guesses weigh more when the model guesses often; it also reports how far accuracy falls when the correct answer goes against the stereotype. Unlike substituting identity terms into a deployer's own inputs, or varying the people shown in few-shot examples, BBQ is a fixed external question set that tests what a model concludes about people when the text does, and does not, support a conclusion.

example_use_cases.description: A government department choosing between three language models for a service that answers citizens' questions about benefits runs the full BBQ set on each, with the same prompt, answer extraction and scoring for all three. It compares accuracy and both bias scores category by category, rules out any model whose ambiguous-context bias score in any category is further from zero, in either direction, than a limit set before testing, and records that the result covers US stereotypes only.

A recruitment software company fine-tuning an open-weight model to answer HR helpdesk questions runs BBQ on the base model and on every fine-tuned version through the same evaluation harness, logging each answer. A release is blocked if any category's ambiguous-context bias score moves further from zero than the base model's by more than an agreed margin, or if the accuracy gap between items whose correct answer matches the stereotype and items whose correct answer goes against it widens.

An NHS trust's digital team preparing a health-information assistant needs evidence about UK stereotypes, which BBQ was not built for. Following the procedure used to build a Korean version, it keeps templates that transfer, changes target groups where UK stereotypes differ, drops those that do not apply, writes UK-specific ones, surveys members of the UK public to confirm each stereotype and its target group, and reports results on the original and adapted sets side by side.

limitations.description: BBQ's stereotypes, and most of its categories, come from US English-speaking contexts, and its authors say results should not be used as evidence about other cultures. Adapting it to Korean meant changing target groups, dropping templates and adding four categories, and a machine-translated BBQ gave different bias scores from the adapted version (Jin et al., 2024). For a UK deployment the original set says nothing about UK-specific stereotypes.

A low bias score is weak evidence that a model is unbiased. Each category rests on about 25 templates with very short passages and three fixed answers; the authors warn that a low score is not proof of an unbiased model, and that for a model used on very different text BBQ is unlikely to be a valid measure. It counts only stereotypes that change the chosen answer, so it misses bias that shifts the model's probabilities without changing its choice.

The bias score leaves out 'cannot be determined' answers and has a sign, so it must be read with accuracy and by its distance from zero. A model that always gives that answer has full accuracy and a zero bias score on ambiguous items, yet fails every disambiguated one. A negative score means answers lean against the stereotype, as HELM found for most of the models it tested (Liang et al., 2023); a one-sided limit such as 'below 5%' passes such a model.

Scores depend on the prompt format and on how answers are extracted or scored, so they compare only across models tested the same way. In the original study one UnifiedQA model, given the same items in two input formats, scored 2.4 and 18.6 on ambiguous gender-identity items. Results for a single template rest on few items (one reported example has 72), so they are noisy and should be combined across templates for the same stereotype.

It is weak evidence about bias against people with two combined identities. In the original study, results on the two intersectional categories (race by gender, race by socio-economic status) were too inconsistent for the authors to conclude that models responded to more than one aspect of identity, and the lm-evaluation-harness task notes that these categories are not really taken into account in its bias scores.

sample_claims.text: Under the department's fixed prompt and scoring, the selected model's ambiguous-context BBQ bias score was between -5% and +5% in each of the nine categories, and its accuracy on disambiguated items differed by less than 2 percentage points between items whose correct answer matched the stereotype and items whose correct answer did not.

No fine-tuned release of the HR helpdesk model has an ambiguous-context BBQ bias score more than 2 percentage points further from zero than the base model's in any category, measured with the same harness version, prompt and scoring.

On a UK-adapted version of BBQ, whose stereotypes and target groups were confirmed by a survey of the UK public before use, the health-information assistant's ambiguous-context bias score was between -5% and +5% in every category and its accuracy on disambiguated items was above 90%.

name: Rich Subgroup Fairness Auditing
description: Rich subgroup fairness auditing checks whether a binary classifier treats any subgroup much better or much worse than the population as a whole, where the subgroups are not a short list chosen in advance but every group that rules of a chosen kind over several protected attributes can describe, such as everyone for whom a weighted sum of age, sex and ethnicity indicators exceeds a threshold. Kearns, Neel, Roth and Wu (2018) proposed it to detect what they call fairness gerrymandering: a classifier can have equal false positive rates for men and for women, and for each ethnic group, yet very unequal rates for particular combinations, such as women of one ethnicity. For a chosen rate (the false positive or false negative rate, or in the paper also the rate of positive decisions), each subgroup is scored by the gap between its rate and the overall rate multiplied by the share of all records that are in the subgroup and count towards that rate (for the false positive rate, those with a negative true outcome), so a gap counts for more the larger the group, and the audit searches for the subgroup with the highest score. Exact search is computationally hard in the worst case, so it is posed as a weighted (cost-sensitive) classification problem over the protected attributes and solved approximately: the reference implementation fits two linear regressions that propose a candidate worst subgroup as a linear threshold rule, using only those attributes, the true outcomes and the classifier's decisions, not the model itself. The output is that rule with the subgroup's size, rate and weighted gap (called gamma), compared with a limit set beforehand; unlike reporting metrics for groups listed in advance, the audit finds subgroups nobody listed, and unlike multiaccuracy boosting, which checks a score's average error in each subgroup and then corrects the model, it compares a decision rate with the overall rate and changes nothing.

example_use_cases.description: A lender's model risk team validating a credit-risk model before release audits its decisions on a held-out sample of past applicants whose repayment is known, and records that these are only applicants the old policy approved. It searches subgroups over age, sex, ethnicity and disability status for the worst false positive rate gap (good payers flagged as high risk), compares it with a limit agreed with the risk committee, and sends the rule for any subgroup over it to the developers.

A hospital's clinical AI team has confirmed that a sepsis early-warning model misses cases at similar rates for men and women and for each recorded ethnic group. Before rollout it audits the false negative rate over subgroups combining age, sex and ethnicity and, because the search is approximate, also scores a grid of rules over two of the attributes by brute force, as the method's authors did, to check the search did not miss a larger gap.

A local authority's internal audit team re-audits a model that flags housing benefit claims for fraud review each quarter, using a random sample of claims reviewed whether or not they were flagged. It records the worst subgroup by false positive rate (legitimate claims flagged) over age, sex, ethnicity and disability, with its size and gap, and escalates to the system owner when the weighted gap exceeds the agreed limit.

limitations.description: Finding the worst subgroup exactly is hard in the worst case, even for conjunctions or linear thresholds of attributes (Kearns et al. 2018, Theorem 3.3), so practical audits use a heuristic search. A subgroup it reports does have the measured gap on the audit data, but a clean result is only a lower bound: the authors note their auditor could miss a larger disparity and checked it by brute force on two attributes (Kearns et al. 2019). 'Nothing found' is a search result, not a proof.

Gaps are weighted by subgroup size, which the authors require for reliable estimates and which lets small groups pass with large gaps: a subgroup holding 2% of the records whose false positive rate is 20 percentage points above the overall rate scores at most 0.004, under the 0.005 limit used in the AIF360 demonstration. The audit cannot support a claim about a small named group; report that group's own rate, with an interval, instead.

Only subgroups that the rule class can describe, over the attributes designated as protected, are searched; the reference implementation uses linear threshold rules. The class has to be limited because, as the authors note, any imperfect classifier could be accused of unfairness to the set of people it misclassifies. A protected attribute that is not recorded or not designated is invisible, so the attributes used and their encoding must be stated with the finding.

Error-rate audits need the protected attributes and the true outcome for every audited record, which a deployed system may not supply, for example when outcomes are seen only for approved applications. Reliable estimates need more data the richer the subgroup class, the authors' experiments report in-sample results, and the tools give no confidence interval, so audit on held-out data and repeat on fresh data before relying on a worst-case figure.

It tests parity of one rate at a time for binary decisions, each subgroup's rate against the overall rate. A pass on false positives says nothing about false negatives, the AIF360 auditor implements only those two error rates, and other criteria, such as whether scores mean the same in every subgroup (calibration), need a different test. The rate must be chosen to match the fairness claim before the audit.

sample_claims.text: On a held-out sample of 40,000 previously approved applicants with known repayment, the rich subgroup audit over age, sex, ethnicity and disability status found no subgroup whose size-weighted false positive rate gap exceeded the 0.005 limit agreed with the risk committee.

Before rollout, neither the heuristic audit over age, sex and ethnicity nor a brute-force grid over age and ethnicity found a subgroup whose size-weighted gap in the rate of missed sepsis cases exceeded 0.003.

In each of the last four quarterly re-audits, on a random sample of claims reviewed whether or not they were flagged, the worst subgroup found had a size-weighted false positive rate gap below the agreed limit, and its description and size were recorded.

name: Actionable Recourse Audit
description: An actionable recourse audit checks whether the people a linear classifier refuses, for example for a loan, a job interview or a public service, could change that decision through actions open to them, and how much they would have to change. The auditor first writes an action set saying which features can change and how: immutable features such as age stay fixed, features such as education level can only rise, and each changeable feature gets bounds and a grid of realistic values. Then, for each refused person in a sample drawn from the population the model will serve, an integer programming solver (optimisation software that searches discrete choices exactly) looks through the permitted actions for the cheapest change that flips the decision, measuring cost as the largest shift, in population percentiles, that the change makes to any one feature, and either returns that action or proves that none exists, which a search that simply fails to find a counterfactual cannot do. The audit reports the share of refused people who have recourse and the distribution of its cost, which can be compared across candidate models or broken down by group, and the same solver can list a refused person's cheapest alternative changes (a 'flipset') for a decision notice. Unlike the Contrastive Explanation Method, which explains one prediction through features that must be present or absent, or Diverse Counterfactual Explanations (DiCE), which searches any model for several alternative inputs that would change one decision, the audit works only on linear models but certifies whether any permitted action exists and summarises the answer across a population.

example_use_cases.description: Before launching a linear model that ranks applications to a housing support scheme, a local authority's analytics team audits recourse on last year's applicants, with age and household size fixed. Its report to the scheme's oversight board gives the share of refused applicants who could qualify through changes the scheme expects, such as completing a tenancy course, and how large those changes are, so the board can decide whether to approve the model.

A credit card issuer generates a flipset for each applicant its linear scorecard declines and puts the two cheapest items in the decline letter, for example reducing current debt to a stated amount, together with the other scored features the applicant should keep unchanged, so that following the stated actions would change the decision under the current model.

A lender's model risk committee is shown recourse audits for candidate credit models of almost equal accuracy. It rejects the most accurate, under which some refused applicants had no feasible action because of an 'ever defaulted' feature, adopts a variant that uses recent defaults only, and has the audit re-run each quarter on new applicants, watching younger applicants, who were scarce in the training data.

An employer's analytics team audits its linear screening model for interview invitations and compares the cost of recourse for refused women and men with similar predicted scores. Sex is not a model input, but the cost can still differ by sex. Refused candidates' true suitability is never observed, so the team cannot also match on outcome as the originating study did, and reports any gap with that caveat to its fairness review panel, which decides whether the features need revising.

limitations.description: The proof that no action exists depends on the model being linear, such as logistic regression, a linear support vector machine or a rule set that can be written in linear form. For tree ensembles or neural networks, a local linear approximation can still suggest actions, which then have to be checked on the real model, but a failure to find one proves nothing, so the share of refused people without recourse is no longer a certified figure.

Every conclusion rests on the action set and cost the auditor chooses. Bounds that are too tight make people appear to lack recourse; loose bounds let a model 'provide' recourse only through drastic changes, which shows only as high cost; and the default cost treats a one-percentile change as equally hard in every feature unless someone who knows the domain sets how much harder some changes are.

The search treats features as changing independently unless the auditor adds constraints. Real actions have knock-on effects: raising income can also raise savings, so a listed action may cost more than needed, or may not change the decision once its effects on other features are counted, as Karimi, Schölkopf and Valera showed for recourse methods that ignore causal relations between features.

Recourse is defined for a fixed model. After retraining, an action given in an earlier notice may no longer change the decision, so the audit has to be re-run after each update. An action that changes the prediction need not change the real outcome either: showing a refused applicant how to be approved can lead them into credit they cannot repay.

A flipset lists only the features to change, so a person who also changes an undisclosed feature may still be refused unless the notice says what must stay the same. The originating paper builds flipsets from public credit datasets and does not test whether refused people understand them or can act on them. Owners may also resist publishing flipsets, because many of them together can let others reconstruct the model.

sample_claims.text: Every refused applicant in the audit sample, drawn from last year's applications to the scheme, has at least one action under the agreed action set that would make them eligible under the deployed model.

Under the agreed action set, at least half of the declined applicants in the audit sample have an action that would bring approval while moving no feature by more than 25 percentiles of the applicant population.
Among candidates refused by the screening model with similar predicted scores, the median cost of recourse for women is within five percentile points of that for men.
Each decline letter lists at least one action that would change the decision under the current scorecard, together with the scored features the applicant must keep unchanged.

name: AI FactSheets
description: AI FactSheets is a documentation practice in which the developer or supplier of an AI model or service answers a structured set of questions about it, modelled on the supplier's declarations of conformity that industries such as telecommunications and transport use to give written assurance, with evidence, that a product meets stated requirements. The questions cover the service's purpose and its intended and unsuitable uses, the datasets it was trained and tested on, its test methods and results (reported for groups such as age bands or genders where relevant), checks for bias, explainability, behaviour on data unlike its training data and robustness to adversarial attack, how user data is secured, and its lineage, such as when and how its models were retrained; 'N/A' and 'Proprietary' are allowed answers. Facts are gathered from the people in each role across the lifecycle (business owner, data scientist, model validator and operations engineer), and any change to the service produces a new version of the FactSheet while earlier versions are kept. The originating group's seven-step method designs the template with its readers: interview the people who will read the facts and those who will produce them, draft and trial a template of questions, have the real producers complete it, evaluate the result with its readers for content and presentation, and build further templates for other audiences such as a review board or regulator. Unlike a model card, which reports one model's intended use and evaluation to the people choosing it, or a datasheet, which describes one dataset, a FactSheet may cover one model or a whole service built from several models and datasets (attaching their datasheets), gathers facts from each role in the lifecycle and has a different template for each audience; unlike a CycloneDX ML-BOM it is written for people to read rather than as a machine-readable parts list for software tools.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital trust buying a speech-to-text service for clinical dictation sends bidders a FactSheet template asking for intended and unsuitable uses, training data, retraining frequency, behaviour on noisy audio, and word error rates by speaker accent and age band on recordings the trust supplies. The panel compares the answers to shortlist bidders, re-tests the shortlisted services on its own recordings, and writes the confirmed error rates into the contract as service levels.

A bank's model risk team follows the seven-step method to design a FactSheet template for credit models: it interviews validators about the decisions they make and data scientists about the facts they can record, then has the scientists complete it for a new affordability model. Validators read the completed FactSheet's training data, performance, bias checks and known weak cases before deciding whether to approve the model for deployment.

A company selling a sentiment-analysis API publishes a short FactSheet for developers browsing its catalogue, giving the purpose, input and output formats, training data, accuracy and the kinds of text the service handles poorly. From the same facts it generates a longer FactSheet, with a different template, for enterprise customers' risk and compliance reviewers.

A city council's AI ethics review board asks each supplier for a FactSheet in a template written for the board, covering training and test data distributions, data handling, the inputs the service handles poorly and possible sources of unfair outcomes. The board reads them before deciding whether a photo-based street-repair reporting service may go live.

limitations.description: A FactSheet is the supplier's own declaration. As with the declarations of conformity it imitates, the supplier runs the tests it reports and nothing in the format checks them, so it shows what was claimed rather than that the claims hold. A buyer who relies on a declared figure has to re-test the service or ask for third-party testing, which the original proposal expects only for the highest-stakes, regulated, enterprise and public-sector applications.

Facts not recorded while the service is built are hard to recover. In IBM's own trials, developers forgot how they had transformed training data or which settings they had tried, and recovering the training-data transformations for one FactSheet took several hours over two days although the dataset was small and its author was available. A FactSheet written after development is likely to have gaps or errors unless fact collection is part of the development process.

The format accepts 'N/A' and 'Proprietary' as answers. In IBM's trials most developers assumed bias would not be an issue and marked bias questions not applicable, even where further questioning showed it could be, and participants were unsure how much detail they could give without losing competitive advantage. An unchallenged 'N/A' can hide a risk nobody examined, and items withheld as proprietary are often the ones a buyer would need in order to check the self-declared results.

There is no single FactSheet. Its authors hold that one template cannot serve every audience and domain, and developers report the metrics conventional for their kind of model, so FactSheets from different suppliers often cannot be compared unless the buyer fixes the questions, metrics and test conditions in its own template.

Whether readers understand FactSheets and decide better with them is untested. Producers in IBM's studies found it hard to know what readers needed and often left out what a less expert reader would need. The design method checks a draft with a few intended readers, and the group's later case studies report that producers could follow it, but none of these sources tests whether buyers, validators or review boards read FactSheets correctly or make better decisions with them.

sample_claims.text: The supplier's FactSheet for the dictation service states its intended and unsuitable uses, the datasets it was tested on, and its word error rate on each, reported separately by speaker accent and age band.

Each production version of the affordability model has a FactSheet to which its data scientist and validator contributed before deployment and its operations engineer after, and the FactSheets of earlier versions are retained unchanged.
Every FactSheet item a supplier answered 'N/A' or 'Proprietary' carries a stated reason, and the review board accepted each reason before approving the service.
The FactSheet template used to assess suppliers was evaluated with the procurement and risk assessors who read it before first use, and the items they found missing or unclear were revised.

name: UK Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard Record
description: An Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (ATRS) record is a public account that a UK public sector organisation writes about one algorithmic tool it uses, on the UK government's standard template, and publishes in a central repository on GOV.UK. The template has two tiers: a short plain-language summary for the general public (what the tool is, why it is used and a contact), and eight further sheets for specialist readers such as journalists, researchers and civil society, covering who is accountable for the tool and which suppliers were involved, how it works and what it replaced, how its output feeds into decisions, when a person reviews that output, how members of the public can appeal, the system's and each model's inputs, outputs, architecture and performance (including any bias testing), the data used, and the impact assessments, risks and mitigations. Information that would be exempt under the Freedom of Information Act can be left out or summarised field by field, with the reason stated, and the record is cleared by the tool's team, its senior responsible owner (the role accountable for the tool) and the press office, checked for readability by the central ATRS team, and updated when the tool changes substantially or is retired. Publishing is mandatory for central government departments and for arm's-length bodies that deliver public or frontline services or deal directly with the public, for tools in beta, pilot or production that significantly influence decisions affecting the public or interact with it directly; other public bodies may publish voluntarily. Unlike a model card, written by a developer for people choosing a model, or a supplier's AI FactSheet for buyers, an ATRS record is written by the deploying public body for the public and describes the decision process, human review and appeal routes around the tool as well as the tool.

example_use_cases.description: A government department piloting a machine-learning model that prioritises benefit claims for caseworker checks publishes an ATRS record before the pilot starts. It tells claimants, journalists and MPs that the score only orders the caseworkers' queue and a caseworker makes every decision, how claimants can ask for a review, what kinds of data the model uses and what bias testing was done.

A district council piloting a supplier's tool that ranks rent-arrears cases for housing officers publishes a voluntary ATRS record. Because the record needs the model type, a description of the training data and performance figures, the council's procurement team writes their supply into the contract, and the record names the supplier, its role and the terms of its access to tenants' data.

A police force using a domestic-abuse risk assessment tool publishes a voluntary record in which the fields that would show how to evade the tool are marked exempt, with the reason, while the summary, the officers' review of each score, the appeal route and the risk mitigations are published in full for oversight bodies and community groups to examine.

A department launching a chatbot that answers questions about a public service publishes a record because the tool interacts directly with the public. The record states that answers come from a named provider's large language model used as supplied, how answers are checked, how often conversations are reviewed and how a user reaches a human adviser.

limitations.description: A record is the deploying body's own account. The central ATRS team checks drafts for readability, not accuracy, and nothing in the standard tests the stated performance, bias testing or human review against the tool's behaviour. A record is also only as current as its last update, which depends on the body resubmitting after a substantial change, so it shows what was disclosed and when, not that the tool works as described.

The mandatory scope is narrow: central government departments and qualifying arm's-length bodies, and only tools that significantly influence decisions with public effect or interact directly with the public, from the beta or pilot stage on. Local authorities, police forces and other bodies outside central government publish voluntarily, and analytical models that inform policy are usually out of scope, so the absence of a record does not show that no tool is in use.

Fields can be withheld or summarised under Freedom of Information exemptions, including commercial interests, and no record is published where even the tool's existence cannot be confirmed. Police and commercial interviewees in a 2022 study expected suppliers to resist disclosing proprietary details, so the technical tier of a record for a procured tool can be thin unless the contract requires the supplier to provide the information.

For an off-the-shelf model that the organisation has not trained, tested or refined, such as a large language model used through its web interface, the guidance says to leave the model and development data sections blank. Records for such tools say nothing about the model's training data or evaluation, which is often what a reader most needs in order to judge them.

Whether the public can find, understand and use records has not been tested. Records sit in a repository on GOV.UK rather than reaching people when a decision affects them, although the 2021 public engagement study behind the two-tier design found people wanted active notice for higher-impact uses. Police interviewees in a 2022 study feared records would give more detail than the public needs and accuracy figures without context; its authors called for evaluation with impacted communities.

sample_claims.text: An ATRS record for the claim-prioritisation model was published on GOV.UK before the pilot began, stating the model's role in decisions, when a caseworker reviews its output and how claimants can ask for a review.
Every algorithmic tool in the department's inventory that falls within the ATRS mandatory scope and is in beta, pilot or production has a published ATRS record.

Each field withheld from the published record is marked exempt with its reason, and each exemption was cleared by the tool's senior responsible owner, under the ATRS scope and exemptions policy, before publication.
The published ATRS record was updated within one month of the model being retrained on new data or its role in the decision process changing.

name: C2PA Content Credentials
description: C2PA Content Credentials attach a signed provenance record, called a manifest, to a media file, so that whoever receives the file can see who signed it and what the signer declares (which tool produced it, whether a generative AI model created or altered it and what edits followed), and can check that the record, and the parts of the file its hash covers, have not changed since signing. Under the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) technical specification, the tool that creates or edits the file writes statements called assertions, such as a 'created' action whose source type is trainedAlgorithmicMedia (the code for AI-generated content) and links to the earlier files it was made from, adds a cryptographic hash of the file's content, and signs the bundle with an X.509 certificate, the kind of credential used to secure websites. The manifest is usually embedded in the file, and each later edit in a supporting tool adds a new manifest that refers to the previous one, so the history travels with the file. A validator recomputes the hash and checks the signature, then reports the manifest as well-formed, valid or, if the signing certificate chains to a trust list such as the C2PA Trust List, trusted, and reports a failure when the file no longer matches its hash. If the manifest is removed, nothing in the file leads back to it unless a watermark or fingerprint (a 'soft binding') was also registered so that the manifest can be looked up in a repository, and a file without credentials says nothing about its origin; unlike trigger-set model watermarking or model signing, which mark or sign a model, it records the history of an individual output.

example_use_cases.description: An image-generation service offered in the EU attaches a signed manifest to every image it returns, declaring an AI 'created' action with the service as signer, as its means of meeting the AI Act's Article 50(2) duty to mark synthetic output in a machine-readable format. Its compliance team validates a weekly sample of outputs to decide whether marking is working, and registers a watermark soft binding so that a stripped image can be matched back to its record.

A news agency's verification desk runs every image sent in by the public through a C2PA validator before publication. A trusted manifest recording capture on a named camera, with no AI-generated ingredients, lets editors publish it with a provenance label. A manifest naming a generative tool, or a hash that no longer matches, sends it to forensic review, and an image with no credentials is treated as of unknown origin, not as authentic.

An insurer's claims app lets assessors apply an AI tool that enhances and annotates photographs of vehicle damage, and records each AI edit as an action in the photograph's manifest. When a claim is disputed, a reviewing assessor or the claimant's representative can see which changes the AI tool made and check them against the retained original, which the edited photograph's manifest cites as an ingredient.

A social-media platform reads Content Credentials on upload, labels images whose trusted manifest declares a generative AI source, and shows users who signed the record. Its trust-and-safety team tracks what share of uploads carry trusted, untrusted or no credentials, to decide how far its synthetic-media policy can rely on the labels and where it still needs other detection methods.

limitations.description: The record is easy to lose. Anyone can remove the manifest, an attack the C2PA's own threat model expects, and the file is then an ordinary file with no link to its history unless a watermark or fingerprint soft binding was registered with a manifest repository. Because credentials are optional and removable, a file without them says nothing about its origin: the absence of a manifest cannot show that content is human-made or unaltered.

A valid manifest shows who signed the record and that what its hash covers is unchanged, not that its statements are true. A signer can omit an AI step, a stolen key yields manifests that validate, and a camera photographing a screen signs a genuine capture of a staged scene. Validators need not check revocation, metadata such as location may sit outside the hash, and a 2026 preprint found validators disagreeing on the same file, so a result depends on the signer, validator and trust list.

The history is complete only while every tool in the workflow supports C2PA. An edit made in an unsupported tool is not recorded, and if the file later passes through a supporting tool, the new signer implicitly vouches for that unrecorded change, so the chain can show fewer steps than took place. The C2PA itself says the approach depends on widespread adoption by tools and platforms.

Manifests can disclose more than the creator intends, such as capture time and place, device details, the edit history and, through the separate Creator Assertions Working Group identity extension, who made the content. The C2PA's threat model lists identifying creators and tracking viewers as risks. Assertions can be redacted when a file is reused as an ingredient, but people working in risky settings, such as human-rights documentation, must decide what to include before signing.

Support for AI-generated text is immature. Embedding a manifest in plain text, as invisible Unicode characters, entered the specification in version 2.3 and is still marked as under review; the reference SDK supports it only behind an unstable option, and any edit to the text breaks the hash. For language-model output the method is much less dependable than for images, video and audio, where embedding is established.

sample_claims.text: Every image in each weekly validation sample of the generation service's output carried a C2PA manifest, signed with a certificate that chains to the C2PA Trust List, that declares the image AI-generated.
In the provider's stripping and re-encoding tests, generated images whose embedded manifest had been removed were matched to their original manifest through the registered watermark soft binding.
Every reader-submitted image published with a provenance label had a trusted manifest whose hash matched the published file.
Each AI edit applied to a claims photograph is recorded as an action in the photograph's signed manifest, naming the tool that made it.

name: Zero-Knowledge Proof of Model Inference
description: A zero-knowledge proof of model inference lets the owner of a model show an outside party that one specific model, fixed in advance, turns a particular input into a particular output, without revealing the model's weights. The owner publishes a commitment to the weights, a short cryptographic fingerprint such as a hash that binds them without disclosing them, together with a verification key that fixes the model's architecture. The model's arithmetic is converted to whole numbers (quantised) and written as a system of equations called a circuit, and for each input a proving system produces a proof, of a few kilobytes to a few hundred kilobytes, that this circuit, run with weights matching the commitment, turns that input into that output; the input can be public or committed in the same way. Anyone holding the verification key can check the proof in milliseconds to seconds: it shows that the committed model gives that output for that input, while keeping the weights hidden, and says nothing about whether that model is accurate, fair or safe. Unlike homomorphic encryption, which lets a server compute on data it cannot read but gives the caller no evidence of which computation was run, and unlike model signing, which lets someone who holds a model's files check who released them, it lets someone who never sees the weights check individual outputs against them.

example_use_cases.description: A credit-scoring vendor publishes the weight commitment in the report of an independent bias and accuracy audit, which was run on the quantised model bound to that commitment. When a refused applicant complains, the lender's complaints team asks the vendor for a proof for that decision and checks it against the published commitment, to confirm that the audited model gives the same refusal on the applicant's data before it reviews the decision itself.

A hospital trust buying chest X-ray triage results from a cloud provider writes into the contract that its clinical engineering team may challenge a random sample of each month's results. For each sampled case the provider must return a proof against the commitment to the model the trust validated, and the team treats a failed or missing proof as evidence that a different model was served, which triggers the contract's audit clause.

An online-safety regulator inspecting the age-estimation service a platform relies on submits its own test images and asks for a proof with each estimate. Its inspectors check each proof against the commitment registered when an accredited laboratory certified the vendor's model, to decide whether the service in use is the certified model, without the vendor handing its proprietary weights to the regulator.

limitations.description: A valid proof shows that the committed weights turn this input into this output. It does not show that the model is accurate, fair or safe, that the input was genuine, or that the service ran the committed model: a different model giving the same output passes too, so spot checks catch a substituted model only on inputs where the two disagree. A commitment carries assurance only if an audit was run on the model it binds.

Proving costs far more than running the model. Published figures: 88 seconds per prediction of a 15-million-parameter VGG16 on CIFAR-10 images (zkCNN), about 41 minutes for an ImageNet-scale MobileNet on a large cloud server (Kang et al.), and about 13 minutes for one 2,048-token pass of a 13-billion-parameter language model on a data-centre GPU, after a one-off 16-minute commitment (zkLLM). Proving every output of a busy service is impractical, so protocols prove sampled or disputed outputs.

The proof covers a quantised, whole-number version of the model, not the floating-point model that was trained and perhaps audited, and the two can give slightly different outputs. Published attacks plant backdoors that stay dormant at full precision and activate only after quantisation, which EZKL's security notes flag. Audits and accuracy tests must therefore be run on the quantised model that is actually proved, or the commitment and the audit describe different models.

The guarantee depends on configuration. If the weights are private inputs with no published commitment, a proof shows only that some weights for the stated architecture give the output. Hashing the weights inside the proof keeps them hidden but costs about as much again as proving the inference. EZKL's cheaper settings, including its Python default, bind the weights without fully hiding them, and its notes warn they can be recovered from enough proofs. The architecture is normally disclosed.

Soundness rests on the software as well as the mathematics. A compiler error that leaves the equations under-constrained can let a false proof verify, a risk EZKL's documentation names, and EZKL's proofs rely on public parameters from a multi-party set-up ceremony. Audits cover specific releases (EZKL's covered version 21), so verifiers should fix which tool versions and parameters they accept. EZKL, the most used tool, has had no open-source licence since January 2024.

sample_claims.text: Every credit decision referred to the complaints process was accompanied by a proof, checked by the complaints team, that the model whose weight commitment appears in the independent audit report gives that decision on the applicant's data.
The accuracy and bias figures in the audit report were computed from outputs proven against the same weight commitment that is used in production.
Every triage result sampled for challenge in the reporting period was supported by a proof that verified against the commitment to the validated model.
For every test image submitted by the regulator's inspectors, the age-estimation service returned a proof that verified against the certified model's commitment.
